title: Targeting the provirus in HIV-1 latently infected cells with a cell-activation-inducible CRISPR-Cas9 system: An in vitro proof of concept.
authors: Magro, Gloria; Tarabella, Carolina; Garzino-Demo, Alfredo; Trevisan, Marta; Palu, Giorgio; Poletti, Valentina; Galizi, Roberto; Calistri, Arianna; Parolin, Cristina
abstract: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) persists as an integrated provirus in the host cells in a latent state and can reactivate if antiretroviral therapy is interrupted, posing obstacles to an HIV cure. Gene editing technologies can be used to target the provirus. However, several challenges need to be fully addressed, including limiting the nuclease activity to latently infected cells and the possible off-target effects. Here, we provide an in vitro proof-of-principle study to assess the feasibility of a CRISPR/Cas9-based-cell-specific inducible system for the functional inactivation of HIV-1 in latently infected cells. We designed a lentiviral vector expressing the Cas9 nuclease under the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT)-inducible promoter, along with an array of guide RNAs targeting HIV-1-specific genes (gag and tat/rev) and the host chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5), required for viral entry. We demonstrated in different cellular models the inducible expression of the nuclease upon cellular activation and its efficacy in disrupting viral genome and replication. Our findings show the possibility to link Cas9 expression to cellular activation in latently infected cells to reduce the drawbacks of its continuous activity, toward a gene-editing strategy to conditionally inactivate the provirus.

title: Gene-activated matrices as nanomedicine platforms for bone regeneration: Delivery, translation and patent landscape.
authors: Abdelnabi, Hiba; Alkaabi, Salem Mohammed; Alderei, Khaled Saeed; Alaryani, Ahmad Sultan; Mohsin, Sahar
abstract: Protein biologics are constrained in critical-size bone defects not by insufficient potency, but by rapid clearance and the inability to sustain therapeutic signaling at the repair site. Dose escalation does not overcome this pharmacokinetic limitation and instead increases the risk of ectopic bone formation, osteolysis, and soft tissue toxicity. Sustained, localized delivery, not higher dosing, is the unmet requirement. Gene-activated matrices (GAM) address this problem by integrating nucleic acid cargo and delivery vectors within an implantable scaffold, converting infiltrating host cells into local sources of regenerative signals. This review examines GAMs as nanomedicine platforms for bone regeneration, tracing their development from scaffold bioactivity and the limitation of protein biologics to nucleic acid-based delivery. We compare viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, polymeric polyplexes, calcium phosphate nanoparticles, and scaffold-integrated systems across transduction efficiency, expression kinetics, immunogenicity, and bone-site retention. We then examine how scaffold composition, architecture, and fabrication govern vector retention, release, and substrate-mediated transfection. This review then evaluates nucleic acid cargo selection and coordinated osteogenic and angiogenic gene delivery, including pDNA, mRNA, siRNA, miRNA, and explores emerging multi-factor, stimuli-responsive, and CRISPR-based GAMs alongside their translational constraints. A distinct feature of this review is its claim-level patent analysis, which identifies substantial intellectual-property white space in GAM development. Despite strong preclinical evidence, no GAM platform has simultaneously achieved scalable manufacturing, regulatory readiness as a combination product, and validation in a human-scale bone defect model. Clinical translation will require coordinated optimization of vector-scaffold interactions, manufacturing scalability, safety, and clinically relevant validation.

title: HU promotes fidelity and leader-repeat integration during CRISPR adaptation in the type III-A system of Thermotoga profunda.
authors: Seimel, Mario; Willkomm, Sarah; Grohmann, Dina
abstract: CRISPR-Cas adaptive immunity relies on the acquisition of foreign DNA fragments as spacers within CRISPR arrays. Although spacer integration is generally catalysed by the conserved Cas1-Cas2 integrase complex, accurate integration frequently requires accessory factors. In the type I-E CRISPR-Cas system of Escherichia coli, the DNA-binding protein integration host factor (IHF) promotes leader-proximal spacer acquisition. The DNA bending properties of IHF exerted at the CRISPR locus are thought to form the mechanistic basis for the supportive function of IHF. However, many organisms lack IHF posing the questions how integration specificity is achieved in these organisms and whether analogous host factors contribute to adaptation in other CRISPR-Cas systems. Here, we investigated spacer integration in the type III-A CRISPR-Cas system of the hyperthermophilic bacterium Thermotoga profunda. Using reconstituted in vitro integration assays, we show that the TpCas1-TpCas2 complex alone exhibits limited integration fidelity and generates substantial off-target integration events. We identify the highly conserved histone-like protein HU (TpHU) as a critical cofactor for accurate spacer acquisition. Addition of TpHU strongly promotes integration at the leader-repeat junction while suppressing erroneous integration into noncanonical sites. TpHU therefore acts as a determinant of integration fidelity and target-site selection during adaptation.

title: Decoding the implicit paradigm of exosome targeting blood brain barrier in neurodegenerative diseases: Molecular insight and therapeutic perspective.
authors: Koley, Rishika; De, Sriparna; Ghosh, Adrija; Bhattacharjee, Dipanjan; Mitra, Ankan; Mondal, Banashree; Pahari, Agnish; Nandi, Meghasri; Kanri, Rachana; Dasgupta, Sanjukta; Chattopadhyay, Dipankar
abstract: Exosome physiology in the progression of neurodegenerative diseases is intricately tangled with various protein aggregations, including tau protein, alpha-synuclein, and amyloid-beta protein. Exosomes facilitate therapeutic and prognostic avenues through cell-to-cell crosstalk mechanisms, drug delivery, and biomarker isolation strategies in neurodegenerative disease management. The significant implications of molecular insights into neurofibrillary tangles and synaptic dysfunction have been extensively explored through microRNA (miRNA) regulation. The therapeutic potential of exosomes as nano-cargo systems is significant in nervous tissue regeneration and the treatment of neuronal lesions. Advancements in exosome engineering, including genetic modifications, have expanded their capacity to transport RNA molecules, proteins, and novel gene-editing tools such as CRISPR/Cas9, thereby enabling neuroprotective treatment protocols. Integration with immunotherapeutic approaches further highlights exosomes as promising components of combined strategies with important clinical outcomes.

title: Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.
authors: Kumar, Vivek; Batra, Priyanka; Das, Nivedita; Shende, Pravin
abstract: Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Tex11 mutant mouse models of human azoospermia.
authors: Atkins, G R; Hvasta-Gloria, R; Ausavarungnirun, C; Pombar, C R X; Hardy, J J; Sukhwani, M; Barnard, E; Pollock, N; Malizio, M; Sheng, Y; Brieno-Enriquez, M A; Castro, C; Chu, T; Yatsenko, A N; Orwig, K E
abstract: STUDY QUESTION: Do different patient TEX11 mutations lead to non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) when modeled in mice? SUMMARY ANSWER: A frameshift mutation in Tex11 leads to azoospermia in mice (Tex11D); a missense mutation had no impact on fertility (Tex11A); and a splice site mutation caused reduced testis weights and sperm counts with variable sub-fertility (Tex11L). WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY: Half of all NOA cases are unexplained but may arise from unidentified genetic mutations. Several variants in TEX11 have been identified in men with NOA; and Tex11 knockout in mice causes NOA. STUDY DESIGN, SIZE, DURATION: For fertility analysis of the different mutations, the sample sizes were as follows: n = 3 wild-type controls; n = 5 Tex11D; n = 3 Tex11A; and n = 3 Tex11L. Wild-type males and hemizygous mutant male mice in each Tex11 line were bred with two to four different wild-type females for fertility analysis. At 12 weeks, testes and epidiymides were then collected for histological analysis and sperm counts. Additional Tex11L mice (n = 3) and wild-type controls (n = 3) were bred for 52 weeks with 2 new wild-type females every 2-3 weeks, then testes and epididymides were collected for further analysis. Testes and epididymides from Tex11L mice (n = 3 for wild type and mutants) were also collected at 24 and 36 weeks of age for histological analyses. PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING, METHODS: TEX11 variants identified in male patients with NOA were introduced into the orthologous region of the mouse genome using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Lines were expanded onto a DBA/2 background by breeding female heterozygous carriers to wild-type DBA/2 males. Hemizygous males from the third generation and beyond were used for fertility studies, gross tissue morphology, sperm counts, and histological analysis. MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE: Compared to wild-type mice (145.0 +/- 17.56 mg testis weight; 1.72 +/- 0.50 million sperm/cauda epididymis; 6.42 +/- 0.73 pups/breeding), Tex11D mice had reduced testis weight (28.33 +/- 0.68 mg), no sperm in the epididymis, and were infertile with a maturation arrest testicular phenotype. We did not observe any spermatogenesis or fertility defects in Tex11A mice (145.0 mg +/- 0 mg; 1.52 +/- 0.11 million sperm/cauda; 5.83 +/- 0.81 pups/breeding) compared to wild type. Tex11L mice had reduced testis weight (78.33 +/- 16.41 mg) and reduced epididymal sperm counts (0.33 +/- 0.13 million/cauda epididymis) but a variable fertility phenotype (5.42 +/- 1.13 pups/breeding), with 2 out of 6 mice being subfertile. Tex11L mice also had variable testicular and epididymal defects, classified as mild or severe. LARGE SCALE DATA: Not applicable for this study. LIMITATIONS, REASONS FOR CAUTION: The sample sizes were limited for each mouse line. WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS: Our study shows the importance of validating NOA-associated variants in a mouse model. Our data suggest that different TEX11 variants produce a variety of phenotypes which could impact genetic counselling of patients with NOA. FUNDING: This study was supported by the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute for Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) grant HD096723 to A.N.Y. and K.E.O. G.R.A. was supported by NICHD grant HD114406. DISCLOSURES: K.E.O. was an advisor to Paterna Biosciences. The authors declare that the research was conducted in the absence of any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

title: Functional analysis of the U-box ubiquitin E3 ligase gene Gracilariopsis lemaneiformis GlPRP19 in heat stress responses.
authors: Jin, Zhenyu; Chen, Yijing; Li, Shiji; Xiong, Zhijun; Gong, Wencheng; Sun, Xue; Xu, Nianjun; Liu, Shixia
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: High temperature has become a major environmental factor affecting the growth and development of marine algae, including the red macroalga Gracilariopsis lemaneiformis. U-box type E3 ligases are well-known for regulating plant growth and stress responses. In this study, we found that GlPRP19, a PRP19 domain-containing E3 ligase, increased heat sensitivity in the model microalgae Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Heterologous overexpression of GlPRP19 reduced algal growth, photosynthetic activity, and activities of superoxide dismutase (SOD) and ascorbate peroxidase (APX), while increasing MDA content. In addition, compared with wild-type, GlPRP19 overexpression in transgenic P. tricornutum significantly downregulated the transcript levels of heat-responsive genes HSP70A, HSP70B, HSP90, HSF and HSF2 under heat stress. Moreover, metabolomic analysis revealed that the levels of several TCA cycle intermediates, ornithine and derivatives of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) were significantly suppressed in OE lines compared with WT under heat stress. Additionally, fatty acid profiling further demonstrated that overexpression of GlPRP19 significantly decreased saturated fatty acids and induced a marked accumulation of polyunsaturated fatty acids including C16:3, C18:3, C18:4, and C20:5, indicating an impaired capacity to reduce membrane lipid unsaturation in response to heat stress. Collectively, these results indicated that GlPRP19 might be a negative regulator of thermotolerance. This study lays a foundation for the direct functional characterization of GlPRP19 in G. lemaneiformis using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout, which represents a promising strategy for breeding heat-tolerant algal strains in the future.

title: Identification of mitophagy inducers for Alzheimer's disease via high-throughput endogenous ATP5B tagging system.
authors: Wang, Bingliang; Wu, Zijian; Huang, Shaojuan; Sio, Choian; Shen, Han-Ming; Chen, Qiang
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Mitophagy, the selective clearance of defective mitochondria via the autophagy-lysosome pathway, is essential for maintaining mitochondrial health and cellular homeostasis. Dysregulation of mitophagy is strongly implicated in aging-related pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), cancer, and metabolic disorders, highlighting the significance of elucidating its regulatory mechanisms. While existing methods using exogenous reporters enable genome-wide and high-throughput screening for mitophagy regulators, they constrain discoveries to specific pathways and introduce artifacts through ectopic expression. OBJECTIVES: To overcome these limitations, we developed an effective and rapid platform for identifying mitophagy modulators by targeting endogenous proteins. METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, we engineered HeLa cells expressing small molecular tags (GFP or NanoLuc) fused to the C-terminal of ATP5B, a mitochondrial inner membrane protein. Genome-wide screening for mitophagy regulatory genes were performed using a genome-wide CRISPR library coupled with flow cytometry. Additionally, an FDA-approved kinase inhibitor library was used to screen for mitophagy inducers. To evaluate the efficacy of a screened drug in Alzheimer's disease, cognitive behavior, pathological features and mitophagy events in 3 x Tg-AD mice with or without treatment were examined using the Morris water maze assay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). RESULTS: These ATP5B-tagging cells provided a robust readout of mitophagy and enabled high-throughput genetic or pharmacological screening. With this platform, we identified several promising genes that regulate mitophagy and are significantly associated with Alzheimer's disease. Moreover, the FDA-approved drug Flupentixol emerged as a novel mitophagy inducer that acts by promoting adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) localization to mitochondria and exhibited strong therapeutic potential in a model of Alzheimer's disease. CONCLUSION: This study establishes a novel system for identifying mitophagy modulators, with the potential to accelerate the discovery of therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer's disease.

title: Multilayered genetic engineering strategies for tunable gene expression in Yarrowia lipolytica: advancing high-performance cell factories for sustainable biomanufacturing.
authors: Xia, Wenxin; Zhang, Zhongmin; Zhi, Yongyan; Lin, Lu; Zhang, Zhi-Gang; Ledesma-Amaro, Rodrigo; Wang, Kaifeng; Ji, Xiao-Jun
abstract: Yarrowia lipolytica has become an important chassis for the biomanufacturing of high-value chemicals because of its strong lipid metabolism, abundant precursor supply, and broad carbon-source utilization. However, efficient cell factory construction requires more than simply introducing a biosynthetic pathway. Imbalanced gene expression, metabolic burden, competing metabolic fluxes, conflicts between cell growth and product formation, and insufficient genetic stability can all limit production performance. Therefore, multilevel fine-tuning of gene expression is increasingly required for the engineering of Y. lipolytica. This review summarizes the genetic engineering strategies developed to meet these demands. We first discuss episomal plasmid expression and different genomic integration approaches, with emphasis on their expression stability and applications. We then review strategies for gene expression enhancement, attenuation, and dynamic regulation, including promoter engineering, multicopy integration, CRISPR activation, weak-promoter replacement, CRISPR interference, antisense RNA, RNA interference, and metabolite- and spatiotemporal-responsive regulation. Finally, future directions are discussed, including the standardization of genetic elements, improved regulatory precision, and enhanced genetic stability of industrial strains. This review provides an overview of genetic strategies for developing efficient and robust Y. lipolytica cell factories.

title: Photoperiodic responses persist in DH-like neuropeptide gene mutants of the band-legged ground cricket, Dianemobius nigrofasciatus.
authors: Shimizu, Yuta; Kataoka, Kosuke; Goto, Shin G
abstract: Seasonal adaptation is essential for the survival and reproduction of organisms inhabiting environments with predictable annual fluctuations. Photoperiodism is a key adaptive mechanism that enables most multivoltine insects to synchronize physiological and developmental processes with seasonal environmental changes, yet its underlying endocrine mechanisms remain poorly understood. Diapause hormone (DH) and DH-like neuropeptides, which belong to the tryptopyrokinin (TPK) family and are characterized by a conserved C-terminal WFGPRXa motif, play a pivotal role in photoperiodically regulated maternal embryonic diapause induction in several insect species. In some lepidopteran insects, DH has also been implicated in the regulation of photoperiodic responses beyond diapause induction, raising the possibility that DH/DH-like neuropeptides function as a common regulator of multiple photoperiodic responses across insects. However, whether this mechanism is conserved across insect taxa remains unclear. The band-legged ground cricket Dianemobius nigrofasciatus exhibits multiple photoperiodic responses, including maternal embryonic diapause induction, wing morph and rate of nymphal development. Here, we investigated the involvement of DH-like neuropeptides in photoperiodic responses in D. nigrofasciatus. Two genes encoding TPKs were identified from the genome sequence of D. nigrofasciatus. One corresponded to capa, whereas the other was designated Din-dh because it encoded seven TPKs (i.e., DH-like neuropeptides). We established three mutant lines carrying distinct Din-dh alleles derived from two G(0) founders and investigated whether Din-dh is involved in photoperiodic responses. All mutant lines retained detectable photoperiodic responses. These results indicate that disruption of Din-dh does not abolish photoperiodic responses examined in D. nigrofasciatus.

title: HvNCED12 positively regulates salt tolerance in barley by modulating abscisic acid biosynthesis and ion homeostasis.
authors: Shi, Wenxia; Du, Xuye
abstract: Abscisic acid (ABA) biosynthesis is essential for plant salt tolerance, but the roles and upstream regulation of individual 9-cis-epoxycarotenoid dioxygenase (NCED) genes in barley remain unclear. To determine whether HvNCED12 contributes to barley salt tolerance and identify its upstream regulator, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 knockout and overexpression lines in the barley cultivar Golden Promise. Wild-type and transgenic plants were exposed to 150 mM NaCl for 14 d, with or without 100 muM ABA. ABA content, physiological traits, ion accumulation, and gene expression were measured, while promoter regulation was examined by yeast one-hybrid, electrophoretic mobility shift, and dual-luciferase assays. Salt induced HvNCED12 expression approximately sixfold at 24 h, and HvNCED12-GFP localized to chloroplasts. Under salinity, knockout lines showed reduced ABA and chlorophyll, 49.3% higher malondialdehyde content, disrupted Na(+)/K(+) homeostasis, and reduced biomass, whereas overexpression lines showed opposite responses. Exogenous ABA partially alleviated these defects and reduced malondialdehyde by 29.1% in knockout lines. HvNCED12 also affected ABA biosynthesis-, ion transport-, and stress-related gene expression. HvMYB10 bound the HvNCED12 promoter and activated transcription. These findings identify an HvMYB10-HvNCED12 module that promotes salt tolerance by regulating ABA biosynthesis and ion homeostasis.

title: Dual proximity-activated immuno-LAMP-CRISPR for ultrasensitive protein detection on an integrated microfluidic chip.
authors: Du, Jungang; Zhu, Yuanyuan; Yu, Xiaoping; Wu, Jian
abstract: Sensitive detection of proteins is critically important in biomedical research, food safety, and environmental monitoring. However, conventional protein detection methods are typically heterogeneous and exhibit lower sensitivity than nucleic acid-based assays, rendering them unsuitable for on-site analysis of low-abundance proteins. Herein, a dual proximity-activated immuno-LAMP-CRISPR (DPILC) technology was developed for ultrasensitive detection of Listeria monocytogenes p60 protein. To improve the detection sensitivity in DPILC, the nucleic acid amplification template could only be generated through two consecutive proximity-activated extension events, which substantially reduced background signals compared with the single-extension approach. Moreover, the two extension reactions produced a longer template than the single extension, enabling coupling with LAMP technology and thus simplifying the assay workflow. To further facilitate on-site application, the dual proximity-activated immuno-LAMP was integrated with CRISPR/Cas12a and a gravity-driven microfluidic chip for contamination-free visual detection. The DPILC assay achieved a detection limit of 1 x 10(3) CFU mL(-1) for Listeria monocytogenes in 10-muL samples, with no cross-reactivity against six non-target bacteria, demonstrating excellent sensitivity and specificity. Validation in spiked pork, lettuce, and skim milk samples showed detection performance comparable to that in pure culture. By combining the advantages of dual proximity-activated extension, isothermal amplification, CRISPR-based signal transduction, and pump-free microfluidic operation, DPILC offers a promising platform for ultrasensitive protein detection in resource-limited field settings.

title: Engineering split activators for controlled-background CRISPR/Cas12a molecular logic biosensing of AFB1 and OTA.
authors: Guo, Fang; Xu, Fengfeng; Zhou, Wenjiao
abstract: Mycotoxin co-occurrence of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) and ochratoxin A (OTA) in dairy products threatens food safety. Conventional methods suffer from complex procedures and limited multi-target analysis. Current CRISPR/Cas12a sensors face nonspecific background and poor programmability. We developed a CRISPR/Cas12a logic gate biosensing platform with split DNA activators, enabling individual AFB1 and OTA quantification via dual YES gates and logic-based qualitative multi-target analysis via OR, AND, INHIBIT, and NOR gates. Integrating aptamer recognition, target-triggered strand displacement amplification (SDA), and Cas12a trans-cleavage, the split activators reduced nonspecific activation, enabling low background for target-dependent logic gates. YES, OR, AND, INHIBIT, and NOR gates were constructed. Linear ranges were 0.1-500 ng/mL for OTA and 0.05-500 ng/mL for AFB1, with detection limits of 0.0755 and 0.0381 ng/mL, respectively. The platform showed good selectivity and satisfactory recoveries in spiked pretreated milk. This work provides a programmable, low-background strategy for CRISPR-based multi-mycotoxin analysis in pretreated milk matrices.

title: An engineered probiotic yeast converts extracellular ATP into adenosine to alleviate experimental colitis.
authors: Liu, Huiye; Zhang, Mingxin; Wu, Weizhen; Deng, Qingyun; Li, Xiaofang; Ma, Rongwei; Bai, Lan; Huang, Bing
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic relapsing intestinal disorder characterized by mucosal inflammation, epithelial barrier disruption, and gut microbial dysbiosis. Excessive extracellular ATP (eATP) accumulates in inflamed intestinal tissues and amplifies immune activation through purinergic signaling, whereas adenosine generated from extracellular nucleotide metabolism exerts immunoregulatory effects. Here, we engineered the probiotic yeast Saccharomyces boulardii to sense eATP and convert it into adenosine through a CRISPR-engineered dual-enzyme pathway consisting of apyrase and 5'-nucleotidase. The engineered strain showed ATP-responsive pathway activation and efficiently generated adenosine from eATP, allowing extracellular nucleotide metabolism to be modulated in inflammatory settings. Oral administration of this strain significantly alleviated disease severity in acute dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis and showed beneficial effects in a repeated-DSS model, improved barrier-related epithelial features, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and supported mucosal recovery. Integrated microbiome and transcriptome analyses further showed partial restoration of gut microbial community structure, partial recovery of predicted microbial purine-related pathways, and attenuation of mucosal T-cell activation. Together, these findings indicate that engineered Saccharomyces boulardii can regulate extracellular purine metabolism in the inflamed gut and provide a microbial strategy for modulating intestinal inflammation.

title: Generation and validation of B2M knockout human iPSC line, LVPEIi001-C-2 that lacks the cell surface expression of HLA-Class I antigens.
authors: Agrawal, Trupti; Maddileti, Savitri; Mahato, Sudipta; Pidishetty, Divya; Srihari, Preeti; Sawarn, Krishna; Sivacoumar, Akschya; Chakraborty, Debojyoti; Mariappan, Indumathi
abstract: MHC Class-I molecules present self antigens to CD8 + T cells and mediate self vs non-self recognition and this mechanism plays a major role in mismatched graft rejections. Beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) binds non-covalently with MHCI heavy chains and stabilizes the peptide-binding groove on cell surfaces. Loss of B2M expression destabilizes the MHCI complexes and could render the cells hypoimmunogenic. Here, we report a B2M(-/-) iPSC line, LVPEIi001-C-2, generated using CRISPR/Cas9-based editing of a healthy control human iPSC line. This line lost the MHCI expression on cell surfaces, retained the stemness, pluripotency, genetic identity, displayed normal karyotype and tested negative for mycoplasma.

title: NANOG and OCT4 dosage shapes non-monotonic gene expression responses during stem cell differentiation.
authors: Yan, Jielin; Cho, Hyein S; Luo, Renhe; Zhao, Jiahui Hazel; Beer, Michael A; Li, Wei; Huangfu, Danwei
abstract: Precise regulation of transcription factor (TF) expression is critical for maintaining cell identity, but studies on how graded expression levels affect cellular phenotypes are limited. To address this gap, we employed human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) as a dynamic model to study gene dosage effects and systematically titrated key TFs NANOG and OCT4 expression using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi). We then profiled transcriptomic changes in hESCs under self-renewal and definitive endoderm (DE) differentiation conditions using single-cell RNA-seq. Quantitative modeling of these Perturb-seq datasets uncovered distinct response patterns for different types of genes, including a striking non-monotonic up-regulation of on-target lineage genes during DE differentiation. This behavior extended to the ESC-to-neuroectoderm transition, suggesting non-monotonic responses of lineage genes to pluripotency regulator dosage are a recurring feature of lineage transitions. Together, these findings underscore the importance of characterizing TF function across a gradient of expression levels.

title: Integrative Genomic and Stem Cell Frameworks for Variant-to-Function Discovery in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Narrative Review.
authors: Uddin, Jalal; Singh, Randhir; Nair, Chandralekha; Rahamathulla, Mohamed; Ahmed, Mohammed Muqtader; Nafiz, Iqbal Hossain; Merghani, Tarig Hakim; Alawad, Azza Osman; Dwivedi, Dyumn; Das, Uddalak
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition shaped by de novo protein-truncating variants, inherited missense substitutions, recurrent copy number variations (CNVs), and distributed polygenic risk. These alterations converge on a limited set of neurobiological processes, including synaptic refinement, excitation-to-inhibition balance, chromatin state regulation, and glial-mediated neuroimmune signaling. Experimental paradigms now exist for systematic variant-to-function interrogation through CRISPR-engineered isogenic human pluripotent stem-cell libraries incorporating Cas9 nucleases, programmable transcriptional modulators (dCas9-KRAB and dCas9-VP64), base editors, and prime editing systems. Coupled with single-cell multi-omic platforms such as Perturb-seq, scATAC-seq, and CITE-seq, and with circuit-level phenotyping through multielectrode arrays, calcium imaging, and quantitative morphometry, these systems resolve ASD-relevant cellular states at single-cell and cell-type-specific resolution. In this narrative review, we distinguish deliberately between what these platforms have already established and what remains proposed. To date, a small number of studies constitute the demonstrated evidence base: in vivo Perturb-seq of 35 ASD/neurodevelopmental risk genes in mouse cortex, mosaic knockout of ASD genes in human cortical organoids, the CHOOSE organoid screen of 36 risk genes, assembloid CRISPR screening of 425 neurodevelopmental-disorder risk genes, a 63-line mouse embryonic stem-cell CNV resource, and a CRISPRi screen of 102 ASD risk genes in human induced pluripotent stem-cell (iPSC)-derived microglia implicating ADNP in synaptic pruning. We summarized these in a dedicated comparison table. Against this, integration of polygenic and noncoding architecture, causal-inference frameworks, such as Mendelian randomization and do-calculus, and cross-laboratory reproducibility, remain aspirational rather than realized. We therefore frame the field's principal near-term requirement not as further gene discovery but as harmonized protocols, shared reference lines, arrayed validation capacity, and interpretable statistical frameworks capable of converting perturbation atlases into causal mechanism.

title: CRISPR-AsCas12a with crRNA-Free Collateral Cleavage Activity for Electrochemical Diagnosis of HER2-Positive Breast Cancer.
authors: Wu, Shuai; Xu, Jialin; Sun, Yanting; Zeng, Tianyu; Li, Zeying; Zhou, Tianci; Deng, Ying; Ye, Chang; Li, Genxi; Yin, Yongmei
abstract: The CRISPR-Cas12a system has revolutionized molecular diagnostics; however, the strict requirement of crRNAs and target DNA for collateral cleavage activation restricts its flexibility in non-nucleic acid diagnostics. Herein, we demonstrate that AsCas12a exhibits an RNA-free collateral cleavage activity with the presence of manganese ions (Mn2+), which preferentially cleaves single-stranded DNA efficiently. Mechanistically, kinetic analyses reveal that AsCas12a exhibits a significantly higher binding affinity for Mn2+ than for magnesium ion (Mg2+), while molecular dynamics simulations suggest that Mn2+ coordination induces conformational changes to expose the RuvC endonuclease domain. Harnessing this unique property, an enzymatic cascade-amplified electrochemical biosensor integrating manganese nanoflowers is reported for the diagnosis of human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive breast cancer. By equipping screen-printed gold electrodes with DNA reporters, this diagnostic tool enables high-precision HER2 quantification and successfully distinguishes various HER2-related cell lines. Furthermore, the biosensor has been extended to analyze HER2-positive exosomes, facilitating the dynamic tracking of serum exosome levels in tumor-bearing nude mice to evaluate therapeutic efficacy and accurately distinguish HER2-positive breast cancer patients in clinical samples. This RNA-free Cas12a system may provide new insights into CRISPR-based non-nucleic acid detection, emerging as a powerful tool for dynamic tumor monitoring and precision oncology.

title: Integrative analysis of pooled CRISPR screens provide functional insights into AD GWAS risk genes.
authors: Wang, Rebecca Y; Wozniak, Glenn; Wang, Xiaoting; Mustafa, Meer; El-Khatib, Malak; Kahn, Elias; Heutink, Peter; Long, Hua; Kenkare-Mitra, Sara; Rosenthal, Arnon; Khan, Zia; Kuhn, Julia A; Gulbranson, Daniel R
abstract: Microglia pathways such as lipid transport and metabolism, phagocytosis, and lysosomal function are implicated Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology, but the mechanisms underlying these pathways remain poorly understood. To map these pathways, custom CRISPR activation and interference (CRISPRa/i) libraries were constructed targeting 203 microglial and genome-wide association study (GWAS)-associated risk genes. Pooled CRISPRa/i screens in THP-1 cells identified core functional regulators of lipid metabolism and lysosomal function, a subset of which were validated in primary macrophages. We also captured transcriptomic changes caused by these genes by performing Perturb-seq in primary macrophages. Through non-negative matrix factorization, we identified five gene programs altered by our perturbation library. We then used an integrative analysis of functional screen data with Perturb-seq data that enabled us to uncover novel functions and genetic relationships between perturbations. This multidimensional resource links genetic perturbations to phenotypes and transcriptional programs, establishing a scalable framework for systematic gene discovery in neurodegeneration and beyond.

title: Ultrasensitive endogenous miRNA imaging in live cells by an allosteric orthogonal CRISPR probe.
authors: Zhang, Xiaoyue; Rha, Hyeonji; Zhang, Yuanzhi; Gao, Ming; Kim, Jaewon; Zheng, Wenjing; Bakan, Yesim; Chi, Jingtian; Cai, Yueyuan; Wang, Xingang; Wang, Chengqin; Wang, Jie; Yue, Bin; Chen, Zhi; Kim, Jong Seung; Qiu, Meng
abstract: Sensitive and multiplexed visualization of endogenous RNA in living cells remains challenging because of insufficient signal amplification, background activation, and interference between parallel readout pathways, particularly for low-abundance regulatory RNAs. Many current CRISPR-based RNA imaging strategies rely on stoichiometric RNA binding, limiting sensitivity and often yielding a poor signal-to-background ratio for low-abundance endogenous microRNAs (miRNAs). Moreover, limited orthogonality between sensing modules and readouts complicates interference-free multiplexing. Inefficient intracellular delivery further limits their applicability in complex biological environments. Here, we introduce an allosteric CRISPR probe for orthogonal and amplified miRNA imaging in living cells, which is built on an allosterically gated crRNA that integrates a CRISPR-Cas12a system with a Zn(2+)-dependent DNAzyme module. Mechanistically, miR-210 selectively unlocks the caged crRNA to activate Cas12a trans-cleavage, providing amplified red (Cy5) fluorescence, while miR-21 independently activates DNAzyme cleavage to generate green (FAM) fluorescence with minimal cross-talk. Black phosphorus nanosheets serve as a biocompatible nanocarrier for efficient intracellular probe delivery. This orthogonal architecture enables precise discrimination of breast cancer subtypes in living cells and clinical tissue sections. Together, this work overcomes a central limitation of live-cell miRNA imaging by enabling sensitive and multiplexed visualization of endogenous miRNAs, opening new possibilities for dissecting RNA-mediated regulation in complex cellular systems.

title: Bloom syndrome helicase facilitates efficient HIV-1 infection in macrophages.
authors: Leal, Andrew A; Tafrate, Samantha; He, Xianbao; Bryant, Daniel L; Herring, Melissa B; Andrade, Maria; McWhirter, Joseph B; Quinones-Molina, Andres A; Gummuluru, Suryaram; Sagar, Manish; Flynn, Rachel L; Leshchiner, Ignaty; Henderson, Andrew J
abstract: The induction of DNA damage by HIV-1 prior to integration suggests a role for DNA damage responses (DDRs) during early infection; however, this role remains incompletely understood. Initial experiments, using specific inhibitors for DDR pathways, demonstrate that both ATM and ATR are necessary for efficient HIV-1 infection of macrophages with ATM acting at the late reverse transcription step. To identify DDR factors associated with ATM/ATR pathways that influence HIV-1 infection, a CRISPR knockout screen using a DDR-focused sgRNA library was performed. Approximately 30 DDR genes that impacted HIV-1 infection were identified with 13 factors that facilitated HIV-1 infection and 17 DDR factors that restrict HIV-1 infection. Several hits were factors associated with the Fanconi anemia pathway, such as BTR complex proteins, including the RecQ helicase Bloom syndrome helicase (BLM). BLM was specifically demonstrated to enhance HIV-1 infection and replication with knockdown of BLM expression diminishing integration and the establishment of intact HIV-1 proviruses in macrophages by 50%. BLM is associated with HIV-1 late reverse transcription intermediates, the step that proceeds HIV-1 integration, identifying BLM as a cofactor in this key step required for efficient infection.

title: Research progress on the epidemiology and diagnostic technologies of urinary tract infections in kidney transplant recipients.
authors: Fan, Liqi; Zhou, Yiming; Shen, Bin; Zhou, Yunheng
abstract: In recent years, the increase in poor lifestyle and dietary habits (such as smoking, unhealthy eating) coupled with the high prevalence of chronic comorbidities including diabetes and hypertension has led to a rising number of patients with kidney disease. Kidney transplantation (KT), as an important means to improve the quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), has been widely applied in clinical treatment. However, post-kidney transplantation urinary tract infections (Post-KT UTIs), as a serious postoperative complication, severely threatens the safety of transplant recipients and the long-term function of grafts. Post-KT UTIs refer to an inflammatory reaction resulting from pathogen proliferation in the urinary system after transplantation, which may include cystitis, pyelonephritis, and in severe instances, can advance to bacteremia or sepsis, endangering both patient and graft survival. Post-KT UTIs are commonly caused by Gram-negative bacterial infections, notably by species such as Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli (E. coli). Currently, the clinical detection and treatment of Post-KT UTIs remain based primarily on traditional urine culture and empirical antimicrobial therapy. This review introduces advanced detection methods such as next-generation sequencing and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), aiming to offer new strategies for diagnosing Post-KT UTIs. Moreover, it reviews recent advancements in the epidemiology, treatment methods, and preventive strategies of Post-KT UTIs, and the role of gut and urinary microbiota in infection development, aiming to facilitate the development of novel therapeutic agents, vaccine formulations, and refined treatment strategies for precise management of Post-KT UTIs.

title: CRISPR/Cas in food microbial biotechnology: from genome editing to precision microbiology.
authors: Juszczuk-Kubiak, Edyta; Pilka, Natalia; Zielinska, Ewelina; Roszko, Marek
abstract: CRISPR/Cas technologies have opened new opportunities for the precise genetic engineering of microorganisms relevant to food biotechnology. Their programmability enables targeted genome modification, transcriptional regulation, sequence-specific antimicrobial activity, and nucleic acid detection, offering new strategies to improve fermentation processes, microbial safety, and the functional properties of food-associated strains. However, experimental evidence varies considerably across microorganisms and applications, and successful genome editing does not necessarily translate into improved technological performance. This review examines recent advances in CRISPR/Cas-based engineering of starter cultures, probiotic strains, and production microorganisms, alongside emerging strategies for bacteriophage resistance, pathogen and biofilm control, and food diagnostics. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing applications experimentally validated in food-related settings from proof-of-concept studies conducted in laboratory or biomedical contexts. The review also evaluates the major barriers to industrial implementation, including strain-specific editing efficiency, genetic stability, process robustness, and validation in food matrices. It also considers the distinct biosafety and regulatory implications of production microorganisms removed or inactivated during processing versus viable engineered cultures retained in final products. By integrating advances in molecular engineering with evidence of functional performance and practical implementation requirements, this review highlights both the opportunities and current limitations of CRISPR/Cas technologies in food microbial biotechnology.

title: Betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase regulates metamorphosis and vitellogenesis via juvenile hormone biosynthesis in Locusta migratoria.
authors: Yan, Qiang; Ma, Jiajie; Gao, Lulu; Liu, Mingzhi; Wang, Guoxin; Man, Yu Bon; Zhou, Shutang; Song, Jiasheng
abstract: Juvenile hormone (JH) is a major endocrine regulator of insect metamorphosis and reproduction. The biosynthesis of biologically active JH requires S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation, coupling JH production to cellular methyl metabolism. In animals, betaine-homocysteine S-methyltransferase (Bhmt) regenerates methionine from homocysteine, yet this enzyme has long been considered absent from insects. Here, we show that not all insects lack Bhmt. Transcriptome profiling of the corpora allata (CA), the JH-synthesizing gland, in Locusta migratoria revealed that Bhmt is specifically and highly expressed in the CA, with its developmental expression closely mirroring the JH synthesis pattern. A genome-wide survey confirmed Bhmt retention in basal insect species but loss in derived lineages. To investigate its function, we generated Bhmt knockout locusts using CRISPR/Cas9. Bhmt knockout significantly reduced JH titer and caused multiple developmental defects, including precocious metamorphosis, shortened nymphal duration, reduced body size, delayed ovarian development, reduced egg size, and decreased hatching success. Consistently, the JH synthesis genes Hmgr and Jhamt were markedly downregulated in the knockout CA. Together, these findings establish Bhmt as an important regulator of JH biosynthesis and reveal a previously unrecognized function of the betaine-dependent remethylation pathway in insect endocrine regulation.

title: An NLR Associated With Defence Against Turnip Mosaic Virus in Nicotiana benthamiana.
authors: Lin, Jiajia; Guo, Ziying; Mao, Wenqi; Fang, Xinxin; Jia, Zhaoxing; Rui, Penghuan; Rao, Shaofei; Lu, Yuwen; Zheng, Hongying; Chen, Jianping; Yan, Fei; Wu, Guanwei
abstract: While the role of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) proteins as intracellular immune receptors in plants is well documented, information on NLRs involved in antiviral defence remains scarce. Here, we conducted a high-throughput virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) screen of 301 NLRs in Nicotiana benthamiana using turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) to identify NLRs potentially involved in TuMV infection. Genetic analyses identified that NLR39-2, a previously uncharacterized Toll/interleukin-1 receptor NLR, enhanced antiviral defence: overexpression suppressed TuMV accumulation, whereas CRISPR-Cas9 knockout enhanced susceptibility. This enhanced defence is probably specific to TuMV, as NLR39-2 manipulation did not affect infection by the related potyvirus chilli veinal mottle virus or the unrelated potato virus X. Mechanistically, NLR39-2 was transcriptionally upregulated upon infection and physically interacted with the viral protein VPg. Co-expression with individual TuMV proteins did not trigger hypersensitive cell death. During infection, NLR39-2 partially redistributed from the plasma membrane to cytoplasmic P-bodies, which are tightly associated with the viral replication complexes. Our study establishes a scalable platform for antiviral NLR discovery and provides a new NLR resource for engineering TuMV resistance.

title: CRISPR/Cas9 Editing of Starch Branching Enzyme Genes Remodels Starch Structure and Improves Nutritional Quality in Sweet Potato.
authors: Fan, Weijuan; Li, Yanshen; Xu, Ziyin; Nie, Haozhen; Gao, Yusen; Yang, Jun; Wang, Hongxia
abstract: Starch branching enzymes (SBEs) play a central role in determining amylopectin architecture and starch functionality, yet their contribution to starch nutritional quality and crop performance in sweet potato remains unclear. In this study, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to target SBEI and SBEII in sweet potato, generating lines with reduced SBE activity. Edited lines showed markedly increased amylose and resistant starch contents compared with the wild type. Amylopectin chain length analysis revealed a decrease in short chains and a relative increase in longer chains, indicating substantial remodeling of branch structure. Microscopic observations further showed reduced birefringence and structural irregularities in starch granules. These structural changes resulted in altered physicochemical properties, including decreased swelling power and solubility, elevated gelatinization temperature, and modified pasting behavior. In vitro digestion assays demonstrated significantly reduced starch digestibility and lower predicted glycemic index values. Whole-genome resequencing confirmed the stable integration of T-DNA and predicted limited insertion-associated effects, further supporting that the improved starch traits were primarily derived from targeted SBE editing. Importantly, storage root yield remained comparable to that of wild-type plants. Collectively, these results demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated SBE editing effectively improves starch nutritional quality without compromising yield, providing a promising strategy for developing health-oriented sweet potato varieties.

title: From Nitrate Perception to Environmental Adaptation: Functional Elucidation and Regulatory Networks of the Plant NLP Family.
authors: Ahmad, Hafiz Ishtiaq; Liu, Ying; Chen, Chunrui; Jia, Lijie; Zhu, Huihui; Yang, Jianli
abstract: Nitrogen is a necessary macronutrient that limits plant growth and crop productivity, yet excessive fertilizer application has resulted in serious environmental consequences. The NIN-like protein (NLP) family consists of plant-specific transcription factors that serve as central regulators of nitrate signaling. In 2022, the discovery of NLP7 as an intracellular nitrate receptor represented a major conceptual shift from transcriptional regulation to signal perception. This review systematically summarizes the molecular architecture of NLP proteins, focusing on the conserved RWP-RK DNA-binding domain, the PB1 protein-protein interaction module, and the GAF-like domain associated with the integration of multiple signals. It also examines the species-specific expansion and evolutionary diversification of the NLP family, as well as the multilayered mechanisms that regulate NLP activity, including phosphorylation as a signal-dependent molecular switch, SUMOylation as a negative feedback mechanism, transcriptional regulation of downstream targets, and PB1-mediated protein interaction networks. In addition to nitrate signaling, NLPs serve as central hubs linking nitrogen and carbon metabolism and mediating responses to abiotic stresses including cold, heat, salinity, and iron deficiency. Notably, the NLP7-NIGT1.3 module coordinates a growth-stress trade-off during iron deficiency by modulating nitrate signaling intensity, revealing a previously unrecognized mechanism for balancing stress adaptation with growth maintenance. NLPs also participate in developmental processes, including lateral root formation and symbiotic nodulation. Finally, this review highlights the potential of NLP-based approaches for crop genetic improvement, such as overexpression of key NLP genes or CRISPR/Cas-mediated editing, to improve nitrogen use efficiency, stress tolerance, and yield. Collectively, these insights provide a theoretical foundation for developing crop varieties with improved nitrogen-use efficiency and context-dependent stress adaptation, while acknowledging the inherent trade-offs between productivity and resilience.

title: MicroRNA Gatekeepers: Integrating Growth, Development, and Stress Adaptation in Cotton.
authors: Li, Jiarui; Wang, Xuan; Qin, Jiawang; Wu, Yifan; Wei, Mengyao; Li, Chaofan; Jia, Yanfeng
abstract: As the primary cash crop for natural fiber, cotton develops under sophisticated endogenous genetic programs, with biotic and abiotic stresses continuously driving its adaptive evolution. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are post-transcriptional regulators that modulate gene expression via target mRNA cleavage, translational repression, and mediation of DNA methylation. miRNAs target transcription factors and hormone signaling pathways to regulate cotton plant architecture and fiber development. In addition, miRNAs mitigate biotic and abiotic stresses through ROS, lignin, and hormone pathways, as well as by forming competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) modules with long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs). This review establishes an miRNA-centered regulatory framework that coordinates cotton growth, development, and stress resistance. A series of technologies, including multi-omics combined with machine learning, gene overexpression, STTM, MIM, MIGS, CRISPR editing, foliar dsRNA spraying, and bionanocarriers, are proposed to facilitate the breeding of cotton varieties with high yield, superior fiber quality, and broad-spectrum stress tolerance.

title: A LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a Assay for Specific Detection of Escherichia coli in Whole Blood: Analytical Performance and Clinical Evaluation in Suspected Bloodstream Infection.
authors: Quyen, Dao Thanh; Thau, Nguyen Sy; Trung, Pham Quang; Huy, Nguyen Quang; Huyen, Dao Thi; Hoan, Phan Quoc; Trang, Do Thu; Parkes, Le Mai; Song, Le Huu; Trung, Ngo Tat
abstract: Background/Objectives: Blood culture is slow and real-time PCR (qPCR) needs a thermal cycler, while loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) is rapid but prone to non-specific amplification. We developed a LAMP assay with CRISPR/Cas12a read-out targeting the Escherichia coli dxs gene and compared it with qPCR and blood culture. Methods: Reaction conditions were optimised and specificity tested on 15 E. coli and 40 non-target isolates. The limit of detection (LOD) was determined in spiked whole blood (20 replicates per level, 1-10 CFU/mL) by hit rate and probit regression, with conversion to dxs copies by growth phase. Fifty-two patients with suspected bloodstream infection were tested by all three methods. Results: The assay detected all 15 Escherichia coli isolates tested (inclusivity 15/15; 95% CI 79.6-100) and none of 40 non-target isolates (exclusivity 40/40; 95% CI 91.2-100); the exclusivity panel did not include Shigella spp. or Escherichia fergusonii, which the in silico analysis predicts the assay would detect. The probit LOD(95) was 14.2 CFU/mL (95% fiducial limits 6.7-156;  approximately 43 dxs copies/mL for the mid-exponential spike culture used here) for LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a and 5.8 CFU/mL (2.6-958) for qPCR; a positive was read within 5 min of starting the Cas12a detection step. LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a was positive in 19/33 qPCR-positive and 0/19 qPCR-negative patients (positive and negative percent agreement 57.6% and 100%; kappa = 0.50); all 13 samples at or above the qPCR LOD(95) were detected. Conclusions: LAMP-CRISPR/Cas12a detects E. coli in whole blood specifically and rapidly, but its clinical sensitivity is limited by the very low bacterial loads of bacteraemia, so that it is suited to use as a rapid confirmatory test alongside blood culture rather than as a rule-out test.

title: Metadata-Driven Project-Level Analysis and Noise Modeling for Amplicon Sequencing Data Using CRISPResso2.
authors: Volodina, Olga; Smirnikhina, Svetlana
abstract: Here we present a lightweight workflow designed to improve the robustness and scalability of high-throughput amplicon sequencing analysis while leveraging CRISPResso2. To handle large batch processing without sensitive runtime interruptions, our pipeline processes samples sequentially, allowing the analysis to resume from the last successfully completed sample if an error occurs. The workflow implements a fallback mechanism for failed runs, automated extraction and separate processing of control samples, and a background noise model derived from control libraries within defined editing windows. Validation using spike-in datasets across Cas9, base editing, and prime editing demonstrated that our noise-adjusted estimates deviated from the ground truth by only 0.1-0.6%, whereas native CRISPResso2 caused a 1.5-3.7% overestimation. Unlike existing tools such as CRISPECTOR, which focus primarily on CRISPR-Cas9, our approach supports multiple editing modalities and enables project-level organization of large datasets. Input complexity is reduced through configurable flags and modular metadata tables, minimizing manual parameter entry. Together, these features provide a flexible, fault-tolerant, and highly accurate framework for analyzing large genome editing datasets.

title: Combined Effect of Hadron Therapy and PCSK9 Inhibition Therapy on the Immune Response in STK11-Deficient Lung Adenocarcinoma.
authors: Gantsova, Elena; Arutyunyan, Irina; Soboleva, Anna; Mikhailovskaia, Viktoriia; Kananykhina, Evgeniya; Artemova, Daria; Mironov, Kirill; Vishnyakova, Polina; Elchaninov, Andrey; Bao, Xuhui; Makarov, Andrey; Gordon, Konstantin; Fatkhudinov, Timur
abstract: Lung cancer is the most common type of cancer worldwide. Tumors carrying a mutation in the STK11 gene are associated with severe prognosis and resistance to therapy. New treatments for pulmonary adenocarcinoma highlight the efficacy of High-LET neutron therapy, often combined with drug therapy. PCSK9, whose inhibitors are used to treat dyslipidemia, may also be a new target in lung cancer therapy. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated STK11 mutation was performed in murine LLC1 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Human A549 cells that naturally carry a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the STK11 gene were also used. Cells were irradiated with protons, neutrons, and photons (2 Gy) and analyzed for survival, apoptosis, clonogenic survival assay, and evolocumab (PCSK9 inhibitor) sensitivity. In vivo xenograft (Nude) and syngeneic (C57BL/6) subcutaneous tumor models were neutron-irradiated (5 Gy). Tumor cell proliferation, microenvironment, and protein expression were assessed. High-LET irradiation confirmed the STK11-deficient lines radio resistance, which did not reduce under PCSK9 inhibitor treatment conditions in vitro. In animal models, the PCSK9 inhibitor decreased Ki67 index of tumor cells and infiltration of cancer-associated fibroblasts and macrophages in the combination therapy group. Particle therapy resistance serves as a crucial prognostic marker in the management of lung adenocarcinoma. Using cell lines and animal models, we successfully described this resistance phenotype and demonstrated the promising use of a PCSK9 inhibitor to enhance the efficacy of hadron radiotherapy against lung cancer.

title: Genome Editing for Earliness and Plant Architecture in Cucurbit Crops: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives.
authors: Wan, Lili; Wang, Zhuanrong; Ren, Jian; Wei, Jiaqi; Zeng, Hongxia; Li, Xiaoyong; Qu, Jiuhong; Xiong, Jianshun; Tang, Mi
abstract: Earliness and plant architecture are major breeding targets in cucurbit crops because they influence crop duration, early yield, planting density, canopy management, and production efficiency. This review summarizes genetic, molecular, and genome-editing advances related to flowering, sex expression, fruit development, stem elongation, branching, and canopy architecture in cucumber, melon, watermelon, Cucurbita species, and other cucurbits. Current evidence shows that earlier flowering or increased femaleness does not necessarily lead to earlier commercial maturity, while compact growth must be evaluated together with yield, fruit quality, and environmental adaptation. CRISPR/Cas9 knockout remains the most established editing approach, whereas base editing, cis-regulatory editing, multiplex editing, developmental-regulator-assisted regeneration, and DNA-free RNP delivery offer promising routes toward more precise trait optimization. Major constraints include genotype-dependent transformation, pleiotropic effects, limited validation in elite germplasm, and scarce direct evidence for shortening fruit-development duration. An evidence-guided framework is proposed that links trait definition, functional genomics, target prioritization, tailored genome editing, whole-plant evaluation, and breeding deployment. Future progress will depend on quantitatively tuned alleles and coordinated optimization of reproductive timing, canopy architecture, productivity, fruit quality, and environmental stability.

title: Raffinose in Brassica Crops: Integrating Plant Stress Physiology, Food Quality, Nutrition and Precision Breeding.
authors: Czernicka, Maria; Czernicka, Malgorzata
abstract: Raffinose-family oligosaccharides (RFOs) have nutritional and physiological significance that cannot be inferred from concentration alone. In Brassica, interpretation of their food value and definition of breeding targets require consideration of edible organ, environmental history, analytical resolution, and intended use. This critical review integrates evidence on RFO composition, plant physiology, food quality, and nutrition with an evidence-weighted assessment of conventional breeding, genetic transformation, and new genomic techniques. Direct Brassica experiments are distinguished from evidence derived from soybean and Arabidopsis and from prospective applications. Direct studies demonstrate that RFO metabolism in Brassica is manipulable, but they do not support a universal strategy for improving vegetable or meal quality. Genome-editing studies in soybean further show that reductions in total RFOs may coexist with increased raffinose and that lower RFO concentrations do not themselves demonstrate nutritional benefit. Tissue-specific regulation may offer a route to balance seed composition with stress responses, although genotype-dependent regeneration remains an important constraint. A three-tier framework is therefore proposed in which raffinose is interpreted as a stress-responsive metabolite, a potential food-quality indicator, and a context-dependent nutritional component. Compound-specific phenotyping, functional validation, and product-relevant physiological testing should precede deployment of low-RFO or stress-responsive Brassica material.

title: Genome-Wide Association Study Identifies Loci and a Candidate Gene Regulating Tomato Seed Germination.
authors: Liu, Chenxu; Zhu, Yihang; Miao, Jiashun; Wan, Hongjian; Yao, Zhuping; Ruan, Meiying; Ye, Qingjing; Li, Zhimiao; Zhou, Guozhi; Cheng, Yuan; Zhang, Xiaobin; Wang, Rongqing
abstract: Seed germination is the first critical transition in the plant life cycle, strongly influencing seedling establishment, crop uniformity, and subsequent productivity. However, the genetic basis of seed germination in tomato remains incompletely understood. Here, we performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) using 319 diverse tomato accessions to identify new loci and candidate genes associated with seed germination. Five significant variants were detected across the genome. Among them, SNP_59508294 on chromosome 3 was consistently associated with the seed germination index (SGI), and accessions carrying the GG haplotype exhibited a significantly higher SGI than those carrying the TT haplotype. Seven alpha-expansin (EXPA) genes were located within or near the associated interval. Integration of transcriptomic data from contrasting accessions and expression profiles across tomato tissues showed SlEXPA10 to be the most plausible candidate gene. The InDels in the SlEXPA10 promoter were highly associated with its low expression level in low SGI varieties. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of SlEXPA10 significantly reduced the rate and speed of seed germination relative to the wild type. Collectively, these results identify SlEXPA10 as a positive regulator of tomato seed germination and provide a candidate locus for improving seed vigor and emergence uniformity.

title: Genetic and Molecular Regulation of Seed Size in Brassica napus: Current Knowledge and Breeding Perspectives.
authors: Wang, Jin; Ashraf, Sana; Han, Yu; Long, Xinyao; Jiang, Wenlong; Atar, Hasan Huseyin; Ahmad, Mushtaq; Ma, Li; Zhang, Qinxue
abstract: Brassica napus L. (rapeseed), a member of the family Brassicaceae, is the world's third most important oilseed crop for edible oil production, after soybean and palm. Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping is a powerful strategy for dissecting the genetic basis of seed weight. In this review, Previous studies summarized a total of 1905 candidate genes associated with seed weight in Brassica napus. Five candidate genomic regions harboring 204 seed-weight-related genes were identified, among which 21 genes were characterized as differentially expressed genes via transcriptomic analysis. Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) mutant libraries targeting genes related to silique and seed size have been constructed in Brassica napus, revealing that BnaHRD genes play critical roles in seed development. These differentially expressed genes are involved in developmental processes, cell division. and nutrient storage, supporting their functions in seed size regulation. SHB1 and HAIKU2 modulate endosperm proliferation through the IKU pathway, thereby affecting seed weight. BZR1 (brassinazole-resistant 1) acts as a master regulator of seed growth via maternal tissues. Thidiazuron (TDZ), a cytokinin analogue, simultaneously promotes cell proliferation and cell expansion, thereby increasing cell number and cell size. Multiple phytohormone signaling pathways, including auxin, gibberellin (GA), and brassinosteroid (BR), as well as transcription factors such as LEC2, participate in the regulatory network of seed size. Here, we review current advances in the genetic and molecular regulation of seed size and discuss future perspectives for rapeseed breeding.

title: USP1, an MAPK Target with Chaperone-like Activity, Regulates Innate Plant Immunity in Arabidopsis.
authors: Manickam, Prabhu; Alhoraibi, Hanna; Veluchamy, Alaguraj; Almeida-Trapp, Marilia; Rayapuram, Naganand; Hirt, Heribert
abstract: In eukaryotes, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades are highly conserved signaling modules in transducing extracellular signals perceived by receptors/sensors. MAPKs phosphorylate cytoplasmic and nuclear target proteins, modifying their stability, protein-protein interaction, enzyme activity, DNA-binding affinity, and subcellular localization. A comparative phosphoproteomics analysis of wild-type and mapk mutant plants identified a previously uncharacterized protein, USP1, as a novel MAPK target. In this work, we investigated the role of USP1 in pathogen responses. CRISPR-Cas9-generated knockout usp1 mutants displayed enhanced resistance to the bacterial pathogen P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000, reduced apoplast reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and upregulated defense marker genes such as WRKY29 and FRK1. Transcriptome analyses revealed that immune hormone signaling genes, such as salicylic acid (SA) and jasmonic acid (JA), are differentially regulated. These hormones are responsible for primary defense responses against biotrophic and necrotrophic pathogens, respectively. Accordingly, usp1 mutants show enhanced and reduced resistance to bacterial and fungal infection by Pst DC3000 and Botrytis cinerea, respectively. Biochemical analyses showed that USP1 exhibits chaperone-like activity that stabilizes various proteins, including the MAPKs MPK4 and MPK6. Furthermore, usp1 mutants were defective in flg22-mediated immune priming, indicating that USP1 is required for the establishment of PAMP-induced immune memory. Collectively, our findings identify USP1 as a MAPK-regulated chaperone that plays an important role in coordinating plant immune responses.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics Analysis of the Response of Lycium barbarum 'Ningqi-1' to Powdery Mildew Infection and Functional Characterization of LbMLO6.
authors: Xu, Wendi; Luo, Lan; Wang, Jiaqi; Ren, Ruirui; Zhou, Jun; Wang, Cuiping; Qin, Ken; Li, Yanlong; Li, Yunxiang; Zhang, Xin; Wang, Jing; Si, Binbin; Duan, Linyuan; Dai, Guoli
abstract: Powdery mildew severely constrains the production of Lycium barbarum L., yet the molecular mechanisms underlying its response to infection remain poorly understood. Here, 'Ningqi-1' plants were inoculated with the powdery mildew pathogen and sampled at 0, 12, 24, and 48 hpi for integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses. Quantitative PCR and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing were further used to evaluate the candidate susceptibility gene LbMLO6. Infection induced extensive molecular reprogramming, yielding 1299 differentially expressed genes with sustained changes, 75 DAPs shared across all three time points, and 127 shared differentially accumulated metabolites. These molecules were mainly enriched in plant-pathogen interaction, plant hormone signal transduction, MAPK signaling, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and alpha-linolenic acid metabolism pathways, suggesting coordinated roles for Ca(2+) signaling, reactive oxygen species, defense-related proteins, and secondary metabolism in the host response. Integrated multi-omics analysis identified LbMLO6 as a candidate gene associated with powdery mildew susceptibility, its expression was markedly induced from 24 hpi onward. CRISPR/Cas9-edited LbMLO6 lines showed reduced fungal development compared with the control, particularly during the early stages of infection. These findings provide preliminary evidence that LbMLO6 may be associated with powdery mildew susceptibility in L. barbarum.

title: Engineering Modification Enhances the Antibacterial Activity of Yak Gastric Lysozyme and Its High-Level Expression in Pichia pastoris.
authors: Fan, Bing Bing; Zhang, An Rong; Wu, Zhen Long; Yang, Ying
abstract: To broaden the antibacterial spectrum of yak gastric lysozyme (YGL) against Gram-negative bacteria and improve its secretory expression in Pichia pastoris, this study employed a combined strategy of functional short-peptide fusion and host engineering. Four hydrophobic peptides, FFVAP, GVSLANWVCLAK, VVYP, and AWVAWK, were individually fused to the C-terminus of YGL, and the enzymatic activity and antibacterial performance of the modified proteins were compared. AW-YGL was subsequently selected for sequential optimization of the host strain, secretion signal peptide, endoplasmic-reticulum-associated molecular chaperones, and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9)-mediated host-gene knockout, followed by physicochemical stability evaluation of the optimized product. The results showed that AWVAWK modification produced the most pronounced enhancement of YGL activity against Gram-negative bacteria. AW-YGL exhibited inhibition rates of 65%, 68%, and 67% against Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Salmonella enteritidis, respectively. During expression-system optimization, the GS115 host significantly improved AW-YGL secretion, with total enzyme activity and specific activity in the culture supernatant reaching 3.1 x 10(5) U/L and 983 U/mg, respectively. Replacement with the HSS signal peptide further increased total enzyme activity to 4.3 x 10(5) U/L and specific activity to 1264 U/mg. Co-expression of the endoplasmic reticulum molecular chaperone binding immunoglobulin protein (BIP) further promoted functional AW-YGL expression, increasing the specific activity to 1560.3 U/mg. On this basis, knockout of the cell-wall-related gene FKS1 further increased the total enzyme activity in the culture supernatant to 6.9 x 10(5) U/L and the specific activity to 1638.3 U/mg, indicating that stepwise optimization of the signal peptide, folding assistance, and host-cell engineering effectively enhanced AW-YGL secretory expression and enzymatic activity. The optimized AW-YGL retained relatively high activity over defined pH and temperature ranges and showed tolerance to several metal ions and digestion-related proteases. Collectively, C-terminal fusion with hydrophobic short peptides enhanced the inhibitory activity of YGL against Gram-negative bacteria, while the combined strategies of signal-peptide optimization, folding assistance, and cell-wall engineering further improved its secretory expression in P. pastoris. These findings provide an experimental basis for the engineering and scalable production of novel broad-spectrum lysozymes.

title: Wine Yeast Engineering for Improved Polysaccharide Depolymerization and Reduced Urea Accumulation.
authors: Vasyagin, Egor A; Urakov, Valery N; Shalamitskiy, Maksim Yu; Cherviak, Sofia N; Semenova, Karina A; Lutkova, Natalia Yu; Beletsky, Alexey V; Rakitin, Andrey L; Mardanova, Eugenia S; Kushnirov, Vitaly V; Ravin, Nikolai V; Mardanov, Andrey V
abstract: Engineering wine yeasts to combine efficient extracellular polysaccharide degradation with reduced urea accumulation may support improvements in winemaking. This study aimed to replace the arginase-encoding CAR1 locus in the genome of the triploid industrial wine yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae I-328 with an expression cassette for the endopolygalacturonase gene PGU1, placed under the control of the PGK1 gene promoter and terminator. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome editing was performed using an acetamidase-selectable plasmid followed by phenotypic screening and molecular genetic verification. Whole genome sequencing confirmed the replacement of all three CAR1 alleles by the PGU1 expression cassettes. The modified strain I-328-Y21 showed enhanced degradation of polygalacturonic acid relative to the parental strain. Consistently, RT-qPCR analysis showed that the transcription level of the PGU1 gene in strain I-328-Y21 was about 300 times higher than in I-328. Disruption of arginase-the enzyme that generates urea from arginine-reduced urea content in the growth medium by about ninefold. As ethyl carbamate is formed from ethanol and yeast-excreted urea, this strain could help lower ethyl carbamate in wine. Fermentation performance and other technological characteristics remained unaffected by the genome editing. The new strain, in which the arginase gene is replaced by an endopolygalacturonase expression cassette, is a promising candidate for winemaking.

title: DAO2 Modulates Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid Accumulation in Germinating Brown Rice.
authors: Chen, Pingli; Liu, Xudong; Liu, Qing; Li, Chen; Sun, Bingrui; Yu, Hang; Jiang, Liqun; Mao, Xingxue; Zhang, Jing; Lv, Shuwei; Zhou, Yanfei; Yuan, Yilong; Naveed, Shahzad Amir; Khan, Muhammad Ramzan; Li, Jianxiong
abstract: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is a functional non-protein amino acid that regulates plant stress responses and signaling, while offering antihypertensive and hepatorenal benefits in humans. However, the genetic and molecular networks governing GABA accumulation during brown rice germination remain poorly understood. Here, we engineered DAO2 knockout rice lines using CRISPR/Cas9. Mutant brown rice exhibited significantly lower GABA levels alongside a marked accumulation of glutamate (Glu), glutamine (Gln), arginine (Arg), and proline (Pro) compared to the wild type (WT). Spatiotemporal profiling across seven germination intervals revealed that GABA titers peaked at 24 h in both the DAO2-1 mutant (24.24 mg/100 g) and WT (24.95 mg/100 g) before stabilizing. Notably, Glu levels were suppressed in DAO2-1 relative to WT during germination, whereas Pro showed the inverse trend. Transcriptomic analysis indicated substantial temporal variations in GABA metabolic gene expression between the two genotypes. The differences in expression level of OsGAD and OsGABA-T in DAO2-1 likely accounts for its diminished GABA capacity during early germination. These insights clarify the role of DAO2 within the regulatory network of rice GABA metabolism, providing a biochemical blueprint for optimized processing and the targeted breeding of GABA-enriched functional rice varieties.

title: Analysis of the Use of shRNA in Atherosclerosis Therapy: Current Status.
authors: Blagov, Alexander V; Maksaeva, Anastasia O; Kovyanova, Tatiana I
abstract: Atherosclerosis remains the principal pathological substrate of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke and peripheral artery disease, and its progression is driven by an interlocking set of processes, including hepatic and vascular lipid metabolism, chronic vascular inflammation, macrophage foam cell formation and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) proliferation, none of which is fully controlled by currently approved pharmacotherapy. Short hairpin RNA (shRNA) technology, in which a DNA template encoding a stem-loop transcript is delivered to a cell and processed intracellularly into small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that trigger sequence-specific mRNA degradation, offers a route to durable, vector-encoded gene silencing that is mechanistically distinct from transiently acting synthetic siRNA or antisense oligonucleotides and that, although non-permanent at the level of the target gene, is not readily reversible at the level of the vector, which cannot easily be withdrawn once administered. This review analyzes the current status of shRNA-based strategies for atherosclerosis therapy. We summarize the molecular mechanism and vector design principles of shRNA-mediated RNA interference (RNAi); critically examine preclinical studies in which shRNA delivered by lentiviral or adeno-associated viral (AAV) vectors has been used to silence hepatic lipid-metabolism genes (PCSK9, ApoB,), the endothelial gene ANGPTL2, inflammasome and inflammatory mediators (NLRP3, TACE/ADAM17), and genes driving VSMC proliferation in restenosis models (connexin 43); we explicitly distinguish this direct shRNA evidence from complementary target-validation studies that use antisense oligonucleotides (e.g., ANGPTL4), synthetic siRNA, genetic knockout, or antimiR approaches (e.g., lncRNA AK136714, CD36, miR-33, P2X7R); and discuss the principal delivery vectors, their tissue tropism, and the toxicity arising from saturation of the endogenous microRNA-processing machinery. We further place shRNA in the context of competing and complementary RNA-based and gene-editing modalities, including clinically approved synthetic siRNA drugs (inclisiran, patisiran) and CRISPR-based gene editing of PCSK9 and ANGPTL3, both of which have now yielded human phase 1 data, to clarify why, despite two decades of robust preclinical proof-of-concept, no shRNA construct has yet reached clinical use in atherosclerosis; we further compare this with the clinical trajectory of vector-encoded shRNA in other indications, in which anti-CCR5 and anti-HCV constructs have already been administered to patients in phase 1/2 trials, in order to establish that the limiting factor is not the hairpin itself but the risk-benefit case obtainable in a chronic, largely asymptomatic disease for which withdrawable and outcome-validated therapies already exist. We conclude that shRNA remains a mechanistically attractive but clinically immature modality whose translation will depend on vector engineering that limits off-target saturation of the RNAi pathway and achieves durable, cell type-restricted expression in the liver, endothelium, macrophages or vascular wall, and, equally, on the identification of an atherosclerosis indication-most plausibly a small, high-residual-risk or locally treatable population-in which durability outweighs the vector-level irreversibility, immunogenicity and manufacturing burden of a viral vector.

title: CRISPR-Based Engineering of Mesenchymal Stem Cells: Functional Enhancement, Translational Challenges, and Clinical Perspectives.
authors: Facicilia, Geofanny; Sartika, Cynthia Retna; Hadisaputri, Yuni Elsa; Rostinawati, Tina
