abstract: Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are promising platforms for regenerative and immunomodulatory therapies, but their clinical performance is limited by donor heterogeneity, variable potency, and limited persistence. CRISPR-based engineering provides programmable approaches to modify MSC function through genome editing and transcriptional regulation. This review examines CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout and knock-in, dCas9-based transcriptional regulation, and emerging base-, prime-, and epigenome-editing technologies for MSC engineering. These approaches can enhance survival and stress resistance, homing and tissue retention, paracrine and extracellular vesicle activity, immunomodulation, immune compatibility, and lineage-associated functions. Key translational challenges include efficient delivery, engineered-population heterogeneity, genomic safety, immunogenicity, phenotypic stability, scalable manufacturing, and mechanism-linked potency assessment. The appropriate engineering strategy should therefore be selected according to the intended therapeutic mechanism and product development requirements. Clinical translation will ultimately depend on demonstrating reproducible functional enhancement, manufacturing consistency, genomic and phenotypic stability, and validated therapeutic potency.

title: Matrix Metalloproteinase-2 Deficiency Impairs Eye Development in Crispant Zebrafish.
authors: Ren, Chenhui; Wei, Lu
abstract: Matrix metalloproteinase-2 (Mmp2, also known as gelatinase A) is a zinc-dependent endopeptidase, and mutations in human MMP2 can lead to some human diseases. However, the underlying function and mechanism of mmp2 during eye development are still unclear. The present study generated mmp2 crispant zebrafish by CRISPR/Cas9 system. Whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH), immunofluorescence, qRT-PCR, and transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses were performed. Results showed that mmp2 knockdown led to small eyes at 48-96 hpf (hours post-fertilization). WISH and qRT-PCR showed that mmp2 knockdown at 72 hpf (hours post-fertilization) significantly decreased the expression of cone-specific markers (opn1sw1, opn1sw2, opn1mw1, and opn1lw1), the rod-specific marker rhodopsin, retinal cell-specific markers (gnat1 and gnat2), and lens-specific markers (crybgx and crygm2c) in the retina. Immunofluorescence showed increased apoptosis (TUNEL(+) cells), ectopic localization of the neuronal differentiation marker HuC/D at the ciliary marginal zone, and decreased photoreceptor cells (Zpr1) and photoreceptor (RCVRN) fluorescence. Transcriptomic analysis indicated that 520 differentially expressed genes were enriched in phototransduction and retinol metabolism. Metabolomics analysis indicated that mmp2 knockdown led to abnormal lipid metabolism and amino acid metabolism. Integrated omics analysis revealed shared pathways involving PPAR signaling and nucleotide sugar metabolism, while correlation analysis highlighted strong associations between eye-development-related genes (e.g., gnat1, gnat2, opn1sw1) and specific metabolites such as 2-palmitoyl-rac-glycerol and 1-hexadecyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Mmp2 is essential for normal eye development in zebrafish, and its deficiency disrupts retinal cell survival, differentiation, and metabolic homeostasis, providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying Mmp2-associated ocular abnormalities.

title: Point-of-Care Testing for Aquatic Animal Disease Diagnosis: A Socio-Technical Review of Technologies Enabling Sustainable Aquaculture and Blue Food Security.
authors: Jiang, Na; Zhang, Yukun; Yu, Huanhuan; Zhang, Xiaoxiao
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Disease outbreaks are among the principal constraints on the sustainability of global aquaculture, yet diagnostic capacity remains concentrated in centralized laboratories far from the point of production. Point-of-care testing (POCT)-immunochromatographic strips, isothermal amplification (LAMP, RPA/RAA), CRISPR-Cas assays, microfluidics and biosensors-can compress the diagnosis-to-intervention window from days to about an hour. This structured narrative review draws on a documented search of the Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, PubMed and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure (2000-2026), with explicit inclusion criteria and a three-tier evidence-grading scheme (Section Review Methodology and Evidence Grading). We synthesize the evidence in the following three tiers: the technical landscape, comparing eight representative platform classes on sensitivity, turnaround, instrument dependence and deployment maturity; the application geography, tracing how POCT has entered pond-side screening, hatchery biosecurity, border inspection of live aquatic trade and IoT-based surveillance networks across East Asian freshwater, Indo-Pacific shrimp and North Atlantic salmonid systems, with markedly uneven evidence of routine adoption; and the bottlenecks that determine whether analytical performance becomes a sustainability outcome-sample-matrix interference, cold-chain dependence, the absence of unified field-performance standards (with WOAH diagnostic-kit registration suspended from May 2024 to May 2027), ambiguous legal status of POCT results, and smallholder affordability. Adopting a sustainability-transition perspective, we argue that the binding constraint is no longer assay chemistry but socio-technical governance, and that POCT should be positioned as enabling infrastructure for antimicrobial stewardship (SDG 3), loss avoidance and trade resilience (SDG 2/12), and aquatic ecosystem protection (SDG 14). We close with coordinated action imperatives for researchers, standard setters, policymakers and industry, including field-validation-first study designs and use of the 2024-2027 standards window to establish graded performance claims for on-site aquatic diagnostics.

title: Host Factor ANP32A in Avian Influenza Virus Replication and Cross-Species Adaptation: A Narrative Review.
authors: Li, Zeyu; Zhao, Shuang; Cao, Zhi; Song, Jiuzhou; Sun, Hongyan; Zuo, Qisheng; Han, Wei; Chen, Guohong; Li, Bichun; Jin, Kai
journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza virus undergoes continuous evolution with strengthened cross-species transmission capacity, posing a severe threat to global public health security. Host acidic nuclear phosphoprotein 32A (ANP32A) acts as a critical host cofactor for activating influenza viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and plays a central role in viral replication and host adaptation. This review systematically elaborates the molecular features of ANP32A, as well as the mechanism by which its leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domain specifically binds to the polymerase basic protein 2 (PB2) subunit and its low-complexity acidic region (LCAR) interacts with polymerase acidic protein (PA) to facilitate the assembly and functional activation of viral polymerase complexes. It also summarizes the influences of species-specific sequence variations and splicing isoforms of ANP32A on the host restriction barrier of cross-species transmission. Further analyses reveal that ANP32A indirectly modulates the transcriptional levels of genes related to interferons, NF-kappaB and NOD-like receptor pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasomes via chromatin epigenetic modification and transcriptional resource competition, remodeling the cellular antiviral microenvironment as a nuclear transcriptional regulator. ANP32A and acidic nuclear phosphoprotein 32B (ANP32B) exert complementary functions to support viral polymerase activity, while acidic nuclear phosphoprotein 32E (ANP32E) only provides weak auxiliary effects on a small subset of mutant influenza strains with its primary physiological function centered on chromatin regulation; the three proteins jointly participate in the regulatory network of viral replication. Drawing on recent advances in cryo-electron microscopy structural biology and CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technologies, which are discussed narratively in this review, this review highlights the pivotal hub role of ANP32A in viral host adaptation and cross-species spillover.

title: GRB2 Loss Attenuates Downstream TCR Effector Functions Despite Proximal ZAP-70 Hyper-Activation.
authors: Vico-Barranco, Inmaculada; Narbona-Sanchez, Isaac; Fernandez-Aguilar, Luis M; Garcia-Garcia, Ana; Carrasco, Manuel; Munoz-Fernandez, Raquel; Arbulo-Echevarria, Mikel M; Aguado, Enrique
abstract: The adapter protein GRB2 is central to T-cell receptor (TCR) signal transduction, yet its precise role in setting activation thresholds remains controversial. To clarify its functions, we generated stable GRB2-knockout (KO) Jurkat T-cell lines using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. Systematic analysis of TCR/CD3-stimulated GRB2-KO cells revealed widespread signaling hyper-activation: proximal ZAP-70 phosphorylation was drastically increased, and downstream signaling was markedly enhanced, evidenced by elevated ERK and PLC-gamma1 phosphorylation along with heightened intracellular Ca(2+) influx. In contrast, LAT phosphorylation was significantly decreased in GRB2-KO cells, indicating that GRB2 acts downstream or in parallel to constrain activation even when LAT phosphorylation is blunted. Intriguingly, loss of GRB2 was accompanied by reduced THEMIS protein expression, suggesting a potential link between GRB2 and THEMIS levels in human T cells. These findings support a role for GRB2 as an important negative gatekeeper of TCR signaling whose absence promotes hyperactivation despite reduced LAT phosphorylation, while to enhanced activation pathways while highlighting an intriguing association between GRB2 and THEMIS. Together, our results provide new mechanistic insights into the regulatory constraints governing human T-cell activation.

title: Zebrafish as a Model Organism in Space Biology Research.
authors: Er, Tianyi; Zhang, Chen; Wang, Ziming; Ruan, Sisi; Mao, Jian; Ma, Hong
abstract: As deep-space exploration advances, the health effects of the space environment have become a critical concern. Zebrafish (Danio rerio) have emerged as a valuable vertebrate model for space biology owing to their genetic tractability, optical transparency, and conserved organ systems. This review summarizes recent advances in using zebrafish to study spaceflight-associated health risks, focusing on ionizing radiation and altered gravity. We examine effects across the cardiovascular, nervous, musculoskeletal, sensory, reproductive, and other systems. Radiation induces cardiac dysfunction, neurobehavioral deficits, skeletal deformation, ocular damage, and reproductive toxicity, often through oxidative stress, apoptosis, and dysregulated signaling pathways. Microgravity and hypergravity primarily affect the musculoskeletal and vestibular systems, with microgravity reducing bone ossification and impairing otolith development. We also discuss current limitations, including the gap between ground-based simulations and actual space conditions, and the lack of combined-stressor studies. Finally, we highlight future directions, such as in-orbit live imaging, CRISPR/Cas9-based validation, and high-throughput countermeasure screening. This review aims to provide a theoretical framework for using zebrafish to assess space-environment-associated health risks and to inform research on health risks relevant to long-duration spaceflight.

title: BmS6K Regulates Growth and Survival Traits of Silkworm, Bombyx mori.
authors: Wan, Linrong; Yin, Bowen; Xi, Rui; Wen, Yuanyuan; Wang, Lin; Liu, Mengyan; Tong, Xiaoling; Long, Dingpei; Dai, Fangyin
abstract: Ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K) is a conserved effector of the mTOR signaling pathway that regulates cell growth and metabolism. The organism-level function of S6K in the silkworm Bombyx mori has not yet been examined by direct genetic manipulation. Here, we combined CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout, piggyBac-based transgenic re-expression and overexpression, and multi-tissue RNA-seq with weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) to characterize the role of BmS6K in vivo. BmS6K-null mutants were viable but showed 26.5% and 28.6% reductions in pupal weight in males and females, respectively. Furthermore, mutant survival rates were 44.2% (males) and 28.5% (females) lower than those of controls, with mortality concentrated at the late fifth larval stage. Targeted transgenic re-expression rescued these phenotypic defects. Conversely, overexpressing BmS6K in a wild-type background increased the larval growth rate by 16.9% and significantly raised both whole cocoon weight and pupal weights. WGCNA of the three tissue types identified a core co-expression module (MEred) that was significantly enriched for genes involved in proton-transporting V-type ATPase activity and vacuolar complex assembly, mTOR signaling, and oxidative phosphorylation coupled to cellular redox homeostasis, including BmV1-ATPase, BmGabaT, and BmNadDac, whose orthologs represent core components or mediate critical cross-talk in the TOR-S6K pathway, a function conserved in Drosophila and mammals. Since the loss and gain of BmS6K produced opposite effects on growth and viability, it can be regarded as a candidate target for increasing cocoon yield in sericulture, as well as a target for RNAi-based control of lepidopteran pests through the suppression of its orthologs.

title: A Novel Function of Tubulin beta2a and Tubulin beta3 in Regulating Metastatic Properties in Bone-Metastatic Breast Cancer Cells.
authors: Patel, Shreya; Winogradzki, Marcus; Gant, Kayla M; Hazime, Danielle; Arra, Sai Srujana; Patel, Niyati; Blank, Alan T; Pratap, Jitesh
abstract: Background/Objectives: Bone metastasis (BM) occurs in approximately 70% of patients with advanced breast cancer (BCa) and is associated with limited treatment options and a median survival of only 19-25 months. Although microtubule (MT)-targeting agents such as paclitaxel remain a standard therapy, their efficacy is often limited by chemoresistance linked to in part by altered beta-tubulin isotype expression. Among these, tubulin beta2a and tubulin beta3 (encoded by TUBB2A and TUBB3) have been linked to poor clinical outcomes; however, their roles in breast cancer bone metastasis (BMBC) remain unclear. Here, we investigated the functional significance of TUBB2A and TUBB3 in regulating MT dynamics and metastatic behavior in bone-derived BCa cells. Methods: TUBB2A and TUBB3 expression levels were evaluated in primary breast tumors and bone metastases. CRISPR-mediated TUBB2A knockout and TUBB3 depletion were performed in bone-derived MDA-MB-231 cells to assess microtubule dynamics, trafficking, metastatic phenotypes, and gene expression. Results: Elevated expression of both TUBB2A and TUBB3 correlated with reduced patient survival. Immunohistochemical analyses demonstrated increased tubulin beta2a abundance in BM lesions relative to matched primary breast tumors, while the proportion of moderate-to-strong tubulin-beta3-positive cells was also increased in BM. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout/knockdown in a bone-derived MDA-MB-231 cell model, we found that loss of TUBB2A or partial depletion of TUBB3 impaired MT regrowth, altered the cell cycle, and disrupted endosomal trafficking, characterized by enlarged perinuclear Rab5-positive vesicles. Functionally, depletion of either isotype reduced cell migration and invasion while enhancing adhesion, accompanied by increased expression of integrin beta4, beta5, alpha4, alpha5, and talin-1. Exploratory RNA-seq analysis suggests enrichment of cytokine-cytokine receptor signaling pathways, consistent with a potential link between MT remodeling and inflammatory/secretory programs. Conclusions: Collectively, these findings identify TUBB2A and TUBB3 as regulators of metastatic phenotypes and potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets in BMBC.

title: Phosphatidylserine modulation influences syncytia formation in human breast cancer cell lines.
authors: Sieler, Mareike; Huwa, Leonie; Keil, Silvia; Kneissig, Maja; Dittmar, Thomas
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cell-cell fusion is a biological process, crucial for the development and homeostasis of tissue. In contrast, cell fusion is also pathologically associated with viral infections or cancer cell fusion. While physiological cell fusion is strictly regulated, is it not clear how and why cancer cells fuse with other cells. Since the resulting cancer hybrid cells can have new malignant properties, like chemotherapeutic resistance or an enhanced metastatic potential, it is of interest to get to know how cancer cell fusion takes place. METHODS: A breast cancer cell fusion model, relying on the dual split protein cell fusion assay and overexpression of the fusogen Syncytin-1, was used to study the impact of the membrane lipid phosphatidylserine (PS) and lipid distributing proteins. Therefore, the breast epithelial cell line M13SV1 was cocultured with the breast cancer cell lines MDA-MB-231 or HS578T. To mask PS, we added the PS-binding protein Annexin V in the coculturing medium. The most prominent expressed scramblase Ano6/TMEM16F was investigated using the clinically used substances Niclosamide, Clofazimine, Salinomycin and Hexachlorophene to indirectly or directly inhibit the protein's activity. In addition, Ano6 was knocked-out using CRISPR/Cas9. The flippase Atp8a1 was simultaneously overexpressed with its cofactor CDC50a and assays assessing the tumorigenic properties as well as the cell fusion capacity of the differently treated or altered cells were done. RESULTS: While Annexin V was able to significantly decrease Syncytin-1-mediated cell fusion, the four substances Niclosamide, Clofazimine, Salinomycin and Hexachlorophene did not affect the amount of phosphatidylserine on the cells' surface or their capacity to fuse with other cells. The Ano6/TMEM16F KO as well as the Atp8a1-CDC50a overexpression showed rather non-significant effects on the cell fusion. CONCLUSION: Although the effects were mainly non-significant, it was shown, that Syncytin-1-mediated cell fusion could be decreased when M13SV1 cells overexpressing Syncytin-1 were overexpressing Atp8a1-CDC50a, suggesting that less PS in the membrane of these cells is causing the decrease in cell fusion. Vice versa, the loss of Ano6 or the overexpression of Atp8a1-CDC50a in the breast cancer cell lines was able to increase Syncytin-1-mediated cell fusion. This suggests the hypothesis that the localization of PS during fusion may be dynamic and that externalized PS may enhance the function of Syncytin-1 on the expressing cell, while it appears to disrupt cell fusion when exposed on the neighboring cell.

title: Correction to: An Overview of Programmable Epigenetic Editing Based on CRISPR Tools for Gene Expression Regulation.
authors: Djordjevic, Marija; Dinic, Svetlana; Saric, Ana; Uskokovic, Aleksandra; Vidakovic, Melita

title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism.
authors: Chen, George T; Nair, Gayatri; Osorio, Aubrey J; Holley, Sandra M; Ghassemzadeh, Kimiya; Zhou, Yixuan; Gonzalez, Jose; Martin, Jacqueline M; Lu, Congyi; Sanjana, Neville E; Cepeda, Carlos; Geschwind, Daniel H
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: How to train your microbe: editing environmental bacteria.
authors: Flaig, Maximilian L; Hardwick, Molly M J; Burmolle, Mette; Alker, Amanda T P
abstract: Genome editing is an essential tool in microbiology, enabling researchers to assess gene function, link genotype to phenotype, and design microbes with specific features. Most tools have been developed in model bacteria, and adapting them to environmental species remains time- and resource-intensive. This review provides a framework for engineering environmental bacteria, including assessment of genetic tractability, considerations for overcoming challenges in recalcitrant systems, and an overview of techniques with guidance on tool selection. We discuss the emerging field of microbiome editing, where genome modifications can be delivered to bacteria within complex microbial communities and hosts, opening new possibilities for mechanistic studies across diverse environments. These advances promise to shift functional microbiology from reductionist, isolate-based approaches toward contextually informed, mechanistic investigations.

title: Deletion of the immune evasion gene gG enhances cellular immunity and protective efficacy of the quadruple-deleted feline herpesvirus type 1 recombinant FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE/gG.
authors: Gao, Jianuo; Yang, MengFang; Fang, Lingying; Wu, Benyuan; Hu, Xiaoshuai; Liu, Zirui; Shi, Jiale; Zhang, Yidan; Hou, YunLong; Li, Mengxia; Shen, Zhou; Peng, Guiqing
abstract: Feline herpesvirus type 1 (FHV-1) causes feline viral rhinotracheitis (FVR), which can cause severe disease in kittens. Our previously developed recombinant virus, FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE, provided enhanced protection compared with existing vaccines; however, its protective efficacy requires further improvement. Therefore, optimization of this vaccine by deleting additional nonvirulence genes involved in immune evasion is warranted. Glycoprotein G (gG) of alphaherpesviruses has been implicated in immune evasion, but its role in FHV-1 immune modulation and vaccine efficacy remains unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that gG overexpression significantly downregulated the expression of chemokines, including CCL and CXCL family members, interferon-beta (IFN-beta), and interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), whereas gG deletion partially alleviated this suppression. Subsequently, a recombinant virus designated FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE/gG was generated by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of the gG gene from the FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE backbone. The resulting recombinant virus exhibited growth kinetics comparable to those of FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE in vitro. FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE/gG was safe in kittens, and subcutaneous prime-boost immunization provided enhanced protection against the virulent FHV-1 WH2020 strain. Compared with control kittens, those vaccinated with FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE/gG exhibited milder clinical signs, lower viral loads in tissues, significantly elevated serum IFN-gamma levels, and significantly upregulated expression of chemokines and innate immune factors in the nasal turbinates following challenge. Collectively, these findings suggest that FHV-1 gG contributes to the suppression of host innate immune responses and its deletion from DeltaTK/gI/gE backbone enhances cellular immunity, thereby improving protection against challenge and reducing wild-type viral colonization in tissues. FHV-DeltaTK/gI/gE/gG represents a promising live attenuated vaccine candidate against FHV-1.

title: Recent advances in design strategies for rapid mycoplasma detection: Towards point-of-care testing.
authors: Xu, Zhe; Yuan, Yi; Ye, Tingsong; Gong, Xuelin; Li, Dengran; Ding, Yi; Li, Zhengdong; Chen, Rongjie; Deng, Xuemei; Li, Yinjie; He, Kui; Liu, Xiao; Cui, Rongwei; Li, Danyang; Xu, Lizhou
abstract: Mycoplasma pathogens present significant challenges for clinical point-of-care testing (POCT) due to their pathogenicity, public health implications, and the limitations of conventional detection methods. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in rapid mycoplasma detection technologies, with emphasis on sensing design principles, technical bottlenecks, innovative solutions, and clinical performance. Three major technology systems are comprehensively discussed: (1) Molecular diagnostic platforms, focusing on optimization strategies for non-CRISPR isothermal amplification and CRISPR/Cas-based systems that leverage collateral cleavage for ultra-sensitive detection; (2) Emerging biosensing technologies, encompassing colorimetric, fluorescence, and electrochemical modalities, with detailed analysis of transducer functionalization and signal transduction mechanisms; and (3) Lateral flow assays (LFAs), highlighting innovative signal amplification strategies for rapid nucleic acid and antigen/antibody testing. Furthermore, the integration of mass spectrometry (MS) with metabolomics for high-throughput metabolic profiling is examined. Finally, we discuss the core challenges of mycoplasma POCT, including sample preparation, matching detection technologies to the unique biological traits of Mycoplasma, and use cases such as at-home testing. Building on these challenges, we also outline future prospects: discrimination between viable and non-viable organisms, resistance-informed testing, and device-level integration. These insights collectively define a roadmap for next-generation 'sample-to-answer' POCT devices. This review aims to bridge the gap between laboratory innovation and clinical diagnostics for mycoplasma management.

title: Rapid genotyping of FecB mutation in sheep using CRISPR-Cas12a orthology-assisted assay.
authors: Li, Sheng; Shi, Suyu; Yang, Jie; Xing, Dan; Wang, Yuan; Deng, Manfei; Ruan, Jinxue; Li, Xinyun; Xu, Zhenfei; Tao, Dagang; Xie, Shengsong
abstract: Accurate genotyping of the Fecundity Booroola (FecB) gene, a key determinant of ovine fecundity, is essential for effective breeding programs. However, current methods are largely constrained by their reliance on specialized equipment and high operational costs, which collectively limit their applicability for large-scale, on-site genetic screening. To address these challenges, we systematically evaluated five Cas12a orthologs and identified Gs12-19 as the optimal candidate. Based on this, we developed a novel detection platform integrating the CRISPR-Gs12-19 system with allele-specific amplification and fluorescence-based signal readout, which enables discrimination between homozygous wild-type sheep (AA) and FecB mutation carriers (AG or GG, collectively designated as RG). Coupled with a portable blue-light excitation device and a custom-designed Red Channel Quantification (RedQ) analytical program, the platform was field-tested on 153 randomly selected samples from a core crossbred sheep population. The method achieved 98% accuracy in mutation-carrier classification when benchmarked against Sanger sequencing. Collectively, this study offers a rapid, visually interpretable, and field-deployable platform for FecB mutation-carrier screening with high sensitivity and specificity, providing a practical solution to accelerate marker-assisted selection in sheep breeding.

title: Intelligent Modular Dual-Readout Architecture Driven by CRISPR/Cas13a-CHA Cascade and Machine Learning for Portable Multiplex MicroRNA Liquid Biopsy in Early Lung Cancer.
authors: Fan, Min; Ji, Xiangrui; Chen, Jingbo; Ding, Yun; Feng, Shangyuan; Lin, Jinlan; Guo, Tianxing
abstract: Precise detection of trace miRNAs in liquid biopsies is critical for early lung cancer screening, yet current methods are frequently limited by complex reverse transcription procedures and potential enzymatic amplification biases. Herein, we developed a sequencing-free and highly portable dual-mode biosensing platform for decentralized clinical diagnostics by synergizing highly specific CRISPR/Cas13a recognition with exponential non-enzymatic catalytic hairpin assembly amplification (CHA). Trace target miRNAs activate Cas13a to trans-cleave the RNA trigger strand, while intact RNA triggers can precisely initiate downstream assembly networks. The Cas13a molecular lock completely eliminates spontaneous hairpin crosslinking interference. Based on this mechanism, we separately constructed a fluorescence and a multiplex surface-enhanced Raman scattering biosensing platform. The catalytic network drives reporter-embedded bimetallic nanoparticles to specifically bind plasmonic chips, forming sandwich resonance structures for absolute multiplex spectral quantification. The system synchronously processes and analyzes four lung cancer-associated miRNAs within 80 min, achieving an ultralow attomolar diagnostic limit and an exceptionally broad linear dynamic range spanning ten orders of magnitude. Clinical validation using 50 plasma samples demonstrated high quantitative agreement with standard qRT-PCR alongside exceptional anti-interference characteristics. Integrating a machine classification model to extract spectral features successfully clustered distinct pathological stages with the accuracy of 80.00 and 93.33%, respectively. The systematic framework, merging miniature programmable biochemical cascade pathways with multidimensional artificial intelligence predictions, provides a highly powerful novel diagnostic paradigm to overcome traditional barriers in complex liquid biopsy translational applications.

title: Noncanonical enhancers control gene expression and cell fate in human pluripotent stem cells.
authors: Cao, Yang; Dovgusha, Oleksandr; Ebrahimi, Ayyub; Cruz, Carmela Rieline V; Bevan, Stephen; Widmer, Lukas; Torabi, Fereshteh; Kurlovich, Julia; Rodriguez-Polo, Ignacio; Khan, Soumen; Patel, Manthan; Shiels, Oliver T; Pradeepa, Madapura M; Flynn, Sean M; Gunesdogan, Ufuk; Schoenfelder, Stefan
abstract: Enhancers are key gene regulatory elements that ensure the precise spatiotemporal execution of developmental gene expression programs. However, recent findings indicate that current approaches to identify enhancers may not capture the full repertoire of active enhancers in mammalian genomes. Here, we combine massively parallel enhancer assays with chromatin structure and transcriptome profiling to functionally annotate enhancers genome-wide in human induced pluripotent stem cells. We find that a substantial fraction ( approximately 40%) of accessible chromatin regions with enhancer function lack key features associated with active enhancers, including the active enhancer mark histone H3 lysine-27 acetylation and enhancer-associated RNAs. Perturbation of this class of noncanonical enhancers by CRISPR-mediated epigenome editing or deletion results in decreased levels of target gene expression and, in one instance, loss of pluripotent stem cell characteristics. Collectively, our data demonstrate enhancer activity for a class of gene regulatory elements that had, until now, only been associated with a neutral or inactive status, challenging current models of enhancer function.

title: Aneuploidy impairs B cell development but accelerates their MYC-driven transformation.
authors: Weiss, Johannes G; Petermann, Paul Y; Rigato, Irene; Lohmuller, Michael; Honold, Felix; Schapfl, Marina; Spock, Sarah; Kinz, Nadine; Tijhuis, Andrea E; Wardenaar, Rene; Losito, Marilu; Foijer, Floris; Rizotto, Dario; Schubert, Michael; Herzog, Sebastian; Riley, Joel S; Labi, Verena; Finotello, Francesca; Villunger, Andreas
abstract: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is an established driver of aneuploidy and cell death. Here, we investigate the role of apoptosis as a barrier against CIN-driven aneuploidy in B lymphocytes. We found that impairment of their spindle assembly checkpoint via deletion of Mitotic Arrest Deficient 2-Like 1 or mutation of Monopolar Spindle 1 kinase curtails B cell survival. A CRISPR screen identified intermediates of mitochondrial apoptosis as critical, which we confirmed in vivo by overexpression of a B cell-restricted BCL2 transgene, outperforming loss of P53. Notably, cell death inhibition by BCL2 was insufficient to cause aneuploidy-driven B cell transformation, while loss of P53 strongly synergized with tumors featuring stochastic aneuploidies. In contrast, high cell death rates rapidly select for specific karyotypes, facilitating aneuploid tumor cell survival in Emu-Myc transgenic mice. Hence, cell death inhibition fails to allow CIN-driven aneuploidies to prevail. In contrast, BCL2-regulated apoptosis selects viable aneuploid tumor karyotypes in the presence of oncogenic MYC, a notion with implications for the clinical use of BCL2-targeting therapies.

title: GEX1-mediated semigamy induces both maternal and paternal haploids in cotton.
authors: Li, Tengyu; Pan, Jingwen; Li, Yan; Yao, Jinbo; Fang, Shengtao; Cao, Zongpeng; Zhu, Shouhong; Zhang, Yongshan; Chen, Wei
abstract: How semigamy generates haploids during double fertilization has remained elusive for more than six decades. Here, we identify Gamete Expressed 1 (GEX1) as the gene underlying semigamy and show that it mediates dual-origin haploid induction in cotton. A naturally occurring mutation in GEX1 disrupts normal nuclear membrane fusion during fertilization, resulting in delayed or incomplete karyogamy. Cytological analyses reveal that delayed karyogamy allows the closely apposed but unfused gametic nuclei to undergo independent mitotic divisions, giving rise to maternal haploids, paternal haploids, and chimeric progeny. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated disruption of GEX1 reproduced the characteristic defects in nuclear fusion and enabled both maternal and paternal haploid induction within a single generation. Together, our findings uncover a genetically tractable mechanism underlying semigamy that links nuclear membrane fusion dynamics to haploid formation and establish a versatile strategy for rapidly generating doubled haploids from both parental genomes to accelerate crop breeding.

title: Base editing-mediated precision genome engineering in Toxoplasma gondii.
authors: Liu, Fang; Wu, Youlan; Chen, Zhenghe; Liu, Xiang; Yu, Li; Shen, Jilong; Xu, Yuanhong; Yuan, Jing; Li, Jiabin; Cheng, Weisheng
abstract: Functional genomics in Toxoplasma gondii (T. gondii), an obligate intracellular parasite of global medical importance, primarily relies on CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene disruption. However, conventional CRISPR-Cas9 editing relies on generating double-strand breaks (DSBs), which are repaired either by error-prone non-homologous end joining or by homology-directed repair requiring donor templates and time-consuming clone isolation. Here, we established the first two base editor platforms in T. gondii: adenine base editors (ABEs) and cytosine base editors (CBEs), which enable precise point mutations via direct base conversion without DSBs or donor templates. We successfully employed ABE and CBE to introduce high-efficiency A > G and C > T conversions at defined genomic loci, respectively. By targeting the critical virulence gene ROP18, we demonstrate that ABE-mediated i-Silence (start codon disruption) and CBE-mediated i-STOP (premature stop codon introduction) strategies can efficiently generate functional T. gondii null mutants. The resulting base-edited parasite strains exhibited a complete loss of ROP18 protein expression and showed attenuated virulence and proliferation phenotypes equivalent to those of a conventional ROP18 knockout strain, as validated in both cellular and mouse models. We then conducted a genome-wide analysis predicting that the i-Silence and i-STOP strategies enable targeted inactivation of nearly all genes in the T. gondii genome (>99.6% coverage). Since our approach does not require DSBs, it enables researchers to achieve efficient, precise nucleotide substitutions without the risk of chromosomal rearrangements. We propose base editing as a powerful genetic tool in T. gondii, paving the way for high-resolution functional pathogenesis studies and the further development of genetically stable attenuated vaccines.

title: Population structure of group B Streptococcus from semen reveals virulent and resistant lineages with implications for surveillance.
authors: Merces, Ana Clarisse; Costa, Natalia Silva; Oliveira, Laura Maria Andrade; Botelho, Ana Caroline Nunes; Barros, Laylla Graca; Silva, Luisa de Miranda Basto; Teixeira, Lucia Martins; Fracalanzza, Sergio Eduardo Longo; Khan, Uzma; Bentley, Stephen; Jamrozy, Dorota; Pinto, Tatiana Castro Abreu
abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a major agent of perinatal infections. Although extensively studied as a pathogen in pregnant individuals and neonates, little is known about GBS from male adults, despite occasional reports of its occurrence in semen. We characterized 120 GBS isolates obtained from semen samples in Brazil between 2017 and 2022 to determine serotypes, antimicrobial susceptibility profile, virulence-associated determinants, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) diversity and phylogenetic relationships with isolates from other clinical sources. Serotype V was the most frequent, followed by Ia, Ib, III, II and IV. Resistance was observed for tetracycline (84.1%), erythromycin (30.8%), levofloxacin (8.3%) and 12.5% exhibited multidrug resistance (MDR). The most common sequence types (STs) were ST1, ST144 and ST19. The isolates clustered into five major clonal complexes (CC1, CC17, CC19, CC23 and CC24) and six singletons. Serotypes, antimicrobial resistance and virulence-associated determinants markers varied across CCs. Resistance determinants detected included tetM, mefA, msrD, ermA and ermB. Levofloxacin-resistant isolates contained mutations in gyrA and/or parC and were predominantly linked to the serotype V/ST19 lineage. All isolates except one carried at least one alpha-like protein (Alp) gene. Phylogenetic analysis of isolates from semen, rectovaginal samples, urine and invasive infections showed that isolates clustered according to CC regardless of clinical source. CRISPR1 analysis revealed intra-clonal diversity, as isolates within the same CC displayed different CRISPR compositions. These findings indicate that GBS isolates recovered from semen belong to established GBS lineages also identified in other clinical sources and support the co-circulation of GBS lineages across different human niches.

title: Integrative CRISPR-Cas9 dependency analysis identifies CDC45 as a candidate prognostic biomarker with preliminary functional validation in prostate adenocarcinoma.
authors: Xie, Yuxin; Wang, Shuo; Gao, Yukui
abstract: Prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) has become one of the most prevalent malignancies in men worldwide. Although advances in diagnostic techniques and targeted therapies have improved clinical outcomes, a significant subset of patients still develops aggressive, metastatic disease with limited treatment options. At present, identifying reliable biomarkers for early risk stratification remains a critical unmet need in prostate cancer research. This study presents a dependency-informed prognostic prioritization approach by integrating multi-omics data to enhance clinical risk stratification in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD). Integrated analysis of CRISPR-Cas9 dependency screens and bulk RNA sequencing data prioritized tumor-dependent genes associated with PRAD cell viability. Pathway enrichment analysis indicated the involvement of these candidate genes in cell cycle regulation and tumor progression. Subsequently, an 11-gene prognostic signature was constructed via LASSO regression, effectively stratifying patients, with the high-risk cohort demonstrating significantly reduced Progression-Free Interval (PFI; log-rank p < 0.001). Among the prioritized hub genes, CDC45 exhibited marked upregulation in tumor tissues, which was confirmed by Western blotting and qRT-PCR. Collectively, this study provides a dependency-informed prognostic framework for PRAD and nominates CDC45 as a candidate prognostic biomarker, laying the groundwork for future mechanistically resolved investigations.

title: Recent approaches to modulate citrinin biosynthesis in Monascus species: a review.
authors: Mahesh, Trupthi; Subburamu, Karthikeyan; Sundaram, Senthilarasu; Rajendran, Poorniammal; Subramanian, Marimuthu; Vishwas, Pawale Amol
abstract: The filamentous fungi Monascus spp. are rich sources of secondary metabolites that include Monascus azaphilone pigments, monacolin K, and gamma-aminobutyric acid, making them significant in the food, nutraceutical, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries. Despite the industrial importance of this fungus, its production of citrinin, a nephrotoxic polyketide mycotoxin, remains a major drawback and limits its commercial application. Recent research studies have shown that the mechanism that governs citrinin biosynthesis highlights the interactions between Biosynthetic Gene Clusters (BGCs), epigenetic modifications, global regulatory networks, and environmental factors. The current understanding of the molecular and epigenetic mechanisms used to mitigate citrinin production in Monascus spp. is discussed in this review. Emphasis is given on histone acetylation and deacetylation, methylation, chromatin remodeling, the velvet complex, and the modulation of toxin biosynthesis through RNA-level gene expression control. The recent advances are critically evaluated for engineering citrinin-free strains, including transcriptomics, proteomics, multi-omics, RNA interference, CRISPR/Cas genome editing, and synthetic biology. The comparative analysis of these approaches shows that integrating epigenetic engineering with advanced genome and metabolic engineering can regulate citrinin while maintaining other important metabolite yields. Combining multi-omics and artificial intelligence-guided strain design with epigenetic interventions will accelerate the development of safe, sustainable, and high-yielding Monascus-assisted bioprocesses.

title: Gene Therapy: Advances in Delivery Systems, Genome Editing Technologies, and Applications in Human and Veterinary Medicine.
authors: Chandran, Deepak; Appanasamy, Ramanathan; Mohankumar, Pran; Sukumaran, Sreyass Kallemoochikkal; Saleena, Lejaniya Abdul Kalam
abstract: Gene therapy has emerged as a revolutionary therapeutic strategy for the treatment of inherited, acquired, and age-related diseases through the modification, replacement, or correction of defective genes. Advances in molecular biology, viral engineering, and genome-editing technologies have significantly enhanced the efficiency and safety of gene delivery systems. This review provides a comprehensive overview of gene therapy, including its classification, delivery methods, and therapeutic applications in both human and veterinary medicine. Viral vectors such as adenoviral, retroviral, lentiviral, adeno-associated viral, and poxviral vectors remain the most effective delivery platforms owing to their high transduction efficiency, whereas non-viral approaches including physical and chemical delivery systems offer improved biosafety and reduced immunogenicity. Recent developments in gene-editing technologies, particularly clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated protein systems, have expanded the therapeutic potential of gene therapy by enabling precise genome modifications. The review highlights the successful application of gene therapy in treating genetic disorders, cancer gene therapy, retinal diseases, neuromuscular disorders, hemophilia, and metabolic diseases in humans, as well as inherited and acquired diseases in companion and livestock animals. Despite remarkable progress, challenges related to delivery efficiency, immune responses, off-target effects, manufacturing scalability, regulatory approval, and long-term safety continue to limit widespread clinical implementation. Advances in vector design, genome-editing precision, artificial intelligence-assisted development, and regulatory frameworks are expected to address these limitations. Overall, gene therapy and CRISPRbased technologies represent promising platforms for the development of next-generation precision medicines that could transform disease management in both human and veterinary healthcare.

title: Pulmonary Ionocytes Regulate CFTR-Mediated Chloride Transport in Human iPSC-Derived Epithelium.
authors: Rollins, Stuart D; Yeboah, Ruth-Love; Tang, Yang; Wu, Sharon; Yin, Jianing; Little, Alice; Fatima, Anam; Johnson, Casey R; Kotton, Darrell N; Thiagarajah, Jay R; Schlaeger, Thorsten M; Wang, Ruobing
journal: American journal of respiratory cell and molecular biology
abstract: RATIONALE: Pulmonary ionocytes, representing approximately 1% of airway epithelial cells, exhibit high CFTR expression and unique transcriptional markers, including FOXI1, ASCL3, and V-ATPase. Their exact role in human airway physiology is incompletely understood. OBJECTIVE: This study employs induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived airway epithelial models (iPSC-airways) to elucidate the role of FOXI1 in pulmonary ionocyte differentiation and function. METHODS: CRISPR-Cas9 was used to generate FOXI1-knockout iPSCs, into which a doxycycline-inducible FOXI1-overexpression cassette was introduced. Edited and control lines were differentiated into airway epithelia to evaluate ionocyte formation, epithelial composition, and ion transport. Rescue studies assessed the effects of FOXI1 re-expression in a FOXI1-KO background, and the addition of inducible WT-CFTR ionocytes to F508del/F508del cystic fibrosis (CF) cultures on restoring chloride transport. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: FOXI1 deletion abolishes ionocyte formation and alters airway epithelial composition, with increased mucus-secreting goblet cells and decreased ciliated cells. Functional assays confirmed ionocytes as key regulators of chloride homeostasis, with FOXI1-deficient airways displaying diminished ion transport. Induction of FOXI1-overexpression restored CFTR-mediated chloride transport. Introduction of WT ionocytes into CF airway models rescued chloride transport deficits, with no rescue observed in vehicle-treated controls lacking ionocyte induction. CONCLUSIONS: These findings highlight FOXI1's essential role in pulmonary ionocyte development, airway cell composition, and airway chloride transport. We present a fully manipulable, gene-edited iPSC-derived system that enables investigation of ionocyte biology and function within a human airway context, highlighting them as promising therapeutic targets for respiratory disorders.

title: Biological Functions of Phytosulfokine Signaling in Plants.
authors: Alabd, Ahmed; Wang, Xuxu
abstract: Peptide hormones are signaling molecules that play a crucial role in regulating diverse physiological processes underlying plant growth, development, and stress adaptation. Among these, the widely distributed peptide hormone phytosulfokine (PSK) has emerged as a key regulatory factor. Here, we provide a brief overview of the biosynthesis and characteristics of PSKs. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive overview of the methodologies for predicting and identifying PSKs in plants and the diverse functions of PSKs in plants. We examine how PSKs govern critical biological processes, including plant growth, root development, and reproduction, and further explore their emerging roles in fruit ripening, senescence, and the mitigation of chilling injury. In addition, the involvement of PSK in both biotic and abiotic stress responses is discussed. Despite significant progress in identifying PSK-related genes through high-throughput approaches, the functional characterization of many remains incomplete. Future research should focus on the application of advanced genetic engineering techniques, such as overexpression, RNA interference, and CRISPR/Cas9, to validate gene functions, elucidate regulatory mechanisms, and identify key transcription factors downstream of PSK signaling. A more comprehensive understanding of these processes will provide a solid foundation for the development of PSK-based strategies in agricultural applications.

title: CRISPR opens the door to targeted therapy against glioblastoma (Review).
authors: Zhang, Chunzhi; Zhang, Yixin; Song, Nachuan; Zhang, Le; Zhao, Yunying; Yao, Chi
abstract: The progression in molecular understanding of glioblastoma (GBM) enables the identification of key therapeutic targets, allowing the advances of targeted therapy in GBM. However, to date, most clinical trial results have been disappointing. The clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) system is a revolutionary genome‑editing tool that has the potential to improve basic research and therapy for GBM. In the present review, the current status and challenges of targeted therapy in GBM are examined. As a potential approach to address the challenges, the development process and application scope of CRISPR are investigated. Furthermore, the application of CRISPR in the study of GBM is explored, mainly by conducting CRISPR screens and employing CRISPR to target genes associated with the malignant phenotype of GBM. Finally, delivery of CRISPR/CRISPR‑associated protein 9 (Cas9) for the treatment of GBM is briefly reviewed.

title: Structure-activity relationship and antibacterial mechanism of saponins from quinoa husks against Bacillus cereus and their application in rice.
authors: Han, Chengcheng; Wang, Yan; Yang, Lijing; He, Yi; Song, Linmeng; Zhang, Ruoyu; Lu, Hao; Xue, Peng
abstract: Bacillus cereus (B. cereus) is a major foodborne pathogen and a persistent food safety concern. Although plant saponins are promising natural antimicrobials, the antibacterial activity of Chenopodium quinoa Willd. husk saponins against B. cereus remains poorly understood. This study investigated the structure-activity relationship and antibacterial mechanism of quinoa husk saponins against B. cereus and evaluate their potential application in rice preservation. In this study, less polar saponins exhibited stronger antibacterial activity against B. cereus than more polar saponins among the twelve tested saponins. Among them, phytolaccagenic acid (Q8), isolated from quinoa husks for the first time, exhibited the strongest antibacterial activity, with minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration values of 125 and 1000 mug/mL, respectively. Q8 showed low cytotoxicity in GES-1 and effectively inhibited B. cereus proliferation and spoilage in rice. Further assays showed that Q8 disrupted membrane stability, causing membrane potential dissipation, protein leakage, cell deformation, and reactive oxygen species accumulation. Metabolomic and lipidomic analyses revealed Q8 mainly affected glutathione metabolism, cysteine and methionine metabolism, fatty acid degradation, and glycerophospholipid/glycerolipid metabolism. Molecular docking, RT-qPCR, CRISPR-Cas9 knockout, and genetic complementation analyses confirmed that squalene-hopene cyclase is essential for hopanoid biosynthesis, and hopanoids protect B. cereus against Q8-induced membrane damage. These findings support the potential application of quinoa saponins as natural antibacterial agents in food systems.

title: Suspension-Based Intracellular Immunofluorescence Staining Coupled With Genome-Wide CRISPR-Cas9 Screening to Identify Regulators of O-GlcNAcylation.
authors: Liu, Peiyu; Lei, Qin; Zhang, Na; Yu, Haibin; Chen, Fang; Yuan, Kai
abstract: Protein O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic and reversible post-translational modification that regulates diverse cellular processes, including transcription, signal transduction, metabolism, and cell fate determination. Systematic identification of genes that modulate global O-GlcNAc levels remains technically challenging at the genome scale. Here, we describe a pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screening protocol that combines the human genome-scale CRISPR knockout (GeCKO) v2 knockout library with intracellular immunofluorescence staining using the anti-O-GlcNAc antibody RL2 and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). In this workflow, HEK293T cells are transduced with the GeCKO v2 lentiviral library at a low multiplicity of infection to ensure predominantly single-sgRNA integration. Following puromycin selection, cells are fixed, permeabilized, and stained in suspension with RL2. The top 5% of cells with the highest intracellular RL2 fluorescence are collected as the RL2-high population, while a corresponding unsorted/input sample is retained as the reference for downstream sgRNA enrichment analysis. Genomic DNA is recovered from the RL2-high and unsorted/input samples, and integrated sgRNA cassettes are amplified through a two-step PCR and library-preparation workflow for Illumina sequencing. This protocol enables the identification of candidate genes whose knockout is associated with increased intracellular RL2 fluorescence. Key features * A genome-scale pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screening workflow using the human GeCKO v2 library in HEK293T cells. * A suspension-based intracellular RL2 immunofluorescence staining protocol optimized to minimize cell loss during fixation, permeabilization, and washing, thereby preserving sgRNA library representation for downstream sorting. * Isolation of the top 5% RL2-high population, with a corresponding unsorted/input sample retained as the reference for downstream sgRNA enrichment analysis. * -Fixed-cell genomic DNA recovery and sgRNA sequencing coupled with model-based analysis of genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout (MAGeCK) enable robust hit identification.

title: Discernible phenotypic alterations following linc-10 knockout in Caenorhabditis elegans.
authors: Zhou, Chenxi; Sun, Xiaoman; Wu, Ruikun; Wu, Zifan; Chen, He
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) are regulatory molecules that play vital roles in various cellular processes. Although the loss of function of most annotated lncRNAs in several model organisms does not result in severe phenotypes, suggesting they are not essential for survival or reproduction, lncRNAs may still act as responsive elements under diverse physiological and pathological conditions. In this study, we investigated the role of the linc-10 gene in Caenorhabditis elegans and found that its deletion is associated with altered gene expression and impaired reproductive fitness. Knockout (KO) mutants of linc-10 exhibited mild but notable abnormalities, including reduced brood size, altered developmental trajectories, and increased sensitivity to stress, along with occasional sterility and a slightly elevated male ratio. We characterized the expression patterns of linc-10 across developmental stages and performed high-throughput sequencing to detect differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following linc-10 deletion. We found that several immune-related genes were dysregulated. Notably, linc-10 mutants showed increased susceptibility to Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 infection and other stressors. Small RNA sequencing further revealed alterations in piRNA and miRNA profiles after linc-10 deletion. Importantly, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated insertion of a Plinc-10::linc-10 rescue transgene into a neutral intergenic site partially rescued the reduced brood size and stress-sensitive phenotypes of linc-10 mutants, supporting the functional relevance of the linc-10 transcript. Together, these findings suggest that linc-10 contributes to reproductive fitness, immune homeostasis, and stress resilience in C. elegans.

title: AAV8-mediated CasRx delivery and expression in the cochlea and cochlear nucleus of mice.
authors: Zhou, Shuang; Huang, Tao; Yao, Wei; Huang, Shan; Jiang, Junjie; Liao, Hua; Xia, Zhongfang
abstract: CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing has made substantial progress in recent years and has enabled the treatment of a variety of genetic diseases, including hearing loss in congenitally deaf mice. However, successful gene editing for hereditary deafness may still induce off-target mutations in genomic DNA, which limits its clinical translation. CasRx, also known as RfxCas13d, is a compact RNA-targeting CRISPR effector that can be packaged into AAV vectors for in vivo delivery. CasRx, a recently identified member of the type VI CRISPR system, modulates target RNA expression without altering DNA sequences, thereby avoiding permanent off-target mutations and offering broad therapeutic potential. Here, we used adeno-associated virus serotype 8 (AAV8) to deliver CasRx into the cochlea and cochlear nucleus (CN) of C57BL/6J mice and evaluated its expression pattern and short-term safety. Two weeks after viral injection, the number and morphology of neurons and other cell types in the CN remained normal. Importantly, auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds were unchanged after viral delivery, indicating that AAV8-mediated CasRx expression did not detectably impair auditory function during the short observation period. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the feasibility and short-term safety of AAV8-mediated CasRx delivery and expression in the cochlea and cochlear nucleus, providing a delivery platform for future guide RNA-directed transcript-modulation studies in auditory disorders.

title: Unlocking genetic accessibility in Halomonas bluephagenesis: A high-efficiency transformation chassis enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing.
authors: Xu, Tong; Guo, Feng; Xiang, Hua; Han, Jing
abstract: Halomonas bluephagenesis has emerged as a promising chassis for industrial biotechnology distinguished by its halophilic robustness and capacity for open and continuous fermentation. However, its poor transformability has substantially limited rapid, iterative, and automatable strain engineering. Here, we develop a "restriction release" strategy that increases transformation efficiency from approximately 10(2) to 10(7) cfu/mug DNA, rivaling the efficiency of standard laboratory Escherichia coli. A spontaneous IS30 insertion disrupting the type II restriction endonuclease gene notI increased plasmid transformation efficiency by about 2000-fold. Targeted deletion of notI reproduced this phenotype, confirming its role as a major barrier. Further deletion of the DNA phosphorothioation restriction locus dptFGH yielded an additional 10 to 37-fold improvement, generating the highly transformable DeltaEPSDeltaFlgDeltaNotIDeltaPTRes chassis. Notably, the enhanced chassis further facilitated two linear-DNA-based editing strategies: direct RecET-mediated pyrF deletion using a linear donor coupled with phenotypic selection, achieving a recombination efficiency of 16.7%, and CRISPR/Cas9-assisted ribDHBA promoter replacement via co-delivery of a gRNA plasmid and a linear donor, achieving an efficiency of 11.1%. Together, these results identify endogenous restriction systems as primary barriers to genetic manipulation in H. bluephagenesis. Stepwise restriction release markedly improves plasmid transformation and enables linear DNA-mediated genome editing, providing an improved genetic platform for the iterative engineering of this industrial halophile. More broadly, this study suggests a practical strategy for overcoming the genetic inaccessibility of other non-model microorganisms and accelerating iterative strain engineering.

title: Decoding multispecies oral biofilms: molecular architecture, host modulation and systems-guided precision anti-biofilm strategies.
authors: Almusallam, Abdulrahman Abdullah; Allemailem, Khaled S
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
abstract: Oral biofilms are spatially ordered microbial communities whose pathogenic behavior is shaped by more than taxonomic composition. Their development reflects the combined effects of adhesin-receptor recognition, interspecies coaggregation, matrix formation, metabolite exchange, local physicochemical gradients and host-derived selection. Here, we synthesize molecular and ecological evidence on the bacterial cell surface-matrix interface and consider how these interactions contribute to cariogenic, periodontal and peri-implant biofilms. Particular attention is given to glucosyltransferase-dependent polysaccharides, extracellular DNA, amyloidogenic proteins, sortase-anchored surface factors and outer membrane vesicles, together with metabolic interactions involving lactate, arginine, hydrogen peroxide and heme. We further evaluate functional-genomic and systems-level approaches (including transposon sequencing, CRISPR interference, metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics, spatial imaging, genome-scale metabolic modeling and machine learning) while distinguishing association and prediction from experimentally demonstrated mechanism. Emerging interventions are assessed according to their biological target and evidence level, including adhesion blockade, specifically targeted antimicrobials, matrix synthesis inhibition and degradation, quorum interference, probiotics, catalytic nanoparticles, antimicrobial photodynamic therapy and antibiofilm dental materials. Across these approaches, reduction in biofilm biomass is not equivalent to ecological restoration or clinical benefit. Key translational barriers include model fidelity, donor-to-donor variation, spatial heterogeneity, treatment durability, endpoint selection and the limited external validation of many computational and preclinical findings. Future precision strategies should therefore integrate microbial identity, matrix architecture, spatial metabolism and host context, with experimental perturbation used to establish causal vulnerabilities before therapeutic translation.

title: Pseudorabies virus as vaccine vectors for delivering foreign antigens: methodology and application.
authors: Tian, Xiao-Xiao; Yang, Yong-Bo; An, Tong-Qing
abstract: Pseudorabies virus (PRV) is the etiological agent of pseudorabies (PR). It belongs to the Herpesviridae family and has double-stranded linear DNA encoding more than 70 proteins. Many of these proteins are non-essential for viral replication and provide insertion sites for foreign genes to enable heterologous protein expression. PRV is a promising viral-vector platform for expressing foreign proteins and developing vaccines against multiple pathogens. However, no recombinant PRV-vectored vaccines are commercially available to date. Here, we summarize the biological characteristics of PRV, recombinant PRV construction methodology, foreign gene insertion sites and optimization, immune responses, and applications of recombinant PRV-vectored vaccines. This study provides insights into the development of PRV recombinant vaccines and the latest research progress, offering novel perspectives for advancing preventive medicine through vaccinology.

title: S100A4 facilitates influenza A virus replication by interacting with M2 in human alveolar epithelial cells.
authors: Wu, Li; Tao, Yingying; Li, Jianing; Yang, Rui; Song, Jiasheng; Shu, Jianhong; He, Yulong; Feng, Huapeng
abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) replication depends on host cells and is regulated by numerous host factors. Therefore, investigating and understanding the role of these host factors is a significant topic. In this study, we found the IAV replication was attenuated after host factor S100 calcium-binding protein A4 (S100A4) was knocked down with RNAi or knockout with CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing technology. Conversely, IAV replication was enhanced upon the overexpression in A549 cells. The interaction between S100A4 and the IAV M2 protein was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation. Meanwhile, confocal microscopy experiment demonstrated that the viral M2 protein co-localized with endogenous S100A4 in IAV-infected A549 cells. Truncation analysis confirmed that amino acids 45-62 of the M2 protein constitute the main interaction region with S100A4. Further study showed that viral entry was reduced after S100A4 deletion. And the polymerase activity was significantly decreased in S100A4-knockout A549 cells compared to that in wild-type A549 cells. The S100A4 overexpression resulted in the downregulation of IFN-beta, while the mRNA levels of the interferon-stimulated genes ISG15 and BST2 were also significantly reduced. Therefore, the host factor S100A4 was a positive modulator of IAV replication and was involved in the viral entry, polymerase activity maintenance and innate immune regulation. Collectively, our findings shed new light on the molecular mechanisms governing IAV infection and suggest a previously underexplored avenue for antiviral therapeutic intervention.

title: FLT3 Kinase Inhibition Reshapes the Neuronal Transcriptome to Suppress Seizures.
authors: Cruite, Kate; Moore, Madeline; Gallagher, Michael D; Lin, Shuqi; Yin, Yuqin; Coleman, Emanuel M; Shahbo, Ellie; Lungjangwa, Tenzin; Ge, Xinzhou; Hovestadt, Volker; Jaenisch, Rudolf; Maguire, Jamie; Tang, Xin
journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
abstract: Approximately one-third of individuals with epilepsy are refractory to current anti-seizure medications, highlighting the need for new, mechanism-based therapeutic approaches. Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3), a receptor tyrosine kinase classically studied in hematopoiesis and leukemia, is also expressed in neurons, although its function in the brain remains largely unexplored. Our prior work identified small-molecule FLT3 inhibitors (FLT3i) as unexpected enhancers of potassium-chloride cotransporter 2 (KCC2), a neuron-specific chloride transporter essential for maintaining GABAergic inhibition. Here, we applied a functional genomics framework in mouse primary neurons and human stem cell-derived neurons to define FLT3i-induced transcriptional programs, revealing conserved gene networks governing synaptic function and ion channel regulation. A complementary CRISPR/Cas9-based screen of candidate transcription factors identified FLT3-responsive neuronal gene regulatory networks linked to epigenetic remodeling and neuroinflammatory signaling. We further demonstrate that KW-2449, an orally bioavailable FLT3 inhibitor, penetrates the blood-brain barrier, elevates KCC2 expression in vivo for up to 24 hours, and significantly reduces seizure susceptibility in a kainic acid-induced mouse model of epilepsy. Together, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for FLT3 in neuronal function and establish proof-of-principle for FLT3 inhibition as a mechanistically supported candidate strategy warranting further development as a next-generation anti-seizure therapy.

title: Gene therapy strategy to treat Cornelia de Lange syndrome due to Hdac8 Deficiency.
authors: Presa, Maximiliano; Lecordier, Sarah; Zuberi, Aamir; Ryan, Jennifer; Tata, Saurabh; Savage, Holly; Chhaya, Dweet; Piec, Pierre-Alexandre; Soule, Sara; Hackett, Neil R; Lutz, Cathleen
abstract: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is a rare, multi-system genetic disorder characterized by developmental and cognitive impairments with systemic manifestations. Among the genes associated with CdLS, loss-of-function variants in HDAC8 account for approximately 4% of cases (referred to as CdLS5), causing the dysregulation of the cohesin complex, a core pathogenic mechanism of the disorder. Currently, no gene-based therapeutic strategy exists to directly address CdLS resulting from HDAC8 deficiency. Here, we created a new CdLS5 mouse model by introducing a clinically reported HDAC8 p.Ile19Ser variant in the mouse Hdac8 gene using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Comprehensive molecular, morphological, and behavioral characterization revealed that the new Hdac8I19S mouse strain exhibits a robust phenotype, including marked alterations in deacetylase activity and pronounced developmental and behavioral deficits. This model was subsequently used to evaluate a gene augmentation approach aimed at increasing HDAC8 protein levels and restoring cohesin function through delivery of human HDAC8 transgene. Two AAV vectors driving expression of human HDAC8 were assessed. Although efficient delivery and robust expression were achieved, only modest effects on Smc3 acetylation, a key HDAC8 substrate, were observed, and no significant improvement in cognitive or behavioral phenotypes was detected. Overall, these findings demonstrate that postnatal HDAC8 gene augmentation resulted in limited biochemical correction and minimal phenotypic improvement under the conditions tested. These results highlight important biological considerations, including target engagement and developmental timing, that should be considered in the development of effective therapies for cohesin-related disorders.

title: Serglycin regulates macrophage differentiation and is associated with human atherosclerotic plaque stability.
authors: Gialeli, Chrysostomi; Fountas, Panagiotis; Bocci, Matteo; Sun, Jiangming; Shami, Annelie; Nitulescu, Mihaela; Persson, Ana; Bengtsson, Eva; Knutsen, Erik; Pietras, Kristian; Kolset, Svein O; Theocharis, Achilleas D; Edsfeldt, Andreas; Goncalves, Isabel
journal: American journal of physiology. Cell physiology
abstract: Inflammation contributes to the destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques and increases the risk of cardiovascular events such as myocardial infarction and stroke. Extracellular matrix components modulate inflammation and immune responses within the plaque microenvironment. Serglycin (SRGN), is a proteoglycan primarily expressed by immune cells that regulates inflammation, but its role in human atherosclerotic plaques remains unclear. SRGN protein levels were quantified by ELISA in carotid endarterectomy samples from patients in the Atherosclerotic Plaque Imaging Project and compared between symptomatic and asymptomatic plaques. SRGN spatial localization was evaluated by multispectral imaging and histology. Glycosylation patterns were examined by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting. Functional effects were investigated using CRISPR-mediated SRGN knockout in THP-1 monocytes differentiated into macrophages and exposed to oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL). SRGN levels were higher in plaques from asymptomatic patients compared with plaques from symptomatic patients and localized primarily to macrophage- and lipid-rich regions. Plaque SRGN was positively associated with histological markers of plaque stability, displayed heterogeneous molecular forms and showed an inverse association with the plaque vulnerability index. In vitro, SRGN deficiency was associated with a more pro-inflammatory macrophage profile, impaired M2-like polarization, and increased lipid retention following oxLDL exposure. These findings indicate that SRGN is associated with inflammatory cell presence, lipid accumulation, and features of plaque stability in human plaques, and suggest a role for SRGN in macrophage differentiation and lipid handling in atherosclerotic lesions.

title: RBP1-driven retinol metabolism in tumor-associated lymphatic endothelial cells orchestrates triple-negative breast cancer progression and lymphatic metastasis.
authors: Montenegro-Navarro, Nieves; Del Cerro, Estefania Diaz; Jordan-Perez, Carmen; de Alava, Enrique; Garcia-Caballero, Melissa
abstract: BACKGROUND: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive breast cancer subtype and is characterized by a high metastatic potential and limited treatment options. TNBC frequently metastasizes to lymphatic vessels and the presence of breast cancer cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes (LNs) is an important prognostic factor. Nevertheless, the molecular and metabolic reprogramming of TNBC-associated lymphatic vasculature remains poorly understood. METHODS: A comprehensive single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of 44,000 endothelial cells from human breast tumor datasets was performed. RBP1, a retinol-binding protein, was identified as a metabolic gene highly and specifically upregulated in tumor-associated lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs). Then, RBP1 expression in human TNBC biopsies was assessed, and its association with LN status and overall patient survival was investigated in a cohort of 1,474 breast cancer patients. We further evaluated the in vivo relevance of RBP1 by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout in a pre-clinical TNBC mouse model. In vitro functional studies were performed using co-culture systems and RBP1-silencing in LECs. Finally, RBP1 mechanism of action in the lymphatic vasculature was determined by bulk-RNA sequencing and validated by applying different cellular and molecular approaches. RESULTS: Single-cell profiling revealed that the metabolic gene RBP1 was upregulated in LECs within the human breast tumor microenvironment. Further analysis showed that lymphatic RBP1 expression was associated with LN metastases, and correlated with poor prognosis and reduced survival in TNBC patients. In the pre-clinical TNBC mouse model, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Rbp1 knockout reduced lymphangiogenesis, tumor growth and metastatic burden, and increased necrosis. Moreover, functional assays demonstrated that direct co-culture of LECs with TNBC cells, or exposure to their secretome, induced lymphatic RBP1 upregulation and enhanced pro-lymphangiogenic activities, whereas RBP1 silencing compromised their biological, redox and metabolic properties. Mechanistically, bulk RNA sequencing of RBP1-silenced LECs combined with experimental validation revealed that RBP1, through its retinol-binding domain, modulates the VEGFR3 and NOTCH pathways, while also involving lipid mobilization. CONCLUSIONS: We define lymphatic RBP1 as a key "switch" that couples LEC metabolism to molecular programs, thereby driving tumor-associated lymphangiogenesis, breast tumor growth and lymphatic dissemination in TNBC. Our findings underscore the potential of RBP1 as both a novel prognostic biomarker and a tractable therapeutic target for blocking TNBC progression and lymphatic metastasis.

title: Functional characterization of EtAMA3 in Eimeria tenella and immunogenicity of its knockout line.
authors: Du, Shiqi; Pang, Ying; Dong, Rongqing; Tang, Xinming; Ou, Changbo; Si, Hongbin; Song, Xingju; Hu, Dandan
abstract: BACKGROUND: Avian coccidiosis, predominantly caused by Eimeria species, imposes severe economic burdens on the global poultry sector. EtAMA3 is an apical membrane antigen specific to Eimeria tenella sporozoites, yet its functions in parasite invasion, intracellular development, and utility as a target for rationally attenuated vaccine design remain poorly characterized. METHODS: In this study, we utilized targeted gene knockout and overexpression to dissect the biological functions of EtAMA3 during E. tenella invasion and endogenous development. RESULTS: Our results show that EtAMA3 localizes primarily to the sporozoite apical pole. EtAMA3 deletion only moderately attenuates in vitro sporozoite invasion but severely disrupts cecal schizont formation, drastically curtails oocyst excretion, and mitigates clinical disease and cecal pathology. Importantly, the knockout strain retains robust immunoprotective capacity at standard immunization dosages. Transcriptomic profiling of EtAMA3-deficient sporozoites uncovered suppressed transcription of core moving junction (MJ) components RON2, RON4, and RON8, alongside elevated RON2L2 expression. Loss of EtAMA3 also triggered widespread transcriptional reprogramming of ApiAP2 transcription factors and numerous transmembrane protein-coding genes. CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate that EtAMA3 is an important component of the molecular networks governing E. tenella invasion and development, and that the EtAMA3 knockout strain combines reduced virulence with preserved immunogenicity, providing an experimental basis for dissecting invasion mechanisms and developing next-generation genetically attenuated live anticoccidial vaccines.

title: Programmable RNA targeting with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) effector Cas7-11 in zebrafish embryos and mammalian cells.
authors: Yan, Huan; Hassan, Imtiaz Ul; Yan, Kai; Cheung, Man Yee; Deng, Jiani; Wuyang, Dio Daniel; Jiang, Ke; Zhou, Liangji; Yuan, Luowei; Cai, Dongqing; Qi, Xufeng; Lei, Yong; Wei, Ping; Zhao, Hui
abstract: BACKGROUND: The CRISPR/Cas7-11 system is a recently characterized RNA targeting tool that exhibits low toxicity, minimal off-target effects, and reduced collateral RNA cleavage. While Cas7-11 has been recently tested in zebrafish embryos as ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, its use as mRNA-single guide RNA (sgRNA) formulations and its application in human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) have not been explored. RESULTS: In this study, we evaluated the efficiency and specificity of Cas7-11 in zebrafish embryos and hESCs. In zebrafish,injection ofCas7-11and sgRNA resulted in evident reductions of target transcripts, accompanied by clear phenotypic outcomes. ExogenousEGFPmRNA levels were reduced to 31.90%, while endogenous tbxta was reducedto 19.89%, and tyrosinase to 33.18%, respectively, resulting in the no-tail phenotype and reduced pigmentation. Theno-tail phenotype was partially rescued by mRNA overexpression. RNA sequencing confirmed minimal off-target effects. Moreover, Cas7-11 decreased exogenousGaussia luciferasemRNA in human embryonic and HEK293T cells, to 23.52% and to 63.75%, respectively, and correspondingly reduced luciferase activity, without collateral cleavage activity. Targeting pluripotency factor genes, OCT4 and SOX2, in hESCs decreased their mRNA levels and induced differentiation. CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these findings establish Cas7-11 as a precise and efficient RNA knockdown tool for functional studies in embryonic development and stem cell biology, providing a versatile alternative to DNA-based gene-editing approaches.

title: Repurposing of abemaciclib to overcome C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma.
authors: Li, Hsin-Jung; Ho, Chao-Chi; Chen, Ci-Ling; Chen, Chi-Yuan; Cheng, Ting-Jen Rachel; Chang, Ya-Hsuan; Huang, Yu-Han; Lin, Ming-Shiu; Lin, Zi-Ling; Yang, Shuenn-Chen; Huang, Shih-Chien; Hung, Yu-Ya; Huang, Kuo-Yen; Yang, Pan-Chyr
abstract: BACKGROUND: Acquired resistance to osimertinib mediated by the EGFR C797S mutation remains a major therapeutic challenge in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), with limited effective treatment options. This study explored whether abemaciclib, an FDA-approved CDK4/6 inhibitor, can overcome C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. METHODS: A high-throughput screen of approximately 125,000 compounds was performed using Ba/F3 cells expressing EGFR triple mutations (L858R/T790M/C797S and Del19/T790M/C797S). The impact of abemaciclib on EGFR kinase activity was evaluated via in vitro kinase and Western blot assays. Apoptosis induction was assessed using flow cytometry. The activity of abemaciclib was evaluated using biochemical assays, cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA), molecular docking analyses, CRISPR-engineered isogenic models, xenografts, and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. RESULTS: Abemaciclib was identified as a potent inhibitor of EGFR triple-mutant cell growth and exhibited preferential activity toward mutant EGFR-dependent models. IL-3 rescue assays demonstrated that its antiproliferative effects were dependent on suppression of oncogenic EGFR signaling.
