Abemaciclib inhibited mutant EGFR kinase activity, reduced EGFR phosphorylation, and induced apoptotic cell death in osimertinib-resistant models while exhibiting substantially weaker activity toward wild-type EGFR. CETSA and molecular docking analyses supported direct engagement of mutant EGFR by abemaciclib. Importantly, abemaciclib significantly suppressed tumor growth in CRISPR-engineered isogenic xenografts and PDX models harboring EGFR C797S-mediated osimertinib resistance. CONCLUSIONS: Abemaciclib selectively suppresses C797S-mutant EGFR signaling and demonstrates robust antitumor activity in preclinical models of osimertinib-resistant EGFR-mutant NSCLC. This breakthrough not only overcomes the existing therapeutic barrier but also demonstrates minimal interference with WT EGFR, offering a transformative and precise therapeutic strategy with significant translational and clinical potential. These findings support the therapeutic repurposing of abemaciclib as a potential treatment strategy for EGFR C797S-mediated resistance and provide a translational strategy for overcoming resistance-associated EGFR alterations using clinically available targeted agents.

title: A self-driven probiotic nanosystem reshapes extracellular matrix by knockdown of DDR1 for enhanced tumor immunotherapy.
authors: Cao, Lei; He, Yuefeng; Li, Wenhao; He, Yu; Li, Gang; Duan, Yangying; Chen, Mingqi; Liu, Congrui; Yang, Ke; Wu, Wencheng; Pu, Yinying
abstract: Immunotherapy represents a promising therapeutic approach for tumor suppression, yet its efficacy is significantly limited by the immunosuppressive extracellular matrix (ECM) characteristic of solid tumors. To achieve simultaneous ECM remodeling and immune activation within a single system, we have developed a self-driven probiotic nanosystem (PL@LDH-CB) based on the probiotic Clostridium butyricum (CB), which incorporates a plasmid-loaded layered double hydroxide (PL@LDH) gene-editing module. Following intravenous administration, the PL@LDH-CB system actively targets tumor sites by leveraging CB's natural tropism toward hypoxic conditions, thereby efficiently delivering the PL@LDH gene-editing module for ECM reshaping. Within tumors, CB and its metabolites significantly enhance anti-cancer immune responses. Concurrently, the released PL@LDH enables stable nuclear expression of CRISPR-Cas9, precisely knocking down Ddr1-a gene encoding discoidin domain receptor 1 (DDR1) that mediates immune exclusion through promoting collagen fibrillogenesis and fiber alignment. The depletion of DDR1 ultimately reduces intratumoral solid stress (a compressive force exerted by collagen fibers), leading to comprehensive ECM remodeling. This process markedly improves the infiltration of activated T cells within tumors, thereby significantly enhancing immunotherapeutic outcomes.

title: Deciphering the landscape of human pathogenome in non-typhoidal Salmonella through multidimensional genomics.
authors: Liu, Haibing; Rui, Ke; Wang, Ting; Zheng, Lijie
abstract: BACKGROUND: Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) is a leading foodborne pathogen causing severe gastrointestinal and systemic infections, posing a significant global health burden. This study employed a genomic approach to investigate the functional and distribution characteristics of human pathogenome in NTS, aiming to provide molecular targets and a theoretical foundation for novel anti-salmonellosis strategies. RESULTS: Analysis of eight NTS strains revealed 2,000 virulence genes encoding 263 factors, predominantly effector delivery systems (41%), of which type III secretion system (T3SS) genes constituted the majority (66.3%). A total of 217 partial sequences from 13 salmonella pathogenicity islands (SPIs) were identified, with SPI-2 (26.7%), SPI-1 (24%), and SPI-13 (10.6%) being most prevalent. Key virulence genes in SPI-1 (35 T3SS1-related genes), SPI-2 (30 T3SS2-related genes), and SPI-5 (sopB/sigD, pipB) were conserved across all strains. We identified 7,868 human pathogenicity-related genes, functionally enriched in metabolic/cellular processes, catalytic activity, and binding. Human pathogenicity-related virulence genes were mainly classified as delivery systems, adhesion factors, and nutrient metabolism factors. Enzymatic analysis showed human pathogenicity-related protease genes were primarily serine, cysteine, and metallopeptidases, while human pathogenicity-related carbohydrase-active genes were associated with glycoside hydrolases, glycosyltransferases, and carbohydrate esterases. Functional annotation with the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes indicated human pathogenicity-related protease genes enrichment in signaling, cellular, metabolic, and genetic information processing pathways, particularly in antibiotic resistance and infectious diseases, while human pathogenicity-related carbohydrase-active genes were enriched in carbohydrate metabolism and glycan biosynthesis. A structurally conserved, metal-chelating non-ribosomal peptide metallophore (NRP-metallophore) gene cluster was present in all strains, containing biosynthetic virulence genes (entA, entC, entF, entB, entE, fes) and transport-related virulence genes (fep family, entS). Functional type I-E clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) and CRISPR-associated (Cas) systems with variable numbers of CRISPR arrays but conserved direct repeats were identified in most strains. CONCLUSIONS: NTS strains carried conserved T3SS effectors, human pathogenicity-related factors enriched in metabolism, catalysis, antibiotic resistance, and infection pathways, a conserved NRP-metallophore gene cluster for iron acquisition, and a functional type I-E CRISPR-Cas system, collectively defining key genetic determinants for pathogenesis.

title: Translating pathogen biology into diagnostic and management strategies for gummy stem blight in cucumber production.
authors: Ranjan, Aastha; Lu, Alison; Hutton, Charles; Bricknell, Oscar; Redman, Andrew; Tissue, David T; Plett, Jonathan M
abstract: Gummy stem blight (GSB) is a major disease of cucurbits caused by Stagonosporopsis spp. and is increasingly problematic in intensive cucumber production systems, particularly where warm, humid environments favour infection, sporulation and rapid disease spread. GSB can infect vegetative and reproductive tissues and remain latent in fruit for several days before visible symptoms develop, creating a distinctive commercial challenge: disease may be difficult to detect before harvest yet cause significant post-harvest losses, reducing grower and retailer confidence. Compounding these problems, current diagnostic tools for detecting pre-symptomatic infection are often insufficiently validated for species specificity, sensitivity, turnaround time, cost, crude-sample compatibility and practical use by production staff. Many of these limitations reflect the relative lack of genomic resources for Stagonosporopsis. Therefore, this review integrates evidence from other pathosystems with current knowledge of Stagonosporopsis taxonomy, infection biology, epidemiology, diagnostics, fungicide resistance, effector biology and host resistance to identify pathways towards grower-ready tools. Specifically, we focus on how recent advances in genomics, paired with previously designed detection systems such as loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated proteins (CRISPR/Cas), could be adapted for species-specific detection of the causal pathogen and, simultaneously, provide a regional profile of fungicide resistance. In parallel, we explore how a deeper functional genomic understanding of the disease, particularly of effector proteins expressed during the early stages of infection, could provide valuable insights into the dynamics of this host-pathogen interaction and support strategies to disrupt these interactions through novel fungistatic compounds and the development of disease-resistant cultivars. Together, these approaches could support a staged technology-development and adoption roadmap for more precise, rapid and sustainable GSB management in cucumber production.

title: Coupling hfCas13d with Circular gRNA Array Precursors Extends RNA Knockdown and Improves Biocatalysis in Yeast.
authors: Thi Le, Xuan-Mai; Truong, Vy Anh; Dang, Quyen Thuc; Huang, Siang-Cing; Nguyen, Mai Thanh Thi; Hu, Yu-Chen
abstract: CRISPR-based RNA cleavage holds promise for gene knockdown but its applications in metabolic engineering remain largely unexplored. Here we reconstitute three mammalian CRISPR-based RNA cleavage systems to arrest the intermediate metabolic reactions in the yeast Candida viswanathii to produce hydroxydecanoic acid (HDA), an important nylon precursor. We identify hfCas13d as the optimal effector and next develop a circular guide RNA (CgRNA) precursor architecture to enhance and extend the knockdown of genes involved in HDA production. This hfCas13d/CgRNA precursor platform also represses genes in other yeasts and E. coli, demonstrating broad microbial applicability. Single and dual CgRNA precursor arrays enable multiplexed pathway repression, with dual arrays reducing byproduct formation and increasing HDA titer to 17.8 g/L in shake flasks. Bioreactor fermentation further boosts HDA production to 37.2 g/L. Together, this work establishes hfCas13d/CgRNA as a programmable RNA regulatory platform for engineering microbial cell factories.

title: Structural basis for loop-dependent inhibition by AcrIIC1 anti-CRISPR proteins.
authors: Wang, Shen; Zhang, Zhiyu; Luan, Chenyu; Zhu, Cheng; Liu, Chang; Li, Wenling; Wang, Qianfan; Liu, Xiaoqian; Yang, Haitao; Xiao, Yunjie; Wang, Zefang
abstract: Most characterized anti-CRISPR proteins act via well-defined core inhibitory mechanisms, yet how auxiliary structural elements modulate and potentiate these canonical processes remains poorly understood. Here, we show that AcrIIC1(Boe) represses Nme1Cas9 activity through an integrated, loop-coupled regulatory mode. Based on canonical occlusion of the HNH catalytic site, the extended loop of AcrIIC1(Boe) provides an additional coupled regulatory layer to remodel sgRNA spacer arrangement and R-loop progression, thereby enhancing Cas9 inhibition. Loop deletion largely abrogates robust inhibition, indicating that this loop module is indispensable for full AcrIIC1 inhibitory potency. Consistently, transplantation of this functional loop into the weakly active AcrIIC1(Nme1) efficiently elevates its inhibitory performance. Our findings identify a loop-mediated regulatory strategy that potentiates the canonical HNH occlusion mechanism, clarify the structural basis for functional divergence across AcrIIC1 homologs, and offer a modular engineering principle for the rational design and optimization of anti-CRISPR proteins with enhanced potency.

title: Quercetin suppresses radial glial stem-like cell functions through an HSPB1-associated mechanism in glioma.
authors: Liu, Bohan; Wang, Zheng; Huang, Lijie; Ni, Ruoxuan; Tao, Rui; Peng, Dazhao; Liao, Chihyi; Chen, Yuge; Huang, Ruoyu; Wang, Chen; Chen, Yankun; Sun, Zhiyan; Chen, Jiashu; Li, Qiuling; Hu, Yuedong; Liu, Shiyu; Yang, Siyuan; Zheng, Yujinglin; Hu, Huimin
abstract: Glioma is a highly malignant tumor characterized by pronounced intratumoral heterogeneity. By integrating multi-omics analyses, we identified radial glial stem-like (RG-like) cells as a putative upstream developmental-like state in inferred glioma differentiation trajectories. Integrated spatial transcriptomic and histopathological analyses further linked the molecular features of RG-like cells to their spatial distribution and associated tissue morphology. A CRISPR-based knockout screen highlighted heat shock protein beta-1 (HSPB1) as a potential molecular target associated with RG-like cell functions. We subsequently investigated quercetin (QUE) and found that it inhibited glioma cell growth and suppressed mitotic somal translocation (MST), a characteristic RG-like cellular behavior. Mechanistic analyses showed that QUE reduced HSPB1 protein expression and was associated with a reduced detectable interaction between HSPB1 and vimentin (VIM). Together, these findings characterize RG-like cells at the molecular and histopathological levels and suggest that QUE may represent a potential pharmacological approach for modulating their associated functions in glioma.

title: Epigenetic Allostasis in Alcohol Use Disorder: A Metabolic-Chromatin Framework Linking DNA Methylation, Circuit Remodeling, and Precision Therapeutics.
authors: Ye, Jiang-Hong; Duman, Lea; Zuo, Wanhong; Li, Dongchen
abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is a chronic relapsing disorder characterized by persistent dysregulation of reward, stress, and executive circuits. Although acute ethanol effects on neurotransmission are well established, the molecular mechanisms that stabilize long-term vulnerability remain unclear. Building on established allostatic and epigenetic-allostatic models, we develop an expanded framework in which repeated alcohol exposure can drive a transition from adaptive, transient chromatin remodeling toward more persistent epigenetic states across key neural circuits. We integrate evidence from histone modifications, DNA methylation, and metabolic regulation, highlighting how alcohol-induced oxidative stress and disruption of one-carbon metabolism lead to S-adenosylmethionine depletion and methylation instability. These processes converge to form a metabolic-epigenetic trap, reinforcing transcriptional repression of plasticity-related genes. We synthesize circuit-specific changes in the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, and hippocampus, and incorporate emerging human postmortem and single-nucleus multiomic data that support cell-type-specific epigenetic remodeling. In addition, we examine neuroimmune-epigenetic interactions and developmental and sex-dependent exposures as amplifiers of epigenetic vulnerability. Finally, we evaluate therapeutic strategies ranging from selective histone deacetylase inhibition to locus-specific epigenome editing, emphasizing the critical importance of treatment timing and circuit specificity. Together, this expanded framework conceptualizes AUD as a disorder in which maladaptive genomic stability may contribute to persistent circuit dysfunction and identifies epigenetic-metabolic coupling as a testable target for next-generation therapeutics.

title: TRIB2 supports a high glycolytic phenotype in melanoma cells.
authors: Mayoral-Varo, Victor; De Sousa-Coelho, Ana Luisa; Lopes, Carla; Martinez-Costa, Oscar H; Amenabar, Carlos; Oliveira, Paulo J; Aragon, Juan J; Ferreira, Bibiana I; Link, Wolfgang
abstract: BACKGROUND: Metabolic adaptation is a crucial driver of melanoma progression and therapy resistance. The pseudokinase Tribbles homolog 2 (TRIB2) is highly expressed in melanoma and is associated with poor outcomes and treatment resistance. However, its specific role in the metabolic profile of melanoma cells remained unexplored. This study aimed to investigate the impact of TRIB2 on cellular metabolism, and its role in metabolic adaptation in melanoma. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The study used UACC-62 human melanoma cells with high endogenous TRIB2 expression and isogenic TRIB2-knockout (KO) clones generated via CRISPR-Cas9. Cell proliferation was assessed using trypan blue exclusion assays under treatment with metabolic drugs including 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG), and dichloroacetate (DCA). Metabolic phenotypes were evaluated by measuring glucose consumption, lactate production, and real-time analysis of glycolytic flux (ECAR) and mitochondrial respiration (OCR) using a Seahorse bioanalyzer. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were measured by dihydroethidium (DHE) fluorescence. Gene expression was analyzed by qPCR, and protein levels were determined by western blot. Citrate synthase activity was measured enzymatically. RESULTS: TRIB2-KO cells exhibited significantly reduced basal proliferation compared with wild-type (WT) cells. KO cells were also more sensitive to the glycolytic inhibitor 2-DG. Conversely, WT cells were more susceptible to DCA treatment. Metabolic analyses confirmed that TRIB2-KO cells had lower glucose consumption, lactate production, and glycolytic capacity than WT cells. Mitochondrial respiratory function and the protein levels of key respiratory complexes were unchanged. Despite the reduction in glycolytic activity, TRIB2 depletion did not increase mitochondrial respiratory capacity and was associated with elevated basal intracellular superoxide levels. Among the molecular alterations identified, PDK4 was consistently reduced at both the mRNA and protein levels, whereas citrate synthase activity was significantly decreased despite preserved protein abundance, indicating selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. CONCLUSIONS: TRIB2 expression promotes a glycolytic phenotype and contributes to metabolic adaptation in melanoma. Loss of TRIB2 does not induce a metabolic shift towards oxidative phosphorylation but instead results in broader metabolic rewiring characterized by reduced glycolysis together with selective alterations in mitochondrial carbon metabolism. These findings identify the TRIB2-PDK4 axis as a previously unrecognized component of metabolic regulation in melanoma and provide a rationale for further investigating its therapeutic potential.

title: Protection against diet-induced weight gain by a single-point mutation in Kir2.1 channels.
authors: Beverley, Katie M; Munoz, Marcos D; Ahn, Sang Joon; Granados, Sara T; Le Master, Elizabeth; Phillips, Shane A; Fancher, Ibra S; Xu, Pingwen; Levitan, Irena
abstract: High-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity remains a significant global health challenge. In this study, we show that a global knock-in CRISPR mouse with the Kir2.1(L222I) single-point mutation exhibits remarkable resistance to HFD-induced weight gain. Specifically, Kir2.1(L222I) mutation preserves Kir2.1 currents in endothelial cells isolated from resistance arteries of overweight mice and confers protection against suppression by palmitic acid (PA), a fatty acid prevalent in obesity. Kir2.1(L222I) mutation also preserves endothelium-dependent flow-induced vasodilation (FIV) both in mice on HFD and in the presence of PA. Moreover, Kir2.1(L222I) confers significant protection against HFD-induced weight gain and adiposity in male mice independent of caloric intake: mutant mice gain significantly less weight on HFD, maintain body composition with higher % lean and lower % fat mass and have significantly smaller fat depots. These protective effects were independent of the food intake (the frequency and the size of the meals) and calories excreted in the feces, as no differences were found between Kir2.1(WT) and Kir2.1(L222I) mice on HFD. Notably, Kir2.1(L222I) mutation resulted in increased Respiratory Exchange Rate (RER), enhanced physical activity during wheel exercise and spontaneous movements in metabolic cages, as well as increased energy expenditure. These findings highlight Kir2.1 channels as potential therapeutic targets for obesity and related metabolic disorders. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62892-7.

title: Epigenetic regulation of DOT1L methyltransferase activityremodels lipid metabolism to alleviate ferroptosis-induced liver injury.
authors: Hu, Jia-Ming; Liu, Shuo; Pan, Zheng-Ze; Gao, Yi-Jia; Cui, Wei-Wei; Zhuang, Xiao; Wang, Rong; Han, Ya-Jing; Liu, Jia-Xing; Fan, Xiang-Chuang; Song, Dan-Dan; Zhang, Zi-Yang; Sun, Wan-Yang; Zhang, Zong-Li; He, Rong-Rong; Xu, Yun-Fei; Gu, Wei; Pan, Chang; Chu, Bo
abstract: Epigenetic modifications contribute to lipid-related disorders by modulating the expression of key genes involved in lipid metabolism. Accumulating evidence suggests that lipid metabolism-mediated ferroptosis drives the progression of metabolic associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and liver injury. However, whether epigenetic mechanisms remodel lipid metabolism to regulate ferroptosis-induced liver damage remains unclear. Here, through pharmacological screening of epigenetics-related compounds and CRISPR-Cas9-based screening targeting epigenetic factors, we identified DOT1 Like Histone Lysine Methyltransferase (DOT1L) as a key sensitizer of hepatocytes to ferroptosis and subsequent liver injury, whereas inhibition of DOT1L reverses the phenomenon. DOT1L loss remodeled the phospholipid landscape by decreasing PUFA-containing phospholipids while increasing monounsaturated and lysophospholipid species. Mechanistically, DOT1L depletion reduced H3K79me1 and H3K79me2 occupancy at the PLA2G7, ALDH3B1, and PLCXD3 loci, particularly across gene-body regions, while increasing promoter-proximal accessibility and expression of these phospholipid-remodeling genes. These genes suppress ferroptosis by reducing the levels of phospholipids containing polyunsaturated fatty acids (PL-PUFAs). Furthermore, we demonstrated that AMPK phosphorylates DOT1L at Ser786, weakens its association with AF9, and suppresses H3K79 methyltransferase activity and ferroptosis sensitivity. Collectively, our findings reveal the AMPK-DOT1L-H3K79 methylation axis as a novel lipid metabolic pathway that regulates ferroptosis and maintains hepatic homeostasis, offering new therapeutic insights for ferroptosis-related liver injury.

title: A new CRISPR/Cas9 GALC Knockout Cellular Model Reveals Lactosylceramide Accumulation Similar to Twitcher Mice.
authors: Del Grosso, Ambra; Papini, Nadia; De Sarlo, Miriam; Carpi, Sara; Scaccini, Luca; Colagiorgio, Laura; Suman, Adrian Florentin; Mancini, Dorotea Frongia; Fazzi, Davide; Pellegrino, Roberto Maria; Signore, Giovanni; Rocchiccioli, Silvia; Cecchini, Marco; Tringali, Cristina
abstract: Krabbe disease (KD) is a lysosomal sphingolipidosis caused by the deficiency of galactocerebrosidase (GALC), leading to profound alterations in sphingolipid metabolism and severe neurodegeneration. While psychosine (Psy) accumulation is a well-established hallmark of KD, emerging evidence suggests that lactosylceramide (LacCer) may also contribute to disease pathogenesis. Here, we generated a novel human oligodendrocytic model of GALC deficiency by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated GALC knockout in MO3.13 cells and used it to investigate sphingolipid alterations associated with impaired GALC activity. GALC(-/-) MO3.13 cells showed a marked reduction in GALC transcript levels and enzymatic activity, confirming the successful establishment of a disease-relevant cellular model. Our results demonstrated that a) GALC knockout MO3.13 cells accumulated Psy and LacCer, and b) LacCer content was increased in the brain and heart isolated from twitcher (TWI) mice, the most widely used spontaneous animal model of KD. In parallel, AKT signalling was evaluated in both systems, supporting a link between LacCer dysregulation and altered cellular signalling pathways. Overall, these findings identify LacCer accumulation as a conserved feature of GALC deficiency across cellular and animal models and support the use of GALC(-/-) MO3.13 cells as a novel in vitro platform to investigate KD pathogenesis and candidate therapeutic strategies.

title: Machine Learning Guided Meta-transcriptomics Reveals OsRPM1 as a Key Regulator of Rice Blast Resistance.
authors: Usman, Babar; Munir, Adeela; Khan, Naveed; Ikram, Muhammad; Zhao, Neng; Wang, Yiming; Gupta, Ravi; Kim, Yu-Jin; Kwon, Soon Wook; Kim, Sun Tae
abstract: Rice blast, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, is the most destructive fungal disease of rice, responsible for annual yield losses of 10-30% and posing a major threat to global food security. The rapid evolution of blast pathotypes and the polygenic nature of resistance complicate breeding efforts for durable resistance. In this study, we integrated multiple RNA-sequencing datasets, revealing a dynamic transcriptional landscape during infection. Compared with susceptible genotypes, resistant genotypes showed early downregulation of immune receptors (e.g., OsPtr, OsSAH2, OsWRKY64), followed by active upregulation of defense effectors (e.g., OsPR10b, chitinases, OsLsi6, OSMORF8a) during peak response stages. Key pathways, such as immune signaling, receptor kinases, and secondary metabolism, were enriched in resistance modules, whereas susceptibility was linked mainly to primary metabolism. Machine learning (ML) models, especially XGBoost (XGB), achieved high area under the curve (AUC) of up to 0.98 in predicting resistance, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis highlighting known and novel genes, including OsLP2, NB-ARC domain protein, OsRPM1, OsATG8d, and several uncharacterized proteins. Importantly, ML identified regulators that conventional methods missed, underscoring the value of integrated computational approaches. Functional validation of OsRPM1 using CRISPR/Cas9 knockout (KO) and overexpression (OX) lines confirmed its positive role in blast resistance, where KO mutants exhibited increased lesion length and higher pathogen accumulation. In contrast, OX lines showed enhanced resistance and improved photosynthetic performance and hydrogen peroxide (H(2)O(2)) accumulation. These findings provide a comprehensive resource of candidate genes and regulatory modules for functional validation and molecular breeding, offering a robust foundation for developing rice cultivars with broad-spectrum and durable blast resistance.

title: Application of AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 for highly efficient gene editing in soybean (Glycine max L.) and Nicotiana benthamiana.
authors: Nguyen, Cuong X; Do, Phat T; Tran, Thu Minh
abstract: The widespread application of CRISPR/Cas genome editing for commercial crop improvement is currently hindered by a complex and restrictive intellectual property (IP) landscape. The recent development of OpenCRISPR-1, a fully AI-designed Cas9-like nuclease, provides a promising alternative with an accessible licensing framework; however, its efficacy in dicotyledonous plants remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the successful adaptation of the OpenCRISPR-1 system for targeted mutagenesis in soybean (Glycine max L.) and Nicotiana benthamiana. We constructed a plant-optimized binary vector (pBSE-OpenCRISPR-1) and validated its editing capability. In soybean (Glycine max), an Agrobacterium rhizogenes-mediated hairy root transformation assay targeting the GmFAD2-1B gene demonstrated that OpenCRISPR-1 actively induces site-specific mutations. In Nicotiana benthamiana, stable Agrobacterium-mediated transformation targeting the phytoene desaturase homologs (NbPDSa/b) achieved overall editing in 75% of T(0) transgenic lines (27/36). Analysis of individual homologs revealed editing rates of 66.7% (24/36) at both the NbPDSa and NbPDSb loci. Complete editing of the target locus occurred in 13.9% of events for NbPDSb and 2.8% for NbPDSa, including one event (2.8%) displaying simultaneous complete editing across all alleles resulting in a visible albino phenotype. Deep amplicon and Sanger sequencing revealed a characteristic mutation profile dominated by small insertions and deletions occurring two to three nucleotides upstream of the PAM. These results demonstrate that the AI-designed OpenCRISPR-1 system is a highly active and versatile nuclease for dicot genome engineering. By providing expanded freedom-to-operate, this tool broadens access to crop trait improvement worldwide.

title: MicroRNA core machinery maintains mitochondrial integrity to empower cancer escape from natural killer cell cytotoxicity.
authors: Chen, Jun-Yi; Zhao, Ze-Fang; Zhao, Hai-Xin; Zou, Miaowen; Qi, Chuhan Joyce; Peng, Zhen-Gang; Song, Tian-Yu; Cang, Yong
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells offer a promising off-the-shelf platform for cancer immunotherapy, yet their clinical efficacy is often limited by tumor-intrinsic resistance. Here, we show that loss of core microRNA (miRNA) machinery components, Argonaute‑2 (AGO2) or Ankyrin Repeat Domain 52 (ANKRD52), renders tumor cells hypersensitive to NK cell-mediated killing in both co-culture and xenograft models. Mechanistically, genetic ablation of Ago2 or Ankrd52 impairs miRNA-mediated silencing of critical mitochondrial apoptotic regulators and NK-cell-associated ligands in tumor cells, exemplified by the disrupted repression of pro-apoptotic Bim transcripts by miR-24 and miR-29b, thereby unleashing rapid TNF-alpha-driven apoptosis. Additionally, metabolic and ultrastructural analyses demonstrate collapsed membrane potential, diminished ATP levels, and fragmented mitochondria in Ago2- or Ankrd52-mutant tumor cells, accompanied by a lower apoptotic threshold upon TNF-alpha or NK cell challenge. Genome‑wide CRISPR library screen further revealed a selective fitness dependency on mitochondrial electron‑transport and ATP‑synthase genes in mutant tumor cells. Collectively, these findings define defective miRNA machinery as a tumor‑intrinsic vulnerability that couples mitochondrial fragility with increased NK-mediated cytotoxicity, nominate miRNA‑pathway status as a predictive biomarker, and propose that co‑targeting mitochondrial metabolism or apoptosis may potentiate NK‑cell therapies.

title: Discovery and Optimization of Anticancer Dibenzothiazepinones That Target the Ribosome Biogenesis Factor NVL.
authors: Tao, Ye; Guo, Holly H; Cruz, Victor E; Reddy, Divya; Leach, Ashley; Williams, Noelle S; Aurora, Arin B; Khivansara, Vishal; Han, Yan; Erzberger, Jan P; Nijhawan, Deepak; De Brabander, Jef K
abstract: Using inducible forward genetics, we recently discovered a dibenzothiazepinone (1) with activity against cancer cells via inhibition of the ribosome biogenesis factor NVL (nuclear valosin-containing protein-like). Herein, we delineate a comprehensive structure-activity relationship (SAR) study that explores the structural space surrounding the dibenzothiazepinone scaffold. A series of 115 analogs were synthesized and evaluated for activity against the colorectal cancer cell line HCT116 and counter-screened against cells CRISPR engineered to express a compound-resistant mutation in NVL. Our initial medicinal chemistry-driven campaign focused on improving potency, metabolic stability, and in vivo exposure and clearance. A fluorescence polarization assay with recombinant human NVL established a correlation between NVL-binding and antiproliferative activity. Cryo-EM structures of human NVL with select inhibitors revealed a binding mode that is consistent with the SAR data. This study led to the in vivo analog 100 (MM927), which we reported to suppress tumor growth in vivo without detectable toxicity via targeting the NVL.

title: Cell lineages of soybean anther morphogenesis reveal developmental trajectory of microsporocytes at single-cell resolution.
authors: Yang, Shiqian; Li, Ke; Chen, Zhiyu; Pan, Siran; Ye, Rong; Yang, Yan; Huang, Yushan; You, Chenjiang; Guo, Jing; Qi, Ji; Wang, Yingxiang; Wang, Cong
abstract: In flowering plants, anther morphogenesis and microspore mother cell (MMC) specification of the male reproductive organ are critical for fertility and seed-setting or yield, but their underlying mechanisms in soybean (Glycine max) remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we cytologically established a staged developmental framework of early soybean anthers that were collected to generate a high-resolution single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas. We further characterized 11 major cell types annotated by cluster-specific marker genes and validated by RNA in situ hybridization. Pseudotime trajectory analysis reconstructed the differentiation process of microsporocytes, tapetum, and middle layer from archesporial cells, and established a regulatory network governing germline development. Parallel comparison of mitotic dividing cells (DCs) and meiotic MMCs revealed divergent transcriptional and cell-cycle programs. DCs follow a linear mitotic cascade with smooth, continuous transcriptional regulation, whereas MMCs undergo lineage-specific transcriptional reprogramming with an oscillatory activation of cell-cycle regulators to orchestrate meiotic transitions and progression. By comparing the transcriptional regulatory network of DCs and MMCs, we identified a pair of C2H2 zinc finger factors GmKNUa/b, the homologs of Arabidopsis KNUCKLES, as a key switch for MMC differentiation in soybean. The CRISPR-Cas9-edited Gmknua/b double mutants lack meiocytes, and GmKNUa/b might trigger the mitosis-to-meiosis transition by repressing the persistent mitotic cell cycle. Taken together, these results reveal the cellular signatures and molecular basis of early soybean anther morphogenesis and germline specialization, and provide candidate targets for manipulating germline fate and male fertility in soybean.

title: Microbiome-guided rhizosphere engineering for sustainable remediation of agricultural soil contaminants.
authors: Arunkumar, Priya
abstract: Agricultural soils increasingly carry mixtures of pesticide residues, heavy metals, petroleum hydrocarbons and microplastics, and conventional phytoremediation is too slow and too contaminant-specific to address them. Rhizosphere engineering, the deliberate manipulation of root-associated microbial communities, is widely proposed as the alternative, but the literature reports laboratory, pot and field results in a single register, so a reader cannot easily tell which approaches are deployable. This mini-review stratifies that evidence rather than surveying it. Every approach examined is assigned to one of three tiers: field-validated, emerging at pot or microcosm scale, or conceptual. Only two domains prove to be field-validated, namely metal immobilization and phytoextraction through bioaugmentation and bulk amendment, and hydrocarbon rhizoremediation by defined consortia; both rest on cultured isolates rather than engineered organisms. Microplastic rhizoremediation has not been demonstrated in soil, and we separate interception, adsorption, weathering, transformation and mineralization to show why reported removal is usually not degradation. Synthetic biology, CRISPR-based community editing and computational design remain conceptual, and we set out the horizontal gene transfer, containment, non-target and regulatory obstacles that stand between them and field use. We identify the measurements that would move an approach from one tier to the next, and argue that the principal deficit in this field is not technical capability but field-scale evidence reported to a common standard.

title: GmNFYA14 negatively regulates soybean seed oil content by interacting with GmWRI1a.
authors: Gou, Han; Li, Xi; Chai, Shuxin; Chen, Meiling; Chen, Xiaochao; Yang, Yunhua; Du, Huan; Ding, Bao-Jian; Xing, Han; Deng, Ping; Yuan, Fengjie; Liu, Bei
abstract: INTRODUCTION: High oil content determines the commercial value of soybean, so the mechanisms that regulate oil accumulation are important targets for quality improvement. GmWRI1a is a core regulator of lipid biosynthesis in soybean, but the proteins that cooperate with it are still poorly defined. METHODS: Yeast two‑hybrid screening using truncated GmWRI1a as bait identified GmNFYA14. Multiple in-vitro and in-vivo protein interaction assays verified the physical interaction between GmNFYA14 and GmWRI1a. We generated GmNFYA14 overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout soybean lines to analyze seed storage components, and combined dual‑luciferase, EMSA and RNA‑seq assays to dissect the regulatory mechanism. RESULTS: Overexpression of GmNFYA14 reduced seed oil content by 2.96-4.13%, total fatty acid content by 9.90-10.78% and triacylglycerol content by 6.32-8.88%, while increasing protein content by 3.53-6.64%. Conversely, knockout of GmNFYA14 increased total fatty acid content by 13.51-13.90% and triacylglycerol content by 15.82%. GmNFYA14 did not occupy the promoters of these lipid genes itself. Instead, it interacted with GmWRI1a and attenuated both the transcriptional activity of GmWRI1a and its binding to the promoters of downstream lipid biosynthetic genes such as GmPKP-beta1 and GmKAS1. Consistent with this, transcriptome profiling showed that GmNFYA14 suppresses the expression of GmWRI1a-regulated lipid-related genes, restricting seed lipid accumulation. DISCUSSION: GmNFYA14 is a negative regulator of soybean oil accumulation that acts by dampening GmWRI1a activity rather than by binding target promoters directly. The GmNFYA14-GmWRI1a module adds a layer of control to fatty acid synthesis in seeds and provides candidate targets for molecular breeding to improve soybean oil content and agronomic traits.

title: Highly sensitive and specific detection of aminoglycoside resistance methylase gene armA by multiple cross displacement amplification-CRISPR/Cas12a technique.
authors: Gong, Lin; Wang, Juan; Zhang, Yuandong; Xu, Huiqiong; Liu, Xiaoli; Chen, Xiaomin; Li, Meiling; Li, Yao; Wu, Liqun; Wang, Yimei; Shen, Xiantao
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The 16S rRNA methylase armA serves as a key molecular determinant conferring high-level resistance to aminoglycoside antibiotics in bacterial pathogens. Development of a rapid and reliable armA gene detection assay will improve surveillance of enzyme-producing strains and support drug resistance control in diverse ecological settings. METHODS: A multiple cross displacement amplification (MCDA) combined with CRISPR/Cas12a system assay was established to identify armA gene with rapidity, specificity, and sensitivity. RESULTS: The entire experimental process, including genomic DNA extraction (15 minutes), MCDA reaction (40 minutes), CRISPR/Cas12a-mediated cleavage (5 minutes), and fluorescence detection (10 minutes), can be completed within 70 minutes. In terms of analytical specificity, the assay yielded positive results for all armA-positive isolates and negative results for all non-armA samples. The sensitivity of the MCDA-CRISPR/Cas12a assay reached a detection limit as low as 10 copies/mL of armA-positive plasmid DNA. In 129 cultured clinical isolates validated by whole-genome sequencing, the assay achieved 100% concordance for armA detection. DISCUSSION: The technique established in this study provides a rapid and accurate diagnostic approach for laboratory-based surveillance of armA in clinical and livestock settings, with future potential for point-of-care adaptation following further simplification and validation.

title: RPA-primed droplet-partitioned CRISPR/Cas12a assay for low-copy detection of Candida albicans in vaginal specimens.
authors: Long, Ju; Xie, Juan; Liu, Fang; Peng, Jie; Xu, Wen-Fei; Li, Xu-Hui
journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
abstract: Candida albicans is a major cause of vulvovaginal candidiasis, and sensitive detection of low-abundance fungal DNA remains challenging in clinical specimens. In this study, we developed a two-stage assay combining rapid recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with droplet-partitioned CRISPR/Cas12a fluorescence detection. Target DNA was first amplified by RPA for 10 min and subsequently analyzed in vortex-generated polydisperse droplets without microfluidic chip fabrication. Using predefined NTC-based analytical criteria, the operational LoDs were 10 copies/muL for the bulk RPA-Cas12a assay and 1 copy/muL for the droplet-partitioned format under the tested conditions. No cross-reactivity was observed with the tested non-target organisms, including additional clinically relevant non-albicans Candida species. In a preliminary evaluation of 28 residual vaginal swab specimens, the assay showed complete concordance with a routine composite clinical reference using an exploratory cohort-derived droplet-count cutoff. Because the comparator was not species-specific for C. albicans, these findings represent preliminary concordance rather than definitive diagnostic accuracy. The complete workflow was performed within approximately 1 h using basic laboratory equipment. These findings demonstrate that droplet partitioning can improve the low-copy analytical readout of RPA-Cas12a detection and provide a practical approach for qualitative identification of C. albicans DNA in vaginal specimens.

title: Beyond Glycan Binding: Defining Professional Glycoconjugate Counterreceptors in Cellular Systems.
authors: Lee, Elizabeth A; Pang, Jia Meng; Huang, Mia L
abstract: Glycan-protein interactions can regulate important biological processes yet are often described in simplistic terms of glycan-binding preferences that imply broad and promiscuous recognition. This conventional ligand-receptor paradigm often fails to distinguish simple binding events from functional binding with downstream biological effects observed in cellular contexts. In this review, we formalize the concept of professional glycoconjugate counterreceptors (PGCRs), which are defined as glycoconjugates whose glycan composition and protein scaffold together enable selective engagement by glycan-binding proteins (GBPs) to drive biological function. We review emerging chemical biology, proteomic, and genetic approaches including proximity labeling, crosslinking mass spectrometry, and CRISPR-based screening, that enable context-dependent identification of PGCRs. These studies reveal that glycan recognition is frequently scaffold-dependent and mediated by discrete glycoproteoforms rather than generic glycan motifs alone. Representative examples, such as Gal-3-CD9 and CD43-Siglec-7 interactions, highlight the importance of integrating binding with functional validation. We envision that a framework shift from a glycan-centric to a glycoconjugate-centric view of molecular recognition can improve our understanding of glycan-dependent signaling particularly in the landscape of druggable biology.

title: Animal and Cell Models in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Disease: Current Innovations Reviewed.
authors: Rejitha, Christopher; Babu, Lavanya
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) remain major global health challenges due to their complex pathology and lack of curative therapies. Advancing therapeutic strategies requires reliable experimental models that recapitulate disease mechanisms. This review summarizes recent developments in animal and in vitro models for AD and PD, with emphasis on their translational relevance and applications. Transgenic mice (APP/PS1, 3xTg-AD), alpha-synuclein and LRRK2-based models for PD, rat 6- OHDA systems, zebrafish, and non-human primates provide valuable insights into amyloid deposition, tau aggregation, synaptic dysfunction, and motor impairment, though each presents limitations in faithfully mimicking human disease. Complementary in vitro approaches using neuronal and glial cell lines enable targeted studies on oxidative stress, inflammation, amyloid-beta (Abeta) toxicity, tau pathology, and dopaminergic degeneration. Emerging platforms such as CRISPR/Cas9-based editing, induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived organoids, and artificial intelligence-driven drug discovery are further expanding the preclinical landscape. Together, these integrated strategies enhance understanding of neurodegenerative processes and hold promise for the development of effective disease-modifying therapies.

title: Emerging Technologies for Viability Assessment of Foodborne Pathogens: From Molecular Dyes to Artificial Intelligence.
authors: Wang, Ze Yu; Farid, Anum; Chen, Zhi Wei; Qi, Jia Yi; Shen, Xin Xin; Liu, Hong
abstract: To critically examine emerging technologies for assessing foodborne-pathogen viability and to evaluate their relevance for improving food safety monitoring and public-health risk assessment. This review examines the literature on viability-detection using biological indicators such as membrane integrity, infectivity, and virulence. It addresses technologies such as viability dye-based PCR, RNA and CRISPR detection methods, biosensors, bacteriophage assays, Raman spectroscopy, and AI-supported analysis. Compared to conventional culture-based and DNA-only molecular methods, viability-focused techniques support more biologically meaningful detection, particularly for viable but non-culturable (VBNC) cells that may retain pathogenic potential. However, assay performance varies depending on food-matrix complexity, the presence of inhibitors, sensitivity limitations, and the degree of validation. Integrated systems combining multi-modal sensing, microfluidics, and machine learning have shown increasing promise for rapid on-site application, although standardization and regulatory validation remain limited. The emerging viability-focused technologies substantially refine microbial-risk assessment by accurately capturing the infectious potential of foodborne pathogens, including traditionally undetected VBNC populations. Nevertheless, integrating these technologies into routine surveillance remains constrained by matrix interference and the absence of standardized protocols. Future efforts must prioritize developing matrix-resilient methodologies and establishing regulatory validation frameworks to facilitate their practical implementation in food safety management.

title: Regulation of Oxidative Stress Associated with an SSK2 Point Mutation Promotes Amphotericin B Resistance in Cryptococcus gattii.
authors: Deng, Heng Yu; Zang, Xue Feng; Zhao, En Qi; Huang, Ye Mei; Liu, Jing; Zhou, Yang Yu; Yang, Chen; He, Wen Cong; Dong, Xiao Zhuo; Chen, Hui; Zhao, Zi Qi; Zhou, Yu Han; Zang, Xue Lei; Wang, Chen; Zhang, Li Ye; Xue, Xin Ying
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Cryptococcus gattii ( C. gattii) is a pathogenic respiratory fungus that rapidly disseminates through the central nervous system. The current clinical treatments for C. gattii infections are limited by prolonged therapeutic courses, high drug dosages, and insufficient antifungal options. This study aimed to explore the molecular mechanisms underlying amphotericin B (AmB) resistance in C. gattii and provide novel insights for developing targeted antifungal strategies. METHODS: A total of 27 clinical C. gattii isolates were subjected to antifungal susceptibility testing, multilocus sequence typing (MLST) for phylogenetic analysis and resistance-related mutation screening. The CRISPR/Cas9 system was used to construct an SSK2-knockout mutant ( ssk2Delta-G4). Capsule and melanin assays, murine pulmonary infection models, and transcriptomic analyses were performed to verify gene function, evaluate therapeutic efficacy, and explore the underlying regulatory mechanisms. RESULTS: G4 isolates exhibited prominent AmB resistance with a novel SSK2 c.793A>G missense mutation (p.Thr265Ala; hereafter SSK2 (T265A)). SSK2 knockout significantly enhanced AmB susceptibility, whereas SSK2 (T265A) complementation partially restored the resistant phenotype. AmB treatment markedly reduced pulmonary fungal burden and inflammatory infiltration ( P < 0.05) and improved survival ( P < 0.001) in ssk2Delta-G4-infected mice. Mechanistically, this mutation upregulated CAT1 expression and enhanced the reactive oxygen species-scavenging capacity and oxidative stress tolerance. CONCLUSION: SSK2 c.793A>G is closely associated with AmB resistance and functionally contributes to the resistance phenotype. SSK2 could serve as a potential therapeutic target for developing AmB synergistic sensitizers and as a research direction for future synergistic treatments of clinically resistant C. gattii strains.

title: Tetrahedral DNA nanostructure-gated solution-phase CRISPR/Cas12a system for probe immobilization-free, reagent-efficient, and dual-phase electrochemical detection of circulating microRNAs in liquid biopsy.
authors: Chen, Shaohao; Ye, Huajuan; Lin, Bohan; Huang, Dunhao; Chen, Yang; Li, Ning; Zhuang, Junyang; Wei, Yong; Xu, Ning
abstract: Liquid-biopsy nucleic acid biomarkers hold strong promise for non-invasive cancer diagnostics, yet their ultralow abundance presents substantial analytical challenges. Conventional electrochemical biosensors rely on complex probe immobilization, whereas emerging homogeneous strategies remain susceptible to matrix interference and require large reaction volumes. Here, we report a probe immobilization-free, reagent-efficient, dual-phase electrochemical platform that integrates solution-phase CRISPR/Cas12a reactions with a tetrahedral DNA nanostructure (TDN)-based interfacial gating mechanism for detecting circulating microRNAs. We found that TDNs extended with a thiolated blocking fragment (BF) impose a pronounced steric gating effect at the electrode-solution interface: the large, rigid TDN architecture prevents intact BF-linked structures from approaching the gold electrode, whereas smaller Cas12a-generated thiolated fragments readily assemble via Au-S interactions. This size-dependent gating transition switches the electrode from an HRP-accessible to an HRP-blocking state, producing a sharply resolved signal decrease that faithfully maps solution-phase cleavage onto an electrochemical readout. Using a target-competitive binding strategy to generate the activator DNA, this interfacial gating mechanism was developed into a robust dual-phase sensing platform driven by CRISPR/Cas12a. Because target recognition and Cas12a-mediated cleavage occur entirely in solution and only the final reaction products contact the electrode, the architecture retains high homogeneous reaction efficiency while avoiding diffusion-governed limitations and eliminating probe immobilization. The 10 microL reaction volume enables substantial reagent savings and strong compatibility with complex matrices. The assay achieves a detection limit of 4.1 aM and accurately quantifies renal cancer-associated circulating miRNA-21 in peripheral blood, yielding results fully consistent with RT-qPCR.

title: CRISPR screening-informed liver cancer stratification identifies ciclesonide as a novel adjuvant drug to alleviate sorafenib resistance.
authors: Liu, Tian; Liu, Kewei; Hou, Yongying; Chu, Zhaole; Li, Jinyang; Sun, Mengting; Wu, Linyu; Liu, Qin; Zhou, Zhili; Zhang, Qiaoqiao; Wang, Bin; Wen, Qinglian; Wang, Xingwei; Min, Jiang
abstract: Sorafenib remains a standard therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but intratumor heterogeneity and drug resistance limit its efficacy. To identify resistance-associated genes, we performed a CRISPR activation screen and integrated results with TCGA and GTEx data. Using univariate Cox and LASSO regression, we constructed a five-gene (AKR1B15, BMF, GBA, GINS2, SMC2) sorafenib sensitivity-related prognostic signature. In the TCGA-LIHC training cohort (n = 371), patients with high-risk scores showed significantly worse overall survival and reduced sorafenib sensitivity, which was validated in the ICGC-US cohort. High risk scores also correlated with adverse clinicopathological features. Drug perturbation Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (dpGSEA) identified ciclesonide as a potential sensitizer to sorafenib. Cell viability assays and a subcutaneous xenograft model confirmed that ciclesonide enhanced the antitumor efficacy of sorafenib. RNA sequencing further suggested that this effect may be mediated through regulation of the cell cycle pathway. Collectively, the sorafenib DS-related prognostic signature may serve as an independent prognostic biomarker and predictor of sorafenib sensitivity in HCC, while the combination of sorafenib and ciclesonide represents a promising strategy to improve targeted therapy.

title: Prime Editing-Mediated Genome Modification in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
authors: Kaur, Navneet; Langley, Jethro; Billon, Pierre
abstract: Prime editing is a highly versatile genome editing technology that enables precise genetic modifications in eukaryotes. Here, we present a detailed step-by-step protocol for conducting prime editing in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. In particular, we describe the design of prime editing guide RNAs (pegRNAs), yeast transformation with prime editor and pegRNA plasmids, and controlled expression through galactose induction. We demonstrate the protocol by targeting the CAN1 gene and achieving editing efficiencies of 22% and 55% with two different pegRNAs. We provide protocols for genomic DNA extraction, PCR amplification, and editing quantification using both Sanger and next-generation sequencing. Given the important role of yeast in both basic research and biotechnology applications, this protocol provides valuable tools for studying gene function and precise engineering of yeast strains.

title: Plant Prime Editing: Design, Assembly, and Application.
authors: Gupta, Ajay; Yang, Bing
abstract: Prime Editing (PE) is the latest technological advancement in genome editing. With the capabilities of altering the genome with precision and efficiency, PE offers great advantages over conventional CRISPR-Cas9 as well as base editors to achieve all 12 possible base changes and small indels. However, the complicated design and assembly of prime editing constructs is a limiting step in the wider applicability of the technology. In this chapter, we set forth step-by-step protocols aimed at helping the scientific community in designing their constructs as well as assembling them to target up to four genes. With the availability of PE plasmids and design/assembly protocols, PE in plants can be carried out by more labs across the globe to recognize the great potential of PE in their research.

title: All-in-One Prime Editing System for Efficient Generation and Isolation of Single Edited hiPSC Clones.
authors: Theodore, Keith; Tahir, Saleha; Costa, Bruna Lopes da; Quinn, Peter M J
abstract: Prime editing has emerged as the preferred gene-editing technique due to its versatility and precision in introducing genetic modifications such as single-base pair substitutions, insertions, and deletions without the need for double-strand breaks (DSBs) and a donor template. Thus, substantially reduces the likelihood of off-target effects that are generally produced when using the traditional CRISPR-Cas9 system. Here, we describe an in-depth protocol for the generation and isolation of prime-edited single human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) clones. In this example, we transfect a commercial hiPSC line with an all-in-one prime editor plasmid to install a pathogenic PRPH2 mutation using the PE3 approach.

title: Improvement of Genome Editing Efficiency in Mammalian Cells by a Refined Uni-Vector Prime Editing System.
authors: Liao, Li-Zhu; Wu, Kou-Juey
abstract: Prime editing is an advanced technology in the CRISPR/Cas genome editing field. The original multi-vector method utilized in prime editing has less efficiency and precision and is also inherently difficult in generating homozygous mutations in mammalian cells. To overcome these technical difficulties, a Uni-vector prime editing system containing the major components for prime editing has been constructed in two all-in-one plasmids, pPE3-pPuro and pePE5max-pPuro. The Uni-vector prime editing plasmids enhance the editing efficiency of prime editing and improve the generation of homozygous mutated mammalian cell lines. The editing efficiency depends on the transfection efficiency. Remarkably, the Uni-vector ePE5max system can achieve a high editing rate even in cell lines that are traditionally difficult to transfect. This Uni-vector approach simplifies the delivery of all the necessary editing components and greatly improves the editing efficiency. This approach represents an advanced progress in the field of prime editing.

title: Protocol for Prime Editing with Engineered PAM-Flexible Cas9 Variants.
authors: Jang, Gayoung; Kweon, Jiyeon; Kim, Yongsub
abstract: Prime editing (PE) is a precision genome-editing technology that allows all types of editing, such as substitutions, insertions, and deletions, at the target site in the genome of a cell without double-strand breaks (DSBs) or donor DNA. However, the targeting range of existing prime editing systems is limited due to their dependence on the NGG protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) recognized by Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (spCas9). To address this limitation, we have engineered prime editor variants incorporating PAM-flexible Cas9 proteins. These variants significantly expand the range of targetable genomic sites, allowing for the introduction of mutations previously inaccessible to standard editing methods. Here, we provide detailed methods for applying these PAM-flexible PE variants in human cell lines.

title: Rapid Cell-Free Preparation of Circular Vector DNA for pegRNA Expression in Prime Editing.
authors: Oliynyk, Roman Teo; Church, George M
abstract: The expression of prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) is crucial for effective CRISPR-Cas9 prime genome editing, traditionally facilitated by DNA plasmids, which require a time-consuming process of bacterial cloning, validation, and purification. The Circular Vector (CV) protocol represents an efficient, fully synthetic, cell-free method that bypasses these traditional steps, allowing for the preparation of pegRNA expression vectors within 3 h. This approach involves circularizing and purifying linear double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) templates containing a promoter with pegRNA elements into compact, bacterial-backbone-free vectors. These CVs offer significant advantages: absence of a bacterial backbone, absence of endotoxins, and no contamination by bacterial nucleic acids, making them a superior choice for transfection in cell culture experiments, where they have shown performance equal to or better than that of traditional plasmids. The CV protocol not only speeds up the preparation process but also reduces costs and complexity, making it an ideal tool for rapid and efficient pegRNA expression in research settings.

title: pegRNA Online Tool Design and Experimental Assembly: Exploring the Practical Use of PE-Designer for Prime Editing.
authors: Santos Sousa, Ines; Patricio, Daniela; Torres, Mara; Marques, Joao Pedro; Ambrosio, Antonio Francisco; Alves, C Henrique
abstract: Prime editing (PE) is an innovative genome-editing technology that enables precise genetic modifications with greater efficiency compared to traditional CRISPR/Cas9-based systems. The successful application of this method heavily depends on the design of prime editing guide RNAs (pegRNAs). Efficient design of pegRNAs is facilitated by online tools like PE-Designer ( www.rgenome.net/pe-designer/) , which offers a user-friendly interface for designing pegRNA and nicking single-guide RNA (sgRNA) sequences. Notable features of PE-Designer include its flexibility in adjusting the prime binding site (PBS) and reverse transcription template (RTT) lengths of pegRNAs, as well as its ability to assess potential off-target effects across various genomes. This chapter focuses on using PE-Designer for pegRNA design, providing a step-by-step guide to the tool while addressing frequent challenges. Furthermore, using the SnapGene software, we explore the assembly of both the pegRNA and sgRNA construct maps. Finally, the chapter presents the experimental protocol for constructing both the pegRNA and sgRNA vectors, with a detailed explanation of the Golden Gate assembly technique.

title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA.
authors: Donaldson, Gregory P; Lima Dos Reis, Gabriella; Saad, Marwa; Wichmann, Christopher; Mamede, Izabela; Chen, Guo; Harrer, Caroline E; DelGaudio, Nicole L; Zhang, Dayu; Aydin, Begum; Castro, Tiago B R; Grivennikov, Sergei I; Reis, Bernardo S; Liu, Elise G; Eisenbarth, Stephanie C; Birsoy, Kivanc; Tavazoie, Sohail F; Stadtmueller, Beth M; Victora, Gabriel D; Mucida, Daniel
abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis(1). IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function(2,3), with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities(4-8). Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

title: Mediator kinase inhibition exposes a transcriptional vulnerability and synergizes with venetoclax in AML.
authors: Aitchedji, Camille; Moison, Celine; Fortier, Simon; Mendoza-Sanchez, Rodrigo; Gracias, Deanne; Spinella, Jean-Francois; Thavonekham, Bounkham; MacRae, Tara; Mayotte, Nadine; Frechette, Melanie; Blouin-Chagnon, Valerie; Leveille, Koryne; Chagraoui, Jalila; Ruel, Rejean; Hebert, Josee; Marinier, Anne; Sauvageau, Guy
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous and aggressive hematologic malignancy associated with poor survival despite recent therapeutic advances. To identify novel anti-leukemic agents, we performed a high-throughput viability screen of 10,000 small molecules across 56 genetically diverse primary AML samples. Compounds with similar activity profiles were grouped into Compound Correlation Clusters (CCCs), leading to the identification of CCC163, which includes AML874, as a potent and selective hit. Integrated pharmacological and CRISPR-Cas9 approaches identified the Mediator complex as the molecular target of AML874. We demonstrated that AML874 acts as a selective CDK8/CDK19 inhibitor, disrupting Mediator-dependent transcription. FLT3-mutated AML showed increased sensitivity to AML874, suggesting a subtype-specific vulnerability. Notably, CDK8 inhibition synergized with venetoclax in AML cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models, resulting in enhanced anti-leukemic activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CDK8/CDK19 inhibition as a therapeutically relevant strategy in AML.

title: Genome-wide screening identifies unique host-directed drugs and pro-viral signalling pathways for SARS-CoV-2.
authors: Khan, Juveriya Qamar; Rajamanickam, Karthic; Vizeacoumar, Frederick S; Balouchi, Mahrokh; Zhang, Yue; Elhasasna, Hussain; Rohamare, Megha; Dong, He; Glover, Kathleen; Anderson-Woodsworth, Tristan; Bhanumathy, Kalpana K; Lew, Jocelyne; Vizeacoumar, Franco J; Falzarano, Darryl; Kumar, Anil; Wilson, Joyce A
abstract: SARS-CoV-2 is a positive-sense RNA virus that was responsible for the devastating COVID-19 pandemic. Although the current disease burden is less severe, there are limited treatment options, and a looming threat of the emergence of variants and future pandemics. To address these challenges, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens in a novel human lung cell line NCI-H23(ACE2), as well as in HEK293T(ACE2) cells, with SARS-CoV-2 Wuhan strain, and identified several host-dependency factors including NRAS, KAT5, HTR3E and GNL3L. Drugs targeting some of these dependency factors, donepezil, dH-ergocristine, trametinib and sorafenib, showed effective pan-coronaviral inhibition in cell lines. Trametinib also showed inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant in primary human airway tissue model (ALI). We also demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 inhibits IFN-beta induction through an NRAS/Raf/MEK/ERK signaling pathway dependent mechanism. Our study highlights the efficiency of a bilateral approach of gene silencing and antiviral screening to identify host-dependency factors and effective antivirals.

title: A single-nucleus multiome map of the human cerebellum with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.
authors: Feng, Yayan; Chen, Xin; Song, Wenqiang; Yang, Xiaoyu; Dou, Lijun; Bonakdarpour, Borna; Jamshidi, Pouya; Castellani, Rudolph J; Mao, Qinwen; Chu, Xiaona; Gao, Hongyu; Liu, Yunlong; Xu, Jielin; Hou, Yuan; Martin, William; Nelson, Peter T; Leverenz, James B; Hu, Ming; Li, Yang E; Pieper, Andrew A; Cummings, Jeffrey; Flanagan, Margaret E; Cheng, Feixiong
abstract: Although cerebellum is neuropathologically affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and AD-related dementia (ADRD), the cell type-specific genomic and epigenomic changes remain poorly understood. Here, we present single-nucleus multiome (RNA-seq and ATAC-seq) analysis of 103,861 nuclei isolated from both the cerebellum and frontal cortex of diseased individuals and cognitively healthy controls. We identify 431,834 significant peak-to-gene linkages across cell subtypes, revealing cis-regulatory elements linked to cell type-specific and disease-associated transcriptomic and regulatory network changes. Differential trajectory analysis pinpoints disease-associated genes in cerebellar granule cells, such as STMN1 and CLU. Integrating epigenomic, genetic, and three-dimensional genome data, we pinpoint two likely causal variants linked to SEZ6L2 in Purkinje cells and KANSL1 in granule cells. Through CRISPR interference in patient-derived cerebellar organoids, we show that silencing the variant-containing regulatory elements suppresses SEZ6L2 and KANSL1 expression, which perturbs neurodegeneration-associated gene programs. This cell type-specific regulatory landscape provides genomic and epigenomic insights into the pathological role of the cerebellum in AD/ADRD.

title: Subfunctionalization with Partially Overlapping Roles of AGAMOUS Paralogs RdAG1 and RdAG2 of Rhododendron delavayi in Floral Organ Development.
authors: Ao, Qian; Zuo, Weiwei; Zeng, Liang; Guo, Qiqiang; Zhang, Bin; Nan, Hong; Gao, Chao; Li, Huie
journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
abstract: Rhododendron delavayi is an important ornamental plant in Southwest China that produces large showy flowers, yet the molecular basis of its complex floral morphology remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functional divergence of two AGAMOUS (AG) paralogs, RdAG1 and RdAG2, to elucidate floral organ development. Our results support a subfunctionalization model with partially overlapping functions: RdAG1 likely acts as a C-class gene mainly for stamen and carpel identity, whereas RdAG2 likely acts as a D-class gene primarily for pistil and ovule development. Heterologous expression in Arabidopsis thaliana and Nicotiana benthamiana revealed both divergent and overlapping phenotypic effects: the two genes differed in their tendencies to induce stamen-like and pistil-like structures, yet both induced homeotic conversion of sepals into carpels and were associated with downregulation of class A genes. Since an efficient regeneration system has not yet been established for R. delavayi, the C/D-class functional assignment is based on heterologous expression and awaits validation in native floral tissues. Yeast two-hybrid assays confirmed the physical interaction between RdAG1 and RdAG2, while DAP-seq in floral buds identified RdGIK as a shared downstream target. Transcriptomic analysis of calli generated via Agrobacterium-mediated CRISPR/Cas9 editing revealed that the majority of downstream targets were classified as showing additive responses, while a smaller subset deviated from this additive expectation. Collectively, these findings define a subfunctionalization model for RdAG1 and RdAG2, providing a foundation for further investigation of their finely tuned functions in floral organ development in R. delavayi.

title: Functional characterization of os9 reveals its role in zebrafish developmental regulation.
authors: Xie, Qiuting; Wu, Lingxin; Wu, Jiayi; He, Meiling; Li, Wenhua
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD) plays a critical role in maintaining proteostasis during development, yet its in vivo functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of os9, a key ERAD component, in zebrafish development. Sequence and protein-protein interaction analyses revealed that Os9 is highly conserved across vertebrates and participates in ER protein quality control. Using CRISPR/Cas9, we generated os9 knockout zebrafish lines and found that loss of os9 leads to developmental defects with incomplete penetrance. Affected os9 mutant larvae exhibited cardiovascular abnormalities, including pericardial edema, disrupted cardiac structure, and abnormal erythrocyte distribution. In addition, affected os9 mutants displayed microphthalmia with reduced retinal size, while retinal lamination was largely preserved. Ultrastructural analysis revealed pronounced ER dilation and mitochondrial disruption in photoreceptor cells, accompanied by downregulation of photoreceptor marker genes and impaired photoreceptor development. Furthermore, os9 deficiency was associated with increased apoptosis and oxidative stress, as evidenced by elevated Caspase 9 activity, altered expression of apoptosis-related genes, and imbalance of antioxidant markers. Transcriptome analysis of affected os9 mutants revealed extensive gene expression reprogramming, characterized by enrichment of stress- and apoptosis-related pathways and suppression of metabolic and redox-associated processes. Notably, genes involved in protein processing in ER were significantly upregulated, while pathways related to retinol metabolism and phototransduction were downregulated. Collectively, these findings suggest that os9 is required for maintaining cellular homeostasis during zebrafish development and that its loss leads to ER stress, oxidative stress, apoptosis, and tissue-specific developmental defects, particularly in the cardiovascular system and retina.

title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models.
authors: Pauli, Theresa M; von Heyl, Theresa; Rieblinger, Beate; Schleibinger, Sabrina Teresa; Liang, Wei; Schmauser, Antonia; Arullmoli, Mithuoshni; Derrer, Paul; Eckstein, Anika; Jagana, Sirradu; Gatti Correa, Camila; Flisikowski, Krzysztof; Flisikowska, Tatiana; Schusser, Benjamin
abstract: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human-animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

title: CRISPR-based pipeline for generating and validating multi-kb deletions and indels in iPSCs.
authors: Hamerlinck, Lisa; Perez Baca, Maria Del Rocio; Van Loon, Nore; Vantomme, Lies; Daal, Esperanza; Vaughan, Michael B; D'haene, Eva; Vergult, Sarah
abstract: Here, we present a CRISPR-Cas9 protocol for generating both small indels and multi-kilobase deletions to enable genome editing in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We describe steps for a ribonucleoprotein (RNP)-based approach that integrates guide RNA selection, electroporation, and multi-tiered screening to accurately identify indels, deletions, inversions, and mixed genotypes. Human iPSCs provide a versatile genome editing platform due to their capacity for clonal expansion and differentiation. This protocol provides a scalable framework for genome editing and quality control. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Hamerlinck et al.(1).

title: Beyond CAR-T: Multi-layered engineering strategies shaping the next generation of cellular cancer immunotherapy.
authors: Jiang, Yunqi; Zhang, Sai; Arami, Sharareh
abstract: Adoptive cellular immunotherapy has transformed the treatment landscape for hematologic malignancies; however, its broader application to solid tumors remains limited by antigen heterogeneity, inadequate persistence, restricted tumor infiltration, and the profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). While conventional CAR-T cell therapy has demonstrated remarkable clinical success, no single immune-cell platform is likely to overcome all biological barriers encountered in complex solid tumors. Emerging evidence instead supports a shift toward an integrated cellular immunotherapy ecosystem that combines the complementary strengths of multiple engineered immune cell populations. In this review, we present a unifying framework for the multi-layered engineering of next-generation immune cell therapies, encompassing CAR-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells, TCR-engineered alphabeta T cells, gammadelta T cells, CAR-natural killer T (CAR-NKT) cells, and CAR-macrophages. Rather than considering these platforms as isolated technologies, we examine how shared engineering strategies, including cytokine armoring, CRISPR-based genome editing, protein-level receptor optimization, tumor-responsive gene circuits, metabolic reprogramming, and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based manufacturing, can be integrated to enhance persistence, functionality, safety, and resistance to TME-mediated suppression. We further discuss the biological rationale, preclinical advances, and emerging clinical evidence supporting each platform, highlighting their distinct and complementary mechanisms of tumor recognition and immune activation. Finally, we propose that the future of cancer immunotherapy lies not in the optimization of a single cellular modality, but in the development of synergistic, scalable, and off-the-shelf engineered immune-cell networks capable of delivering durable and effective responses against heterogeneous solid tumors.

title: Tumor-Specific Gene Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming.
authors: Yang, He; Zhang, Haoyu; Zhao, Ziyin; Ren, Yuxuan; Xu, Yanhan; Cai, Kaimin; Cheng, Jianjun; Liu, Xun; Chen, Yongbing; Yin, Lichen
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.

title: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Palindromic Repeats-Cas Genome-Editing Systems in Filamentous Fungi: Current Tools, Optimization Strategies, and Future Perspectives.
authors: Du, Rubing; Wang, Wuyue; Xie, Jun; Li, Yuxue; Wu, Na; Xu, Qing
journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
abstract: Filamentous fungi are important microbial cell factories for producing antibiotics, organic acids, enzymes, and other valuable products, with broad applications in food, agriculture, and medicine. However, inefficient and imprecise genome editing remains a major bottleneck limiting rational strain engineering. This review summarizes major genome-editing tools in filamentous fungi, including Cre-loxP, TALENs, and CRISPR-Cas systems, with emphasis on their mechanisms, advantages, and limitations. We highlight CRISPR-Cas9 as the predominant platform and discuss optimization strategies involving sgRNA design, engineered Cas9 variants, promoter engineering, AMA1-based replicative plasmids, and ribonucleoprotein delivery. Emerging technologies, including base editing, prime editing, Cas12a, and Mad7, are also discussed for their potential to broaden editing capabilities. Finally, we outline future perspectives focusing on extending the application of existing genome-editing systems in filamentous fungi and discovering novel genome-editing tools from large-scale omics data sets. This review will accelerate the development of filamentous fungi as versatile platforms for biomanufacturing.

title: Mapping Osteosarcoma Biology With CRISPR/Cas: From Gene Function to Therapeutic Targets.
authors: El-Sehrawy, Amr Ali Mohamed Abdelgawwad; Sapaev, Ibrokhim; Nematov, Ozodbek; Turakulov, Rustam; Bayramdurdi, Sapaev; Turaeva, Nafisa O; Bainsal, Neeraj; Bansal, Pankaj; Smerat, Aseel
