This review discusses CRISPRi mechanisms, applications, advantages and limitations in insects, comparing it with RNAi and CRISPR/Cas9. Overall, current evidences indicate that CRISPRi is a precise and non-mutagenic platform for insect-pest management, particularly where controlled, reversible and species-specific gene regulation is desirable. However, its application in agricultural pest management remains an extrapolation from functional-genomics studies and requires validation in pest species under whole-organism and field-relevant conditions.

title: Archaeal histones coordinate conserved DNA sequence motifs to promote CRISPR adaptive immunity.
authors: Patel, Pranami; Treat, Ariana R; Gonzalez, Reyaz; Rajaraman, Sucheta; Cruga, Briana N; Chinea, Elizabeth B; Onwuka, Amarachi; Nguyen, Cat; Terns, Michael P; Santiago-Frangos, Andrew
abstract: Archaea and bacteria acquire resistance to viruses by integrating fragments of foreign DNA at the beginning of a CRISPR locus. In the archaeon Pyrococcus furiosus, histones bind the leader to promote specific integration at the first CRISPR repeat. However, it remains unknown whether archaeal CRISPR leaders contain conserved DNA sequence motifs required for integration. Here, we analyze 542 archaeal CRISPR leaders found across Thermococcales and Methanococcales. We identify 36 motifs found up to 500 bps upstream of archaeal CRISPR loci. Scrambling or truncating novel motifs or histone binding sites found 100-400 bps upstream of the P. furiosus CRISPR modestly decreases integration efficiency. However, mutation of motif T2, which overlaps with the proximal histone site and is adjacent to the CRISPR, ablates both histone-mediated and histone-independent integration. Mutations tiled across T2 reveal that a pyrimidine at position -3 of the leader is required for histone-independent integration, and basepairs -4 to -19 are required for histone-mediated integration. T2 is found in most Thermococcales, and a similar sequence is found in most Methanococcales leaders, suggesting this motif may be a broadly conserved element that facilitates CRISPR adaptive immunity across taxonomic orders. These data shed light on the sequence requirements for histone-mediated DNA integration.

title: Molecular origami in neuroscience: noncanonical DNA structures and functional nucleic acids in neural regulation and disease.
authors: Roy, Subhajit; Pradhan, Arpit Kumar; Jainarayanan, Ashwin Kumar
abstract: Gliomas are increasingly recognized as network diseases in which aberrant interactions between tumor cells, neurons, and immune populations drive hyperexcitability, seizures, cognitive dysfunction, and disease progression. Simultaneously, advances in structural biology and nucleic acid engineering have revealed DNA to be a dynamic molecular architecture capable of sensing, regulating, and modulating cellular states. In this review, we examine how noncanonical DNA structures and functional nucleic acids including Z-DNA, G-quadruplexes, cruciform structures, aptamers, and DNA origami systems, shape neural regulation and glioma associated circuit pathology. We discuss how activity dependent DNA conformational transitions influence transcriptional programs controlling neurotransmission, ion channel expression, synaptic signaling, metabolism, and inflammatory pathways in glioma cells and peritumoral neural networks. Z-DNA formation appears linked to rapid transcriptional activation and enhancer dynamics, whereas G-quadruplex rich regulatory regions modulate genes associated with excitatory signaling, cellular proliferation, and tumor progression. Cruciform DNA structures additionally interface with genome stability and DNA repair, creating mechanistic entry points for therapeutic intervention. Beyond endogenous DNA architectures, we highlight the emergence of aptamer based diagnostics and therapeutics capable of detecting neurotransmitters, cytokines, and metabolites associated with glioma induced network dysfunction. DNA origami platforms further enable programmable multivalent delivery systems for targeted transport of small molecules, oligonucleotides, CRISPR machinery, and ion-channel modulators across the neurovascular unit and tumor microenvironment. We also explore closed-loop neuromodulatory strategies in which electrophysiological signatures guide state dependent therapeutic actuation through nucleic acid based sensing and delivery systems. Finally, we discuss key translational considerations, including blood brain barrier delivery, nuclease stability, immunogenicity, biodistribution, manufacturing reproducibility, and integration with existing neuro-oncology and anti-seizure therapies. By bridging molecular origami, electrophysiology, and neurotechnology, this review proposes a framework for precision neuromedicine in glioma and broader neurological disease, where programmable nucleic acid architectures are coupled to the dynamic circuit states that drive pathology.

title: Engineering aptamer-based therapeutics for precision cancer immunotherapy: from molecular targeting to clinical applications.
authors: Azhar, Mohammad Asim; Ahmed, Sana; Altuhami, Abdullah; Shabab, Mohammad; Assiri, Abdullah M; Broering, Dieter C; Mir, Tanveer Ahmad
abstract: Although cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer therapy, the clinical efficacy of this approach is restricted due to tumor heterogeneity, immune escape, therapeutic resistance, poor tumor penetration, and toxic side effects. Short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, termed aptamers, have high affinity for a given target, low immunogenicity, and high chemical programmability and are emerging as promising agents for precision cancer therapies and immuno-oncology. This review aims to provide a comprehensive, integrated overview of the development of aptamer-based cancer therapeutics, from molecular engineering and pharmacology to clinical applications and translational potential. The discovery and optimization of tumor and immune-specific aptamers have been enhanced by the development of conventional SELEX, Cell-SELEX, in vivo SELEX, high-throughput sequencing, microfluidic selection, and AI-assisted selection. To enhance nuclease resistance, circulation time, biodistribution, and tumor accumulation, chemical modifications such as PEGylation, 2'-fluoro, 2'-O-methyl, LNAs, phosphorothioate linkages, circularization, and lipid/albumin binding have been developed. Aptamers can directly regulate oncogenic and immune signaling pathways or be used as targeted delivery vehicles for chemotherapeutic drugs, siRNAs, miRNAs, proteins, peptides, and CRISPR-based systems. Moreover, aptamers targeting tumor-associated biomarkers, cancer stem cells, the tumor vasculature, stromal components, and immune regulatory pathways have the potential to selectively remodel the tumor microenvironment. In addition, they are well-suited to other immunotherapy strategies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, photodynamic or photothermal therapy, oncolytic viruses, and cancer vaccines, thereby further supporting a multifunctional, personalized treatment approach. Although there has been significant progress in pre-clinical research, several issues remain regarding pharmacokinetics, tumor penetration, off-target effects, manufacturing, long-term safety, regulatory approval, and clinical validation. Additional advancements in aptamer engineering, nanotechnology, computational design, and biomarker-directed therapy could potentially enable the development of these platforms into successful next-generation precision cancer immunotherapies.

title: A rapid and simple vacuum infiltration system of germinated seeds for plant genetic transformation.
authors: Yang, Heru; Yu, Jiaxue; Wang, Weiyan; Chai, Ye; Jin, Taicheng; Yang, Liping
abstract: Plant transformation methods play a crucial role in molecular breeding that enhances crop yield and quality. The genetic transformation of soybean is mainly achieved through Agrobacterium-mediated methods. To solve the problem of long cycles in plant transformation, this study established and optimized a rapid and simple transformation system, namely the vacuum infiltration system of germinated seeds, in soybean (Glycine max (Linn.) Merr.). The expression of beta-glucuronidase (GUS) in soybean was achieved using this system, which did not need sterile conditions. The results of reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) analysis indicated that the GUS gene was stably expressed in T1-generation transgenic plants. Compared with traditional transformation methods, this system is rapid and simple and does not require tissue culture procedures. Moreover, to explore the CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system in combination with vacuum infiltration of germinated seeds, we used the gene editing vector pHEE-pds to knock out the PDS gene in tobacco (Nicotiana tabacum L.). In addition, the visual RUBY reporter gene combined with the vacuum infiltration of the cotyledons was applied to the soybean transformation, which effectively improves the screening of candidate transformants.

title: Genome Editing of Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurological Disease: Progress and Translational Barriers.
authors: Sharma, Reva; Niranjan, Nirupama; Long, Anika; Sharma, Rishika; Safieh, Fuad; Kumar, Pranesh; Sund, Pranaav; Sellami, Zahra
journal: The Yale journal of biology and medicine
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across neurological disease. Specifically, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial DNA damage are factors in primary mitochondrial disorders and major neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer, and Huntington diseases, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This review surveys the mechanisms driving mitochondrial dysfunction and evaluates the current landscape of gene-editing technologies developed to address them. We examine mitochondria-targeted editors and nuclear-targeted editors, examining the editing capability, delivery constraints, and off-target risk of each. Heteroplasmy-shifting nucleases currently offer the strongest in vivo evidence for mtDNA-directed therapy, while base editors extend correction to homoplasmic mutations at the cost of a narrower editing scope and off-target editing. Nuclear editing platforms avoid the mitochondrial gRNA import barrier entirely, allowing current technologies to achieve the most progress toward functional, behavioral rescue in animal models. Across all platforms, delivery efficiency, off-target specificity, and translation from rodent to primate models remain unresolved barriers to clinical application. Gene editing for mitochondrial dysfunction is highly creditable as a precision therapy for genetically defined disease subsets, including primary mitochondrial disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with a known nuclear driver, rather than as a universal strategy for sporadic neurodegeneration, where mitochondrial dysfunction arises from multifactorial and poorly localized causes.

title: Differential Impact of CRISPR/Cas9-Mediated OsMIR396ef Mutagenesis on Yield Components Across Eight Diverse Rice Varieties.
authors: Su, Fei; Vipasha, Verma; Dong, Yinghui; Huang, Sheng; Jiang, Xinxin; Mei, Fating; Zhang, Jinshan
abstract: Substantial gains in rice productivity are a continual demand for breeders, farmers, as well as consumers. Identifying and introducing favorable yield-related genes in elite cultivars is the most efficient strategy for increasing yield. So far, many yield-related genes in rice have been cloned. However, rice varieties with a vast diversity of genetic constitutions differ tremendously in the levels of grain yield. Here, we edited yield-related MIR396e and MIR396f genes in eight japonica rice varieties and found that mutation efficiency varied with genetic background in the T0 generation. Notably, the knockout of MIR396e and MIR396f genes resulted in increased leaf, panicle, and grain size in all eight genetic backgrounds. However, plant height, culm strength, grain number per panicle, and seed setting rate varied with different genetic backgrounds. Results also showed that among the eight varieties, grain yield increased in five different rice varieties compared to the corresponding wild type, while three of them had decreased yield due to the reduced number of grains per panicle or the seed-setting rate. Thus, our findings broaden the understanding that OsmiR396 can have diverse, even opposing effects on grain yield and plant architecture among genetically distinct rice varieties.

title: Efficient Bioproduction of Citric Acid in Aspergillus niger.
authors: Zheng, Xiaomei; Sun, Jibin; Zheng, Ping
abstract: Citric acid is the most widely produced organic acid in industrial biotechnology, with a global annual output exceeding 2 million tons and broad applications across the food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and environmental sectors. Despite more than a century of industrial development since the discovery of citric acid fermentation by Aspergillus niger in 1917, current production systems are approaching critical bottlenecks in strain performance, process efficiency, and environmental sustainability. Increasing evidence indicates that citrate overproduction is not governed by a single metabolic pathway but emerges as a multi-constraint-driven systems phenomenon involving coordinated regulation of metabolism, cellular physiology, and environmental conditions. Recent advances in systems biology and synthetic biology have enabled a paradigm shift from empirical optimization to rational and programmable biomanufacturing. The integration of multi-omics data with genome-scale metabolic models has substantially deepened the understanding of citrate overflow metabolism. In parallel, the development of CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, dynamic gene regulation systems, and promoter engineering has enabled precise and multiplexed rewiring of metabolic networks. Targeted engineering strategies focusing on carbon uptake, mitochondrial metabolism, citrate transport, and morphology regulation have demonstrated that high-level production requires coordinated multi-layer optimization rather than single-gene modifications. At the process level, emerging strategies, including immobilized fermentation, in situ product recovery, and the utilization of alternative non-food feedstocks, are being increasingly integrated with engineered strains to enhance productivity and sustainability. These advances collectively point toward a transition from conventional fermentation to a multi-scale, integrated biomanufacturing framework. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent progress in citric acid biomanufacturing, covering the evolution of industrial A. niger strains, systems-level mechanisms of citrate accumulation, synthetic biology-enabled tool development, rational chassis engineering strategies, and process intensification approaches. Finally, we discuss future directions, including dynamic metabolic control, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and circular biorefinery systems, aiming to establish a fully integrated, intelligent, and sustainable paradigm for next-generation citric acid production.

title: The gene ivory:mir-193 controls scale type differentiation in Heliconius butterflies.
authors: Hanly, Joseph J; Camino, Leo; Holder, Julia C; Calderon-Onate, Paola; Wagh, Pushkar R; Ruiz, Joshue; Zhao, Leia; Stroh, Eva D; Livraghi, Luca; Loh, Ling S; Arias, Carlos F; Gilbert, Lawrence E; Wray, Gregory A; Martin, Arnaud; McMillan, W Owen
abstract: The ivory:mir-193 locus is a genetic hotspot underlying melanic wing pattern variation across Lepidoptera, acting as a master regulator of melanic scale fate. This includes the genus Heliconius, where aposematic mimicry is driven by three scale cell types: light Type I, dark-melanic Type II, and red Type III scales. We test functions of ivory:mir-193 in Heliconius using CRISPR-induced somatic mosaic knockouts of ivory and mir-193 across multiple pattern morphs. Knockouts convert Type II scales to Type I scales. Effects on Type III scales vary among and within individuals, indicating that ivory:mir-193 is permissive for Type III development. Using single-nucleus RNA-seq, we profile the transcriptional landscape of H. melpomene Delta78k mutants lacking mir-193. Loss of mir-193 produces readthrough transcription, consistent with a model where mir-193 acts as a co-transcriptional terminator. These data show that miR-193, a miRNA under the transcriptional control of the ivory host gene, mediate the diversification of wing patterns across Lepidoptera by modulating scale cell identity during pupal wing development.

title: ATRX deficiency drives aberrant type I interferon signalling through cGAS-dependent transcriptional dysregulation.
authors: El-Daher, Marie-Therese A; White, Eve L; Fellas, Andreas; Grimes, Graeme; Pelliciari, Simone; Zhu, Gaofeng; Tait, Tom A; Uggenti, Carolina; Blair, Natalie; Nita, Erisa; Gautier, Philippe; Dunn-Davies, Hywel; Glen, Sophie; Dhir, Somdutta; Rodero, Mathieu P; Rice, Gillian I; Seabra, Luis; Clark, Richard; Fawkes, Angie; Marsh, Joseph A; Huibers, Minke Hw; Koedijk, Joost B; Van Nieuwenhove, Erika; Livingston, John H; Wassmer, Evangeline; Naik, Swati; Vogt, Julie; Isidor, Bertrand; Deegan, Tom D; Lepelley, Alice; Tillotson, Rebekah; Revy, Patrick; Gibbons, Richard J; Crow, Yanick J
abstract: The X-linked alpha-thalassaemia intellectual disability syndrome (ATRX) protein is a chromatin remodeller involved in transcriptional regulation and genome stability. While the importance of ATRX in development and malignancy is well recognised, its role in innate immunity is less well defined. Here we describe three unrelated patients with ATR-X syndrome carrying missense mutations in the ATPase domain of ATRX, each manifesting features of severe inflammation accompanied by persistent upregulation of interferon-stimulated gene expression in whole blood. Studies in patient-derived cells, CRISPR-engineered fibroblasts and neuronal models demonstrate that ATRX loss-of-function mutations drive enhanced type I interferon signalling through a cGAS-dependent mechanism uncoupled from the DNA sensing activity of cGAS. Mechanistically, ATRX deficiency disrupts the chromatin distribution of DAXX and H3.3, with cGAS essential for the changes in nucleosome composition and gene expression mediated by loss of ATRX. Thus, our study highlights a link between ATRX dysfunction and inflammation involving a non-canonical role of cGAS.

title: RPA-assisted three-channel Cas13a-Cas13b-Cas12a fluorescence architecture for three-channel viral nucleic acid detection.
authors: Chen, Keyu; Gao, Tiantian; Yu, Lei; Zhang, Qiang; Lin, Yingzheng; Wang, Yiting; Xiong, Wei; Wang, Yan; Li, Jian; Sun, Xiaodong; Xue, Junxin; Chen, Qin; Niu, Bing
abstract: Multiplex nucleic-acid analysis requires orthogonal signal channels capable of resolving multiple targets without substantial cross-interference. Here, an RPA-assisted three-channel CRISPR fluorescence readout was developed by coupling the distinct collateral-cleavage activities of LwaCas13a, PsmCas13b, and LbaCas12a to FAM-, ROX-, and HEX-based reporters, respectively, for detection of Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV), tick-borne encephalitis virus (TBEV), and an eastern/western equine encephalitis virus (EEEV/WEEV) group target. The corresponding singleplex assays showed no detectable cross-reactivity with the tested non-target viral templates and achieved operational analytical detection limits of 10 copies/muL for VEEV and TBEV and 100 copies/muL for the EEEV/WEEV group assay. Integration of the three Cas-crRNA-reporter modules into one downstream reaction enabled discrimination of single-, dual-, and three-target combinations, with an analytical detection limit of 100 copies/muL for each target in the equal-concentration three-target mixture. Reporter optimization provided balanced channel responses, while inter-day repeatability and interlaboratory reproducibility yielded coefficients of variation below 10%. In a preliminary matrix evaluation using contrived equine nasal-swab samples, plasmid-spiked samples and unspiked negative controls showed concordant classification between the CRISPR readout and RT-qPCR, indicating compatibility of the assay workflow with the tested sample matrix. The method provides a three-channel analytical architecture that consolidates three downstream CRISPR readouts into one reaction while retaining target-assigned fluorescence interpretation.

title: Engineered CRISPR for nucleic acid imaging at the single-molecule level.
authors: Xu, Jiaying; Yang, Hao; Ma, Yuxi; Xiang, Zhenting; Shi, Bingying; Wang, Siyuan; Liang, Kunneng; Deng, Yi
abstract: Accurate and dynamic visualization of nucleic acids at the single-molecule level is essential for elucidating cellular processes, defining disease-associated molecular mechanisms, and advancing molecular diagnostics. Conventional imaging methods often lack the sensitivity, specificity, or spatiotemporal resolution required in complex biological systems. Engineered clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) technologies, leveraging the high programmability of Cas proteins and guide RNAs, have expanded nucleic acid imaging from repetitive and non-repetitive genomic loci to sequence-variant discrimination and individual RNA imaging. This review summarizes major engineering strategies, including Cas protein labeling, guide RNA scaffold modification, and nanomaterial- or protein-assisted signal amplification platforms. We further discuss biomedical applications in live-cell tracking, spatial nucleic acid analysis, and real-time monitoring of cellular dynamics. By examining the biochemical and engineering principles underlying these platforms, we provide a framework for the rational design of CRISPR-based nucleic acid imaging strategies and identify key considerations for overcoming persistent limitations in complex biological environments. Collectively, these advances position engineered CRISPR imaging as a programmable platform for spatially resolved nucleic acid analysis; however, broader application to clinically relevant specimens will require rigorous validation of quantitative robustness and specimen compatibility, together with standardized imaging workflows.

title: Title: Topoisomerase I Inhibition Serves as a Tumor Vaccine by Inducing the ERVs-dsRNA-Interferon Pathway.
authors: Lin, Yanting; Ren, Yiming; Jing, Dongquan; Gao, Rui; Tian, Siyu; Liu, Yingming; Jiang, Xingyu; Zhao, Qixiang; Gao, Zhenhua; Zhu, Yu; Cai, Jian; Xiao, Pingting; Yang, Yong; Cao, Qiuhua; Gao, Xinghua
abstract: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) can activate potent anti-tumor immunity, but its clinical translation remains challenging. We sought to identify clinically applicable strategies to induce endogenous dsRNA and enhance anti-tumor immune responses. Here, we integrated genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screening data with the Therapeutic Target Database (TTD) and identified Topoisomerase I (TOP1) as a potential inducer of dsRNA. Mechanistically, we found that TOP1 was associated with suppression of endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) in an enzyme activity-dependent manner, and this was accompanied by "viral mimicry" through the induction of dsRNA. Pharmacological inhibition of TOP1 using Irinotecan (CPT-11) triggered dsRNA accumulation across cancer models, including patient-derived organoids (PDOs), activating the RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS pathway and antiviral interferon responses (Type I/III IFNs, ISGs). scRNA-seq revealed that CPT-11 remodeled the tumor microenvironment, promoting infiltration of dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and T cells. Combining CPT-11 with PD-1 blockade in "cold" tumors dramatically improved survival. CPT-11 also generated a potent in situ vaccine effect, establishing immunological memory that prevented tumor rechallenge. Moreover, tumor cells pretreated with CPT-11 in vitro were also able to exert a vaccine-like effect, inhibiting the growth of subsequently inoculated tumors. Collectively, our findings support the repurposing of TOP1 inhibitors such as CPT-11 to harness dsRNA-mediated immune activation for more effective cancer therapy.

title: CRISPR-enabled ultrasensitive surface-enhanced Raman scattering sensing platform for background-free detection of phosphorylated tau in Alzheimer's disease.
authors: Chen, Xiaoyi; Yang, Yuanyuan; Liao, Yimin; Chen, Lu; Cheng, Lingjun; Su, Canping; Shi, Xuan; Chen, Jiaming; Lin, Zhenyu; Hong, Guolin
abstract: Accurate and ultrasensitive detection of phosphorylated tau at threonine 231 (P-tau231), a pathologically validated early biomarker of Alzheimer's disease (AD), is essential for preclinical diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring. However, blood-based detection remains challenging because of the femtomolar physiological abundance, substantial interference from the serum matrix, and the reliance of conventional clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) assays on nucleic acid amplification. Herein, we present an amplification-free CRISPR/Cas12a-assisted surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) aptasensor for the background-free quantification of P-tau231. This platform integrates aptamer-mediated target recognition, programmable Cas12a trans-cleavage-based signal transduction, and hierarchical plasmonic enhancement. Au-4-Mercaptobenzonitrile@Au (Au-4-MBN@Au) core-shell nanoprobes coupled with Ag nanocube arrays provide uniform plasmonic enhancement, while the characteristic C  identical with N peak of the 4-MBN reporter at 2230 cm(-1) lies within the biological Raman-silent window (1800-2800 cm(-1)), thereby minimizing inference from endogenous scattering. This biosensor exhibits a linear detection range of 50 fg/mL to 5 ng/mL and an ultralow limit of detection of 2.53 fg/mL. Overall, this work established an effective amplification-free CRISPR/Cas12a-SERS platform for the highly sensitive detection of serum P-tau231 and offers a promising analytical approach for the blood-based early diagnosis of AD.

title: Visual Detection of Foodborne Viruses in Leafy Greens Using an AsCas12f-Split-G-Quadruplex Sensor.
authors: Kasputis, Tom; Landivar, Mathew; Yuan, Lijuan; Wright, R Clay; Zhang, Chenming; Chen, Juhong
abstract: Foodborne viruses are responsible for a substantial burden of disease worldwide, with fresh produce serving as the most abundant vehicle for transmission. However, rapid detection in solid produce, such as leafy greens, remains underdeveloped, as conventional methods often require labor-intensive sample preparation and specialized instrumentation. Herein, we present a colorimetric CRISPR-split-G4 biosensor for rapid viral surveillance in leafy greens that combines reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA), AsCas12f-mediated trans-cleavage, and a modular split-G-quadruplex (split-G4) reporter system. In this system, target recognition activates the trans-cleavage activity of AsCas12f, resulting in degradation of a blocker strand and subsequent assembly of a catalytically active G4-hemin DNAzyme that generates a visible signal easily detectable by the naked eye. Using norovirus as a model pathogen, the platform exhibited high analytical sensitivity and specificity, enabling reliable detection of viral particles with minimal instrumentation. To evaluate practical applicability, the assay was coupled with a simplified leaf-disk extraction workflow and successfully applied to contaminated romaine lettuce and baby spinach samples without requiring viral nucleic acid purification. The platform achieved detection limits of 1000 and 5000 viral copies per 100 mg of romaine lettuce and spinach tissue, respectively. From sample processing to visual readout, the entire assay was completed in approximately 2 h. By integrating isothermal amplification, CRISPR-based target recognition, and instrument-free signal generation into a streamlined workflow, this strategy provides a promising platform for decentralized food safety monitoring and establishes a flexible framework for the on-site detection of viral pathogens in complex food matrices.

title: Plant molecular farming: from gene design to scalable expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins.
authors: Guan, Chunmei; Ravin, Nikolai V; Jiao, Yuling
abstract: Plant-based expression systems have emerged as low-cost, scalable, and safe alternatives for producing therapeutic recombinant proteins. Among them, Nicotiana benthamiana stands out as a versatile chassis due to its rapid growth, high biomass, efficient transient expression, and weak RNA silencing. In this review, we systematically summarize the key technical procedures and recent advances in the expression of therapeutic recombinant proteins in N. benthamiana, covering gene design and subcellular targeting, expression vector engineering and delivery, host engineering for enhanced yield, and cultivation optimization. We discuss strategies to address major bottlenecks, including codon optimization, endoplasmic reticulum retention, protease knockout, glycoengineering to eliminate immunogenic plant-specific glycans, and the use of viral-based transient expression systems such as magnICON, pEAQ-HT, and geminiviral replicons. Additionally, we highlight emerging approaches such as CRISPR-based multiplexed chassis engineering, artificial intelligence-assisted vector design, and hydroponic cultivation for scalable production. Despite significant progress, challenges remain in achieving coordinated high-level expression of multiple proteins and reducing downstream processing costs. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the current state and future directions of plant molecular farming in N. benthamiana, emphasizing its irreplaceable value for rapid emergency response, personalized vaccines, and safe biopharmaceutical manufacturing.

title: Mycoplasma pneumoniae CARDS toxin hijacks annexin A2 to enhance clathrin-mediated endocytosis and induce a cytopathic effect.
authors: Lin, Yang-Ding; Adel, Fadi; Kirkpatrick, Alejandra; Molotsky, Danielle; Thorndyke, Hannah; Pandranki, Lavanya; Kannan, T R
abstract: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a primary cause of bacterial community-acquired pneumonia. One of its key virulence factors, the community-acquired respiratory distress syndrome (CARDS) toxin, replicates most clinical symptoms of the infection. Although CARDS toxin exhibits multi-receptor binding affinity, the mechanisms governing its cellular entry remain poorly understood. In this study, we characterized the toxin entry pathway mediated by the host protein annexin A2 (AnxA2). Using flow cytometry and biotinylated membrane protein analysis, we demonstrate that CARDS toxin induces a rapid, transient translocation of AnxA2 to the plasma membrane, peaking at 15 min post-exposure. This recruitment occurs via a phosphorylation-independent mechanism, distinguishing it from the Src-dependent recruitment typically observed in other physiological contexts. Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) of the clathrin heavy chain revealed an enhanced AnxA2-clathrin association that accelerates clathrin-mediated endocytosis of toxin. Endosomal fractionation, immunofluorescence, and co-IP studies confirmed the time-dependent co-localization and physical interaction of CARDS toxin with AnxA2 within early endosomes. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of AnxA2 in A549 cells demonstrated that this protein is essential for the internalization of CARDS toxin; its absence not only reduces the toxin binding but also effectively impairs the rapid cellular uptake required to trigger the downstream cytopathic effects and vacuolation. These results establish that CARDS toxin modulates host surface remodeling through AnxA2 cell surface translocation to facilitate efficient cellular entry, identifying a rate-limiting step in M. pneumoniae pathogenesis.

title: Costunolide-Mediated Modulation of the P2X7-NLRP3 Complex Suppresses Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cell Pyroptosis and Rescues Perinatal White Matter Injury.
authors: Zhang, Feng; Wang, Qian; Li, Ting; Li, Xianghong; Sun, Mengya; Li, Liangliang; Qin, Miao; Ma, Shiyi; Sun, Junfang; Yu, Wenyu; Liu, Yan; Jiang, Hong
abstract: BACKGROUND: Perinatal white matter injury (WMI) causes neurodevelopmental disability, driven by oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) pyroptosis. We aimed to identify the molecular mechanism of NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in OPCs and evaluate Costunolide (Cos) as a targeted modulator of the P2X7-NLRP3 complex. METHODS: We integrated molecular dynamics simulations, surface plasmon resonance, primary OPC cultures, single-cell RNA sequencing, and a custom CRISPR/Cas9-generated P2rx7 knockout rat model to assess Cos efficacy. RESULTS: Cos associated with the extracellular domain of P2X7 (K(D) = 3.08 muM, Homo sapiens P2X7), modulating the P2X7-NLRP3 complex, thereby restricting calcium influx and preventing Caspase-1 activation and GSDMD-mediated membrane pore formation in vitro. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis identified an injury-induced P2rx7(+)/Nlrp3(+) OPC subpopulation, revealing a previously unrecognized cell-intrinsic susceptibility to neuroinflammatory injury. Both genetic deletion of P2rx7 and pharmacological treatment with Cos markedly suppressed pyroptotic signaling in vivo, resulting in sustained restoration of myelin integrity and enhanced oligodendrocyte maturation from the acute (P7) to the developmental recovery (P14) stage. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that P2X7 may facilitate NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in developing OPCs. Consequently, modulation of this complex by Cos highlights a potential neurotherapeutic strategy for perinatal WMI.

title: CASM regulates lysosomal expansion and cell fate during senescence.
authors: Cheng, Yu-Wei; Gao, Michael Z; Tan, Jay Xiaojun; Liu, Jie; Finkel, Toren
abstract: Cellular senescence, a hallmark of aging, is accompanied by a striking expansion of the cell's lysosomal compartment, yet the pathway leading to increased lysosomal content remains unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that the master lysosomal transcriptional regulator TFEB is activated during senescence through a pathway that involves conjugation of ATG8 onto single membranes (CASM). Using various senescence inducers, we show that senescence induction triggers robust TFEB nuclear translocation and upregulation of TFEB target genes. In contrast, inhibition of the core CASM machinery by CRISPR-mediated deletion of either ATG16L1, ATG12, or ATG5 markedly reduced senescence-induced TFEB nuclear translocation. In ATG16L1-KO cells, reconstitution with WT ATG16L1 but not the CASM-defective ATG16L1F467A mutant restored both ATG8 lipidation on the lysosomal surface and TFEB activation. Moreover, expression of the Salmonella effector protein SopF, a previously described specific CASM inhibitor, similarly blocked senescence-induced TFEB translocation. Functionally, upon stress, CASM-deficient cells exhibited a pronounced shift away from senescence and toward a cell death fate, a phenotype reversed by expressing a constitutively active form of TFEB. Together, these findings identify CASM-dependent TFEB activation as an essential mechanism enabling senescence-associated lysosomal expansion and suggest that lysosomal capacity modulates cell fate decisions in the aftermath of acute stress.

title: Genomic, single-cell, and functional profiling of the CD48-CD244 axis and NK cell dysfunction in multiple myeloma.
authors: Patino-Escobar, Bonell; Steinbrunn, Torsten; Perez-Lugo, Lucy; Rampersaud, Sham; Waller, Daniel D; Ordonez, Daniela; Geng, Huimin; Salangsang, Fernando; Phojanakong, Paul; Camara Serrano, Juan Antonio; Zeng, Yan; Steri, Veronica; Aguilar, Oscar A; Mitsiades, Constantine S; Wiita, Arun P
abstract: Multiple myeloma (MM) orchestrates immune evasion by subverting natural killer (NK) cell function. CD48, one of the most abundant NK ligands on MM cells, paradoxically enhances NK cell activation yet is associated with high-risk cytogenetics and poor patient survival. We integrated multiomics (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing [ATAC-seq], chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing [ChIP-seq]), genome-wide CRISPR knockout/activation screens, and machine learning to dissect CD48 regulation and function. In human MM and Vkappa*MYC mouse scRNA-seq datasets, NK cells exhibit stepwise increases in inflammatory and exhaustion signatures and loss of cytotoxic potential as disease progresses. In vitro coculture assays show that CD48 overexpression on MM enhances NK cell cytokine secretion, whereas chronic exposure leads to ex vivo NK dysfunction. In vivo, CD48-overexpressing Vkappa*MYC tumors progress more slowly and extend host survival, while NK cell depletion accelerates disease. These findings support a context-dependent role for CD48, potentiating acute NK responses while coexisting with chronic NK exhaustion, and suggest strategies to modulate CD48 for therapeutic benefit.

title: The potential for large-scale genome editing in finfish aquaculture via germline stem cell culture and transplantation.
authors: Raudstein, Mari; Datsomor, Alex Kojo; Stewart, Robert; McGrew, Mike; Fraslin, Clemence; Crespo, Diego; Kleppe, Lene
abstract: Genome editing has emerged as a promising tool to complement selective breeding programmes and accelerate genetic gain in aquaculture. Although CRISPR-based genome editing has been successfully applied in several economically important fish species, its application at an industry-relevant scale remains challenging due to limitations of current delivery methods, which primarily rely on manual embryo microinjection. This approach is labour-intensive, technically demanding, and frequently results in high levels of mosaicism in founder individuals, necessitating additional generations of breeding to establish stable genotypes. In this mini review, we discuss the potential of combining germline stem cell (GSC) culture and transplantation approaches as an alternative platform for further improved genome editing in fish. By enabling genetic changes to be introduced, validated, and expanded in vitro prior to germline transmission, this approach has the potential to improve scalability, reduce mosaicism, and shorten breeding timelines. Although several technical challenges remain, continued progress in GSC culture and transplantation methodologies could facilitate the practical implementation of tailored genome editing for improved genetic gain, fish health, and welfare in aquaculture.

title: Progress and applications of microneedle-based gene therapy.
authors: Shen, Yuyao; Ye, Xiuzhi; Chen, Qi; Yu, Di; He, Li; Lei, Lanjie; Zhang, Qingfei; Zeng, Dashun
abstract: Gene therapy holds considerable promise for treating a wide range of intractable diseases through the modification of specific genes. However, gene therapeutics such as plasmid DNA, messenger RNA, and CRISPR-based systems are susceptible to degradation, face challenges in crossing cellular barriers, and may induce immune-related adverse effects, thereby limiting their clinical translation. Microneedles create microchannels that penetrate tissue barriers and, when combined with various carrier materials, enhance nucleic acid stability and intracellular delivery efficiency. This review summarizes the compatibility of different microneedle configurations with gene-delivery vectors, compares the effects of various fabrication processes on the activity of therapeutic agents, and elucidates the mechanisms underlying barrier penetration and delivery by microneedles. Recent advances in the application of microneedle-based gene therapy in dermatology, oncology, and nucleic acid vaccination are also discussed. Finally, current challenges, including drug loading, mass production, and safety evaluation, are analyzed, and the prospects for smart, responsive, and integrated diagnostic and therapeutic microneedles are highlighted.

title: The Rice CBP60 Protein OsCBP609 Interacts With Pik1-H4 and Supports Salicylic Acid-Responsive Immunity Against Magnaporthe oryzae.
authors: Xie, Huabin; Wei, Danhong; Li, Jiayang; Lin, Chunzi; Zou, Xiaodi; Li, Renhui; Hou, Yan; Jiang, Xianya; Chen, Chun; Guo, Tao; Wang, Jiafeng
abstract: Plant immunity depends on coordination between immune receptors and hormone-responsive transcriptional networks, yet how CBP60 proteins contribute to disease resistance in monocots remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized OsCBP609, a rice CBP60 family protein involved in resistance to Magnaporthe oryzae. Expression of OsCBP609 was responsive to M. oryzae infection and defence-related signals, and the encoded protein localized to the nucleus and exhibited transcriptional activation. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of OsCBP609 increased lesion development and fungal biomass following infection with multiple M. oryzae isolates. Transcriptome profiling showed that loss of OsCBP609 was associated with altered expression of genes involved in plant-pathogen interactions and hormone-related signalling pathways during infection. Although basal salicylic acid (SA) levels were elevated in the oscbp609 mutant, SA-responsive defence transcription was attenuated, and exogenous SA failed to restore resistance to the wild-type level, supporting a role for OsCBP609 in the transcriptional response to SA. OsCBP609 physically interacted with the NLR protein Pik1-H4 in the nucleus, and co-expression of the two proteins produced significantly higher reporter activity than expression of either protein alone. Disruption of OsCBP609 in a Pik-H4 near-isogenic line also reduced blast resistance, supporting a functional contribution of OsCBP609 to Pik-H4-associated immunity. Together, these results identify OsCBP609 as a CBP60 transcriptional regulator that supports SA-responsive defence and Pik-H4-associated resistance to rice blast.

title: CROSS: A cross-species chromosome substitution platform for dissecting chromosome architecture and activity.
authors: Mao, Yihuan; Yang, Ning; Zhao, Yulong; Wang, Libin; Xu, Kai; Chen, Yangcan; Ding, Yali; Zhong, Bei; Ma, Sinan; Liu, Jing; Zhang, Yu; Ni, Qingyang; Feng, Guihai; Zhou, Qi; Zhou, Qi; Li, Wei
abstract: The functional integrity of a mammalian chromosome depends on its long-term co-evolution with species-specific nuclear environment. How chromosomes co-adapt with their native environment to define 3D architecture and transcription remains unclear, largely due to a lack of experimental models that dissect this co-evolution. Here, we report cross-species chromosome substitution (CROSS), a method enabling stable, scarless replacement of host chromosomes with divergent orthologs. We integrate microcell-mediated chromosome transfer with CRISPR/Cas9 to import the intact 152-Mb rat X chromosome into male mouse embryonic stem cells, and subsequently replace the mouse X chromosome, maintaining its stability and integrity. Rat-specific LINE1 and RatSatRep2 repeats recruit mouse SETDB1 inefficiently, causing local H3K9me3 loss. This triggers 3D remodeling, characterized by de novo topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries that aberrantly activate adjacent genes, including Rhox5, impairing differentiation. We provide a platform for dissecting sequence and epigenome cooperation in chromosome regulation, and evaluating fidelity of large-scale heterologous DNA.

title: Reconstruction of PAM-interacting domains to broad PAM compatibility.
authors: Niu, Wenchao; Qian, Yuqiang; Wang, Di; Hao, Yang; Yu, Hongliang; Gao, Xun; Zheng, Wei; He, Guobin; Lai, Liangxue; Li, Zhanjun
abstract: The protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) requirement limits CRISPR-Cas9 targetability. Here, we develop REPAM, an ancestral sequence reconstruction-based strategy that re-engineers PAM-interacting domains to expand PAM recognition. REPAM broadens the PAM specificities of Nme1Cas9 and Nme2Cas9 from N4GATT/N4CC to N4CNH, while additional mutations further extend Nme2Cas9 recognition to N4VHH. Applied to SpaCas9, REPAM expands PAM compatibility from NNGYRA to NNHH, increasing theoretical target coverage by approximately 36-fold. The engineered SpaCas9 achieves up to 76.6% editing efficiency in HEK293T cells, outperforming SpRY. Corresponding base editors efficiently generate protective variants and precise splice-site mutations, highlighting REPAM as a versatile platform for CRISPR engineering.
